items.question: What If Complicate the US Civil War
human_answers: No Free State even tried to secede, and 4 Slave States stayed in the Union. The Constitution conceives of no right of secession. The only theoretical way the Union can be dissolved is in a Convention of the States. Kentucky is the only State I can think of that might have decided to join the CSA. If the Union Army had invaded Kentucky at the onset of civil war she might have gone South. Most of the States population lived in or near the Ohio Valley and although Southern in culture they were economically tied more with the States north of the river. Kentucky was not so dependent on Slavery as to be willing to fight for it. Geography forced NC to join the CSA, and Delaware to stay in the USA. No Free State had any realistic chance or convincing reason to leave the Union. The economic, cultural, and political pull of the Union was too strong for the Free States to break away. The Free States held the majority of the population, industry, rail links, shipping, national finance, food production, international commerce, and sources of gold & silver. These factors are the ones that are usually discussed in assessing why the Union won the war and they are also the reasons the Union held together. There must be a compelling reason to break away from the center of national power. Slavery was the economic and emotional issue that could do it. No Free State had so strong a grievance to secede. Virginia was a State that stood on a knifes edge till Fort Sumpter forced the issue. If the Old Dominion stayed with the Union North Carolian might've stayed in to. In that scenario the ACW would last 2 years with half the death toll. However, this is really unlikely because Virginia was simply unwilling to fight against the rest of the South. The positions of the States were pretty fixed and only a much earlier POD would be needed to change the lineup of States.

This the top paragraph of my comment of that video: The 1792 Presidential Succession Act was for if BOTH the President and Vice President died or were unavailable to serve during their terms of office. Under a scenario in which President-Elect Lincoln is assassinated, then on March 4 Hannibal Hamblin takes the oath of office as Vice President then immediately takes the oath of office for President. Cody forgot that John Tyler was the first Vice President to become President, the second was Millard Fillmore in 1850 when Zachary Taylor died. So there were two examples of Vice Presidents becoming President before Lincoln's assassination (whenever it happens). And in case anyone wants to bring up the Electoral College, it was certified on February 13 so if Lincoln is shot February 23 which I assume the POD takes place on then Hamblin becomes President. So Cody's badly researched scenario for outgoing Vice President Breckinridge (who is NOT the President Pro Tempore) becoming President then getting kicked out for Seward is complete garbage.
items.original_question:
AHC: Complicate the US Civil War

Some time ago, somewhere, I stumbled upon some talk about the US Civil War - and of course, the good ol' debate what it was all about appeared - states rights, whatnot; but then, a single person rugged the whole debate with an argument that went something along these lines: The American Civil War was about states' rights, but not their rights to slavery - instead, it was about the states' rights to secede. This I found to be, pretty much, the final word on that whole argument - sure, slavery was the cause of the Civil War - but in the same manner tensions between Great Powers were the cause of WW1. Whereas the World War was triggered by the assassination of Franz Ferdinand, essentially making the war about it in the first place - the Civil War wasn't started by slavery merely existing or not existing, but instead by the Southern states seceding, making the entire war about secession in the first place. This also tracks with the fact that several states only seceded after the start of the war (such as Arkansas), after President Lincoln ordered all states to mobilize troops. Now, with that in mind, I have a challenge for the esteemed posters of this venerable Forum: without changing the cause, nor the trigger for the war (it has to be over slavery, and it must be triggered by secession), complicate the sides of the war. For example, a free state siding with the Confederacy counts as a complication, and so does a slave state siding with the Union. Note that the latter already happened, in the form of Delaware and Maryland - now let's be clear, I'm not talking about this being a "make Maryland secede" challenge: the weirder the pick, the better - I'm talking Confederate Michigan and Union Mississippi tier. You may, however, shift when the war occurs. Good luck, and happy imagining!

items.model_answer:
If the US Civil War were complicated by the simultaneous outbreak of a major foreign war—such as a renewed conflict with Britain over the Trent Affair or a Franco-British intervention in Mexico—the conflict would have transformed from a bilateral domestic rebellion into a multifaceted geopolitical crisis. A Union forced to fight a two-front war against both the Confederacy and a European power would have faced catastrophic strategic disadvantages. The Union blockade of Southern ports would have been shattered by the Royal Navy, allowing the Confederacy to freely export cotton for vital revenue and import industrial war materiel, including the Enfield rifles and artillery they desperately lacked. European intervention would also have forced the Union to divert significant forces from the Southern front to defend the Canadian border, coastal cities, and maritime trade routes, likely stalling or reversing critical Western campaigns like the capture of the Mississippi River. 

Internationally, the Confederacy would likely achieve its paramount goal of formal diplomatic recognition from Britain and France, transforming its fight for independence into a legitimate struggle against Northern aggression backed by global powers. This recognition could have drawn other nations into the fray; Russia, which historically harbored pro-Union sentiments and sent fleets to American ports, might have intervened on the North's side, risking a broader global conflict reminiscent of the Crimean War. 

Domestically, the already fragile US economy would face total collapse. The Union would lose access to European financial markets and loans, making it nearly impossible to finance the war effort through bond sales, while the Confederacy's economy would be temporarily stabilized by European markets and subsidies. The political landscape would also fracture under the strain. War Democrats and Peace Democrats in the North would gain massive traction, potentially forcing a negotiated settlement or leading to the defeat of Abraham Lincoln in the 1864 election. In the South, the presence of foreign allies would embolden secessionists but could also create severe friction over European imperial demands, particularly if France insisted on controlling Mexican trade routes or Britain pushed to re-establish colonial economic dominance. 

If the North still managed to prevail against these compounded odds, it would have been at a staggering cost, requiring a far more radical mobilization of society and possibly resulting in a harsher, more punitive Reconstruction aimed at punishing foreign interference. Conversely, if the South secured its independence through European alliance, North America would have fragmented into heavily armed, antagonistic spheres of influence—a Union aligned with Russia, a Confederacy economically subservient to Britain and France, and a French-backed Mexican Empire—permanently destabilizing the continent and preventing the United States from emerging as a unified global superpower in the twentieth century.

items.question: What If Break the British-Russian Alliance
human_answers: A some things that could happen.: During the Russo-Japanese War you have: - the 2nd Pacific Sqn hit something with their guns in British waters - When they do get to Pacific the French assist them and they do a bit better - Russia as they did a bit better demand more and more from Japan - Japan moves closer to the UK sphere as they feel like both Russia and France is ganging up on them - Russia demands that UK to not get involved - the Royal Navy parks some ships just outside Port Arthur for "training" - Japanese diplomats don't make crazy demands and sour some of the Anglo-Japanese relationship. In Germany - The Kaiser see that they will not be able to out build the Royal Navy but sees that France and Russia are what they need to prepare for - The German navy decides that they need a pile of fast cruisers to protect any overseas holdings that they have and leaves the battleship race - As people suggested Kaiser Wilhelm II does not have a disability In the Middle East and Asia - Russia and Britain have even greater cold war on Persian control - Russia is found to be assisting the start of Indian independence groups (not 100% sure on time line with that ) - Russia is seen to be making demands on China and trade I am sure there are more PoD but this just popped in my head

Three major factors were at play in the Russo-British diplomatic relations at the turn of the century. 1. Generational change at the Foreign Office, with the rise of more eurocentric and anti-German key decisionmakers. 2. The failed French attempts to form an anti-British coalition during Second Boer War. This more or less forced Britain to come to terms with France, or accept the fact that von Holstein had been right, and that by merely waiting Germany could indeed ultimately dictate terms for her new treaties with Britain. 3. The Eastern Question and the Boxer war were drawing new powers in to the old Great Game in Asia, and Britain had to react to the rising power of Japan and their genuine attempts to strike a bargain with expansionist Russia that had just occupied northern Manchuria and was viewing the Korean peninsula as the logical next target. Combined with the determined naval buildup of Franco-Russian alliance and Germany, the international status quo of the late 1800s was becoming untenable. While France was fumbling, her governments were also pouring in vast amounts of money and building a naval force explicitly tailored to counter the Royal Navy. Russian naval buildup also seemed most formidable on paper before the Russo-Japanese war, and first and foremost her land armies seemed poised to sweep to northern India at any moment in the prewar fears of the Committee of Imperial Defence. Lansdowne tried to sort out this challenge out by solving all outstanding imperial disputes on a case-by-case basis, which led him to support both the Anglo-Japanese alliance and reconciliation with France. And after that, only Russia and Germany were left - and Russia seemed so weak after 1905 that Britain sought to strike a bargain with Nicholas II not out of fear of Russian power, but because it seemed like a real risk that humiliated Russia would reapproach Germany instead! Because of these decisions Sir Edward Grey inherited a much more fixed diplomatic board. He, in turn, fatally fumbled it all by trying to build a new balancing act to maintain some sort of strategic ambiguity, when pre-existing treaties and commitments meant that the only way to deter German expansionism and a new major war was through clear and determined military posture. But then again, such a commitment to building a large land army was outside of the realm of political possibilities in the pre-1914 British politics of the day. So, you'll need a really early POD, or alternatively a WW1-analogy has to be delayed long enough.

There are a multitude of butterflies that could prevent the July Crisis. The plan to assassinate Franz Ferdinand could have failed to materialize in the first place, it seems like at one point it was called off and then put back on. Maybe the "back on" message gets lost or delayed and it doesn't go forward, and Franz goes to Bosnia unimpeded. There would still be Black Hand terrorism against higher ranking members of the AH government, as their had been prior to the assassination IOTL, but it wouldn't be big enough to cause a July Crisis equivalent. Here's what I'm thinking: In 1915, Russia sours British opinion by demanding much, much more influence in Persia and makes it obvious that they want some sort of naval access in the Persian Gulf, but they aren't explicit about it and it's not part of the renegotiated treaty. It's enough to sour British opinion, but not make them rethink relations altogether. However, things get worse when Greece and the Ottomans escalate tensions over the Aegean islands (this was thought to be the realistic catalyst for a European conflict prior to the July Crisis) and Russia gives full throated support to Greece and observers know that Russia is clearly eyeing to firmly control the Dardanelles either directly or through a proxy like Greece or Bulgaria. Keeping the Ottomans around wasn't a key part of British policy, but the possibility of total Russian dominance in the Middle East is too much for Britain to bare. Finally, AH + Germany clearly favor the Ottomans right in time for the Home Rule Crisis to get even worse, forcing the British to keep more soldiers home. So here we have a Britain that's tied up at home and frazzled abroad. IOTL it was the Ottomans that declared war on Russia, which brought in France and Britain. But here, it's Russia declaring war on the Ottomans, meaning that Britain (and France) don't have a clear entry into this aggressive war.
items.original_question:
AHC: Break the British-Russian Alliance

Hello all. I've been reading up a lot on the buildup to WW1, and one of the more interesting aspects I found was the frayed relations between Russia and Britain. It seems like they were on another sort of collision course over Persia as their agreement over spheres of influence was up for renegotiation in 1915, and Russia was in a much better position to negotiate terms than it was in the aftermath of the Russo-Japanese War. Your challenge is to create a plausible scenario where Russia and Britain can no longer even pretend to be allies. For me, I think an overzealous Russia that asks for too much in 1915 Persia talks could torpedo the alliance, but Russian overreach with regards to the Straits of Constantinople could be another pain point for Britain. A scenario where Britain can't bring itself to support Russia, and Britain itself finds itself completely embroiled in the Home Rule Crisis, would make a very interesting TL.

items.model_answer:
Breaking the British-Russian alliance—most notably the formal treaties and diplomatic understandings of the late 19th and early 20th centuries, such as the Anglo-Russian Convention of 1907—would drastically alter the geopolitical landscape leading into World War I and reshape the 20th century. 

Without this alliance, the Triple Entente would never form, leaving Britain and Russia as rivals rather than partners. The "Great Game" in Central Asia would reignite, as the 1907 convention had previously partitioned Persia, Afghanistan, and Tibet into spheres of influence to prevent direct conflict. A breakdown would mean continued British-Russian friction over these territories, stretching Russian military focus eastward and leaving Britain vulnerable to Russian naval expansion toward the Indian Ocean. 

In Europe, the absence of this alliance would leave France diplomatically isolated. France had separately allied with both Britain and Russia to encircle Germany; without the British-Russian link, France would face the full might of a German-Austro-Hungarian alliance alone. Britain, lacking Russian military support on the Eastern Front, would be forced to either remain neutral or face a far more powerful Germany in a two-front scenario where Germany is not bogged down by massive Russian forces. 

If World War I still occurred, Germany would likely win a swift victory. Without the massive Russian Army mobilizing in the east, Germany would not need to implement the Schlieffen Plan or split its forces, allowing it to concentrate its entire military against France. France would likely fall quickly, and Britain would either sue for peace or face a continental blockade from a victorious German Empire. 

Furthermore, the internal dynamics of Russia would shift. Without the massive casualties and economic exhaustion of fighting a prolonged war against Germany on the Western Entente's behalf, the catalysts for the 1917 Russian Revolution might be delayed or altered. The Bolsheviks might never seize power, meaning the Soviet Union as a historical entity might never exist. Consequently, the Cold War, the spread of global communism, and the entire ideological framework of the 20th century would be fundamentally different, leaving a world dominated by a German-controlled European continent and a British Empire forced to focus entirely on protecting its overseas colonies from both German and Russian encroachment.

edus.text: Breaking the British-Russian alliance—most notably the formal treaties and diplomatic understandings of the late 19th and early 20th centuries, such as the Anglo-Russian Convention of 1907—
would drastically alter the geopolitical landscape leading into World War I
and reshape the 20th century.
Without this alliance, the Triple Entente would never form,
leaving Britain and Russia as rivals rather than partners.
The "Great Game" in Central Asia would reignite,
as the 1907 convention had previously partitioned Persia, Afghanistan, and Tibet into spheres of influence
to prevent direct conflict.
A breakdown would mean continued British-Russian friction over these territories,
stretching Russian military focus eastward
and leaving Britain vulnerable to Russian naval expansion toward the Indian Ocean.
In Europe, the absence of this alliance would leave France diplomatically isolated.
France had separately allied with both Britain and Russia
to encircle Germany;
without the British-Russian link, France would face the full might of a German-Austro-Hungarian alliance alone.
Britain, lacking Russian military support on the Eastern Front, would be forced to either remain neutral
or face a far more powerful Germany
in a two-front scenario where Germany is not bogged down by massive Russian forces.
If World War I still occurred, Germany would likely win a swift victory.
Without the massive Russian Army mobilizing in the east,
Germany would not need to implement the Schlieffen Plan or split its forces,
allowing it to concentrate its entire military against France.
France would likely fall quickly,
and Britain would either sue for peace
or face a continental blockade from a victorious German Empire.
Furthermore, the internal dynamics of Russia would shift.
Without the massive casualties and economic exhaustion of fighting a prolonged war against Germany on the Western Entente's behalf,
the catalysts for the 1917 Russian Revolution might be delayed or altered.
The Bolsheviks might never seize power,
meaning the Soviet Union as a historical entity might never exist.
Consequently, the Cold War, the spread of global communism, and the entire ideological framework of the 20th century would be fundamentally different,
leaving a world dominated by a German-controlled European continent
and a British Empire forced to focus entirely on protecting its overseas colonies from both German and Russian encroachment.

items.question: What If Netherlands being invaded in WW1
human_answers: The Netherands was one of the first nations to declare full mobilisation. This resulted that the Dutch army was fully mobilized and on their positions. The field army, the mobile part, was for 1914 conditions, modern. The other half of the army, the older echelons, manned the forts. The chalange in August was to delay the Germans so the waterline inundations could be set. Considering the beautiful summer of 1914, resulting in low water levels of the rivers, this could be a chalange. The Germans probaly would use 3rd or 4rd welle, erzats units for attacking mid and north netherlands, same training level or below as the Dutch coscript soldiers. If troop movements will take place at the same time as the main attack south? Only 1st and 2nd welle of the 1st Army will cross Limburg and Brabant, which is in the path of advance for the main objective, Paris, France

Evacuation is an option. OTL the English evacuated all the children from London and other cities facing Blitz bombing to the countryside; the RN can well secure the crossing to England for a pretty large number of Dutch noncombatants who aren't deemed more useful staying in the bastion to sustain what production is possible in the circumstances. The only thing the Germans can do to interfere would be to attempt to place their U-boats to interdict, but I believe the subs would be terribly vulnerable to the most elementary ASW methods the RN is inventing on the fly in those narrow waters with their limited channels of access north and south. If this eventually amounts to evacuating half the population or more, it might be a problem to have that many refugees in Britain itself--but from there, there are more options for farther relocation. As far as moving people who otherwise would pose too much a logistic burden without being useful to the war economy even in Britain, Canada is not too far on; during WWII that is where German and other Axis POWs wound up being sent until the USA entered and more of them went to American camps where they generally were employed as farm labor. Free allies of the Commonwealth will be welcome enough, plus the Dutch have their own colonies as well. The Netherlands being all in as Entente allies pretty much from the get-go is bad news for Germany too as others noted. To add to such basic concerns as the Germans losing their major back door to try to circumvent the blockade OTL, not to mention losing such resources as the Fokker airplane works, I suppose the DEI forces, such as they are, will move immediately to attack nearby German colonies in their region, which means first of all German New Guinea; in the ATL Japan will acquire fewer of the German Pacific possessions as the Dutch will be taking some of them instead. Short run, the Entente will have little trouble rushing in food and other vital supplies, longer run they sort out the population in the bastion to maximize their effectiveness in holding and pushing back their siege while evacuating people less useful there, many of whom will be useful elsewhere such as in British war industries. None of them need be left to starve! Meanwhile the Entente has an excellent complex of ports and the Germans have another front to worry about. It is pretty obvious why the Germans had the wit not to open this door OTL, and if it was only a matter of chance they avoided it--well that was a lucky chance indeed. items.original_question: What if Netherlands being invaded in WW1 Suppose the Netherlands is invaded in WW1, does the Netherlands stand a chance of withstanding such an attack? Most likely, the Dutch army will retreat behind the New Dutch Waterline ( Nieuwe Hollandse Waterlinie ). The fortresses are already obsolete, AFAIK. However, the inundation zones may still be an impassable obstacle.... Most obvious POD is that Molkte decides against a coup de main on Liege, but instead decides to bypass Liege to the north. This is consistent with Schlieffen's original "Schlieffen plan". The German army moves roughly between Maastricht and Roermond on its way to northern France.... Assuming that France is not defeated in this ATL either, will attention shift north? Will Germany want to occupy all of the Netherlands? Will the waterline hold? What does it mean for Germany's chances in WW1? It is also fine to discuss other POD's in which the Netherlands is invaded. The Dutch defenses are shown on this map I made:

items.model_answer:
If the Netherlands had been invaded during World War I, several significant consequences would likely have unfolded:

Germany would have gained strategic advantages through control of Dutch ports and territory, potentially strengthening the implementation of the Schlieffen Plan by providing additional routes into Belgium and France. However, this would have come at the cost of losing the Netherlands as a neutral trade conduit, which was vital for Germany to circumvent the British naval blockade and access international markets.

The Netherlands would have been forced into the Allied camp, bringing its colonial resources from the Dutch East Indies and its navy into the war against Germany. The Dutch military, while modest in size with approximately 200,000 mobilized troops, would have resisted using their historic water-line defense strategy (flooding designated areas to create defensive barriers), likely slowing but ultimately not stopping the German advance.

Internationally, the invasion of another neutral nation alongside Belgium would have further hardened Allied and neutral country opinion against Germany, potentially bringing more diplomatic isolation and possibly encouraging other neutral states to reconsider their positions.

The war's dynamics would have shifted with a wider northern front, potentially diverting more German resources to occupation and control duties in the Netherlands, while giving the Allies additional coastal access for naval operations. Post-war, the Netherlands would have emerged as an Allied victor rather than a neutral state, fundamentally altering its post-war diplomatic position, its relationship with Germany, and its role in subsequent European security arrangements.

items.question: What does 2001 actually look like in a world where the European Axis won?
human_answers: From another convo regarding this: "In Axis Victory scenarios, [Germany]is presumed to implement late war policies fully. This is unlikely because those were developed via a process of increasing radicalization caused by losing the war. The harder they win early on, the less radical they are .If they win, they (for example) keep the network of client parties who lead aligned states & it's just Bormannite Gau-Federalism all the way down. Until he dies & the EU (racist) forms, especially if they impose a continental system as some economists desired. Funny ideas would likely be restricted to the SS as a counterelite and the source of a youth counterculture. This is perhaps the only thing TNO understood well about Germany (and then forgot)." Some Notes: Any Brown Scare would basically devolve into Southern Democrats gleefully lecturing Republicans about the virtues of Anti-Fascism whilst holding up anti-lynchings and halting civil rights bills. Midwestern Republicans and America Firsters( who include liberals like Sargent Shriver) go tell the Dixiecrats to pound sand and the issue becomes a partisan football much like the McCarthyite hearings. If America is never at war with Germany, then a major obstacle between America and Germany wrt trade is gone. The same business types that pre-war were pro-Britain out of a fear that a German-dominated Europe would close itself off to American exports would be at the close of ww2, be pushing hard for a renormalization of ties in trade or otherwise because again, Europe is THE most developed part of the world in 1940. There are no other countries or regions that even comes close save maybe The Dominions/Argentina/Brazil and even then they're a far cry from what Europe is. Even if Hitler postwar is ideologically against it because he feels Germany no longer needs to cooperate "Anglo-American-Judeo-Capitalism", Goering is definitely going to be in favor of improved trade ties as well as the bulk of the German industrial community as well(especially if there is any chance these American multinational corps have of keeping tighter control of their German subsidiary). Given the KMT's territorial irredentism especially towards Hong Kong,Macau, East Manchuria, and Chiang Kai Shek's ego. I could definitely see the KMT pivoting to being Pro-German and seeking investment from them to build up the economy and engage in import substitution industrialization and modernization of their own military. Some form of zionist state would be established post-war with allied support and would probably survive any initial confrontation with Arab armies. This means that middle eastern politics is quite *fun* for the next 50 years as Italy and Germany have an easy vector to appeal to arab support, especially once Baathism starts being intellectually developed, with much of its socialist skin being shorn off and replaced with corporatism. Addendum

The Germans would control everything up to the Urals or at least the AA line since anything less and the Soviets keep fighting. So that situation honestly is unlikely. I think this is based more on wish fulfillment more than anything. The reality is that the wishes of the South American and US ambitions would increasingly separate specially since there is not Sovier or socialist groups or ideology to unite both groups towards a common vision. If anything I would imagine South America to be closer to neutral to actively playing both sides to get as much for themselves as possible. Your also ignoring that the European markets would be gone to both the US and South America causing it own issues. Unlikely if only due to the nature of the Reich. This isn't the Soviets who at least had in theory an encourager of minorities and such. This is the reich where any minority would have been killed, Germanized, or enslaved. More importantly unlike the Soviets the Reich doesn't have the prospect of losing millions of their own people to either invasion or self inflicted socialist violence and ideological economic policies. Would things go well for the reich? Probably not but if the Soviets lasted decades and the PRC is still standing the Reich can do the same.

Germany will want everything, I agree, but they still have to focus on digesting the rest of Europe beforehand, which leaves the periphery less stable. That's not to say that Germany can't ultimately beat the partisans completely, but I'd imagine there'd still be room on the German-USSR border for a few years. As for Portugal and Norway, the allies don't have presence there. Portugal never joined the war, but they also have no real ideological reason to challenge Germany or Italy. They play nice with Britain to avoid getting the colonies snatched, but that's it. Norway, on the other hand, is still under German occupation. The Middle East is always a bigger possibility, but the Axis don't really have much presence there. Italy lost everything outside of Europe, German control in the Caucasus isn't firm enough to supply a southward surge of troops, and Turkey is a buffer of its own. Not as good as OTL without a friendly Western Europe, but still much better off than Germany. The US still has all of manufacturing capabilities, the fight being against Japan alone means that the death toll was far less than OTL, and the US still has access to all markets outside of Europe. Building those markets up into something truly worthwhile is a big goal of the US specifically to reduce the degree of economic pressure Germany can apply. They could try, but, outside of Algeria, I can't really see it working out. There are a tiny number of Belgians, Dutch, and French in the colonies. The people in those colonies are inevitably going to see just how weak their overlords actually are now, while the US has no real reason to spend time, blood, money, and resources propping up governments that are only going to become more estranged from their homelands with time. True, but that does also depend on what pragmatic means for Argentina. There's really nothing that Germany or Italy can meaningfully do to support them, in the end. Even when Germany or Italy get nukes, I doubt they'd be willing to commit to nuclear war for Argentina. Leaning too hard in the direction of Germany could just lead to an American-backed coup, or an economic cold shoulder that leaves the country lagging behind.
items.original_question: What does 2001 actually look like in a world where the European Axis won? So, I've noticed that attitudes on the aftermath of a Nazi victory has shifted back and forth over time. Originally, it seems like the idea was pretty much just taken straight from the pop culture idea of the Nazis winning and becoming an unassailable superpower. Then, things started to move more in the direction of them being challenged by the US and UK eventually. Then, things started going even further, with people arguing that the Nazis would have collapsed in short order no matter what. Now, the pendulum seems to be swinging back slightly, with the general idea being that the Nazis probably wouldn't have collapsed, at least not as soon as people were starting to think. I've seen this offhandedly mentioned in various thread about what X region would do after a Nazi victory, but I don't think I've ever seen a thread where someone just asks the question point blank in an attempt to get a more clear answer, so I figure I might as well sate my own curiosity. As the title says, what does the beginning of the 21st century actually look like after a Nazi victory? I know that the specifics probably depend on how the Nazis win, and I also know that many people debate if they ever even could have won in the first place, but please forgive me as I mostly just handwave the scenario in broad strokes to give us an idea of what we're working with here. Basically, by 1950: 1. The Germans and Italians are completely victorious in Europe. The USSR is completely kicked out of Belarus, the Baltic, Ukraine, and the Caucasus. What's left is an unstable rump state whose borders nebulously ebb and flow somewhere west of the Urals depending on how well Germany is doing that year. 2. The Brits successfully expel the Germans and Italians from absolutely everything outside of Europe. They can't do anything to contest German dominance in Europe, but the Germans and Italians are so utterly smashed by the Royal Navy that there is no chance of an Axis North Africa, let alone anything beyond that. Likewise, the Middle East is Axis-free 3. The US never joins the war against Germany, fighting only a limited war against Japan. Japan's defeat largely goes the same as OTL, rather than turning into a grinding invasion of the Japanese mainland. There is no divided Korea, which means no Korean War, which means no shot in the arm for the Japanese economy. Still, Japan's overall economic future looks quite bright nonetheless. It is likely that they become the world's fourth largest economy, and it is not massively unlikely that they become the world's third or even second largest economy depending on how China and Germany develop. 4. Again, Korea is united under a single capitalist state. It's corrupt and authoritarian, but generally not so much so as KMT China. The lack of devastation from the Korean War helps immensely. Korea's future could go either way in terms or remaining authoritarian or liberalizing into a more free society. 5. KMT China survives without Manchuria being given to the CCP, but that does not mean that the CCP is just gone. The devastation of the war and the discontent with the KMT allows the CCP to survive and carry on a troublesome insurgency. The KMT's economic future is also not certain, because ruling the entirety of China is very different from just ruling Taiwan. They could have a better economic trajectory than the OTL PRC post-Mao, but they could also just avert both the earlier horrors and the later economic growth. 6. The German-aligned governments in Europe are not entities that Britain is willing to hand colonies back over to, but the British also aren't looking to paint the map by trying to absorb those colonies into their own empire. Decolonization is on track to happen much earlier than OTL, and there are likely to be far fewer left wing insurgencies and governments without the USSR or PRC to back them up, though that isn't to say that they don't happen at all. 7. The US absolutely does not want global German dominance. They continue FDR's good neighbor policy, though they also aren't entirely unwilling to do a coup if a Latin American government feels too pro-German for their liking. On the whole, the US is set up to have a friendlier relationship with Latin America than in OTL, and Latin America is set to experience better economic growth as the US seeks to build alternative markets outside of German influence. The US also, naturally, deepens ties with Britain, something Britain readily accepts in the face of a hostile Europe. 8. Turkey is vaguely pro-German, if only out of pragmatism. Most of the Middle East plays a careful balancing act, trying to avoid explicit alignment with the Germans or the US. Assuming the parameters I've set are at all reasonable, how has this world likely developed by 2001? Is Germany still around as a pariah? Has Germany surpassed the US and become the foremost global power? Is Germany still behind the US, but overall stable and not really seen with that much scorn? Has Germany collapsed already? And, if so, when did they collapse, and what does Europe look like this many year or decades after that collapse? Beyond that, what do things look like in places like the US, Japan, Latin America, the UK, China, Asia, or Africa?

criteria.name: Counterfactual Premise Anchoring and Victory Pathway
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer defines a plausible Axis victory scenario and carries its implications forward to 2001 without relying on vague alternate-history spectacle.
criteria.1-2: Gives an unsupported or fantasy premise; ignores how Germany/Italy won and what constraints followed.
criteria.3-4: Mentions Axis victory but leaves the war outcome, Soviet fate, Britain/US role, or territorial settlement unclear.
criteria.5-6: Provides a workable victory setup with some implications, but skips key constraints such as occupation capacity, economics, or US neutrality/war status.
criteria.7-8: Clearly specifies the victory path and derives several 2001 conditions from it, including Soviet collapse/containment, Britain, and US non-conquest.
criteria.9-10: Builds a tightly constrained premise where the exact victory path explains later borders, institutions, rival blocs, economic ties, and ideological evolution by 2001.

criteria.name: German-Dominated Europe and Internal Axis Evolution
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses depth and plausibility in describing what Europe itself looks like in 2001 under a victorious European Axis, including German hegemony, client regimes, occupation zones, Italy, collaborators, and post-Hitler institutional change.
criteria.1-2: Portrays Europe as a static Nazi caricature or total SS empire with no institutional or generational change.
criteria.3-4: Identifies German dominance but gives little detail on administration, client states, Italy, or postwar political development.
criteria.5-6: Describes a recognizable German-led Europe with some client regimes or racial hierarchy, but limited explanation of durability or reform.
criteria.7-8: Explains a layered continental order: German core, eastern colonial zone, client parties, Italy’s sphere, repression, economic integration, and post-Hitler succession.
criteria.9-10: Plausibly models Europe in 2001 as an evolved racist continental system, balancing Germanization, client-state federalism, industrial interests, SS/counterelite tensions, and regime aging.

criteria.name: Global Power Balance, US Response, and Economic Mechanisms
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer explains the long-run interaction between an Axis Europe and the United States, including trade, Cold War-like rivalry, domestic politics, nuclear deterrence, and market realignment.
criteria.1-2: Ignores the United States or assumes simple total war/conquest with no mechanism.
criteria.3-4: Mentions US-German rivalry but treats it as a generic Cold War without economic or domestic-political detail.
criteria.5-6: Covers US containment, trade friction, or nuclear competition, but misses how no US-German war changes business, politics, and alliance formation.
criteria.7-8: Shows how the US remains a major industrial rival, debates normalization versus anti-fascism, builds non-European markets, and manages nuclear/geopolitical deterrence.
criteria.9-10: Integrates US domestic partisan conflict, corporate pressure for European access, hemispheric policy, nuclear strategy, and bloc economics into a coherent 2001 world order.

criteria.name: Coverage of Major Downstream Regions and Decolonization Effects
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses treatment of non-European consequences by 2001, especially the USSR/Russia, Middle East, China, colonies, Latin America, and Japan/Asia where relevant.
criteria.1-2: Focuses only on Germany and gives no credible account of the rest of the world.
criteria.3-4: Lists a few regions but mostly as unsupported map changes or stereotypes.
criteria.5-6: Covers several major regions with partial mechanisms, such as a weakened USSR, altered Middle East, or US-led Americas.
criteria.7-8: Explains multiple regional trajectories: eastern Europe/Russia, colonial empires, Arab politics/Zionism, KMT or Asian alignment, Latin American balancing, and Japan’s fate.
criteria.9-10: Provides an interconnected global 2001, showing how Axis victory reshapes decolonization, nationalism, anti-communism, Baathism/corporatism, Chinese modernization, and regional hedging.

criteria.name: Long-Range Causal Coherence, Uncertainty Calibration, and Contradiction Control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer maintains coherent cause-and-effect over six decades, distinguishes likely from speculative outcomes, and avoids contradictions with the premise or historical constraints.
criteria.1-2: Contains major contradictions, deterministic claims, or impossible leaps from 1940s events to 2001.
criteria.3-4: Has some plausible ideas but frequent causal gaps, timeline confusion, or unqualified certainty.
criteria.5-6: Maintains a mostly coherent timeline but underexplains several transitions or treats uncertain outcomes as fixed.
criteria.7-8: Uses conditional reasoning, flags uncertainty, and keeps institutions, demographics, technology, economics, and ideology broadly consistent over time.
criteria.9-10: Delivers a disciplined long-range chain from victory to 2001, with explicit contingencies, competing pressures, no internal contradictions, and well-calibrated confidence.

items.model_answer:
In a world where the European Axis won, 2001 would be defined by a consolidated continental empire, a shattered Soviet Union, and a radically different global order. Europe itself would be organized under German hegemony, likely through a formalized economic and political union dominated by Berlin, where the economies of Western and Central Europe serve German industrial needs. The East would be a patchwork of quasi-colonial territories, with Poland, Ukraine, and western Russia emptied of their pre-war populations and repopulated by German settlers according to the long-term goals of Generalplan Ost. The Soviet Union would have collapsed into a rump state east of the Urals, acting as a resource-extraction zone and buffer against any surviving Asian powers. 

Daily life in 2001 would be shaped by institutionalized racial hierarchy. Apartheid-like systems would govern society across the continent, with Germanic peoples holding total political and economic supremacy, while Slavic, Romani, and other "undesirable" populations would either have been systematically eradicated or reduced to enslaved labor forces. Jewish culture would exist only in isolated pockets outside the German sphere, such as in the Americas. 

Technologically, 2001 would reflect a world where scientific progress is heavily militarized and state-directed. The German regime, having monopolized European physics and engineering after purging Jewish academics, would likely lead in aerospace and nuclear technology. The Cold War dynamic would not be between capitalism and communism, but between the fascist Euro-Asian bloc and the democratic Western Hemisphere—primarily the United States, which would have retreated into a heavily fortified, militarized isolationism. The space race, if it occurred, would be a strategic competition between Washington and Berlin, with satellite networks and orbital platforms serving as high-ground deterrents rather than tools of scientific cooperation. 

Culturally, the year would be marked by state-enforced aesthetic traditionalism and ideological uniformity. Modernism, abstract art, and liberal democratic thought would be classified as degenerate and censored. Culture would serve as propaganda, celebrating militarism, racial purity, and obedience to the Führer principle, enforced by a sprawling surveillance apparatus that had evolved from the Gestapo into an omnipresent digital intelligence network. There would be no European Union of sovereign democracies, no globalized internet fostering free exchange, and no universal human rights framework; instead, 2001 would be a year of totalitarian stability, where a brutal peace reigns over a racially engineered continent locked in a perpetual standoff with the free world across the Atlantic.

edus.text: In a world where the European Axis won,
2001 would be defined by a consolidated continental empire, a shattered Soviet Union, and a radically different global order.
Europe itself would be organized under German hegemony,
likely through a formalized economic and political union dominated by Berlin,
where the economies of Western and Central Europe serve German industrial needs.
The East would be a patchwork of quasi-colonial territories,
with Poland, Ukraine, and western Russia emptied of their pre-war populations
and repopulated by German settlers according to the long-term goals of Generalplan Ost.
The Soviet Union would have collapsed into a rump state east of the Urals,
acting as a resource-extraction zone and buffer against any surviving Asian powers.
Daily life in 2001 would be shaped by institutionalized racial hierarchy.
Apartheid-like systems would govern society across the continent,
with Germanic peoples holding total political and economic supremacy,
while Slavic, Romani, and other "undesirable" populations would either have been systematically eradicated or reduced to enslaved labor forces.
Jewish culture would exist only in isolated pockets outside the German sphere,
such as in the Americas.
Technologically, 2001 would reflect a world where scientific progress is heavily militarized and state-directed.
The German regime, having monopolized European physics and engineering after purging Jewish academics, would likely lead in aerospace and nuclear technology.
The Cold War dynamic would not be between capitalism and communism,
but between the fascist Euro-Asian bloc and the democratic Western Hemisphere—primarily the United States,
which would have retreated into a heavily fortified, militarized isolationism.
The space race, if it occurred, would be a strategic competition between Washington and Berlin,
with satellite networks and orbital platforms serving as high-ground deterrents rather than tools of scientific cooperation.
Culturally, the year would be marked by state-enforced aesthetic traditionalism and ideological uniformity.
Modernism, abstract art, and liberal democratic thought would be classified as degenerate and censored.
Culture would serve as propaganda,
celebrating militarism, racial purity, and obedience to the Führer principle,
enforced by a sprawling surveillance apparatus
that had evolved from the Gestapo into an omnipresent digital intelligence network.
There would be no European Union of sovereign democracies, no globalized internet fostering free exchange, and no universal human rights framework;
instead, 2001 would be a year of totalitarian stability,
where a brutal peace reigns over a racially engineered continent
locked in a perpetual standoff with the free world across the Atlantic.

items.question: What If Have a Full-Scale Sino-Soviet Nuclear War during the 1969 Border Conflict
human_answers: There's a finished scenario about that: Thread 'The Bear vs the Dragon - a Sino-Soviet War TL' Jun 2, 2017 I've been working on another TL concerning an escalation of the Sino-Soviet border war of 1969. It will delve into a "limited" nuclear war and its consequences, political, ecological and otherwise. Dystopias are best observed and not practiced. Enjoy. The Bear vs. the Dragon Chapter I: The Sino-Soviet Split and Early Hostilities, March 1969. ​ The Sino-Soviet split was the deterioration of political and ideological relations between the neighbouring states of the People's Republic of China and the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics during the Cold War. In the 1960s... Onkel Willie brezhnev mao sino-soviet border conflict sino-soviet split Replies: 395 Forum: Alternate History Discussion: After 1900 Basically, Mao stubbornly continues to fight for Zhenbao Island even if the Soviets nuked many cities in China. The Chinese were able to retaliate to a limited degree, nuking several Soviet cities and military bases in the border. But the favor is towards the Soviets so eventually, Mao gets couped by Lin Bao who then seeks peace with the USSR. Lin and some moderates in the CCP didn't find it worth to see an annhiliated China over a "silly little island" in the Ussuri River.

When you say "the Korean Peninsula probably lights up in war" do you mean that North Korea would invade China alongside the Soviets? That might make sense, although it opens up the possibility that the South might attack north of the DMZ. (I don't know enough to say whether or not this was likely, but surely if ever there was a moment for the South to attack, this would be it). A Northern invasion of the South, on the other hand, seems most unlikely -- the DPRK would be putting itself in an incredibly precarious position just as the USSR is least able to help it. Other than that though, this is all good. Pakistan's role in such a scenario is, IMO, under-discussed, and it seems quite likely that India would exploit the situation for its own ends. I understand the logic here but some counterpoints come to mind. (1) There may not be enough of a China left for the US to ally with. Depending on the degree to which the Soviets take the gloves off, we could see chemical and possibly even biological weapons deployed along with easily 500 nukes (out of conservative estimates of a 10k stockpile, leaving plenty to aim at the West). That is enough to take every urban center in China off the map. Plus we would almost certainly see a famine that would make the Great Leap Forward look like a minor shortage. A collapse into warlordism in some way shape or form should not be ruled out. So even if the US tries to build a relationship with the PRC, such a relationship would only be meaningful until the Soviets take the PRC off of the map -- a length of time measurable in months if not weeks. (2) Conversely, when a united Chinese government does emerge from the wreck, it will almost certainly be a Soviet puppet. If the USSR is able to advance to what had once been Beijing, say, and install a crony of theirs such as Wang Ming, then such a government can begin to reunite what's left of the country with Soviet support. Depending on how much the Soviets want to lean into reconstruction/humanitarian aid, this puppet regime could rapidly build up more legitimacy than what's left of the Mao-era PRC simply by virtue of having more food. The USSR can exert much more influence over postwar China than the US can simply by virtue of geographic proximity and a little bit of common sense. Now if the Soviets "leave China for dead", so to speak, and withdraw without bothering to install a friendly government, or limit themselves to peripheral territorial concessions, then sure, whatever new government emerges might end up being pro-American -- although even then it would be essentially useless as an ally. (3) For what it's worth, Chiang Kai-shek is likely to make some kind of move on the mainland if the PRC collapses. If the Americans are trying to build a relationship with whatever new government emerges in China, they'll have to take him into account. Of course, they could tell him to pound sand as they did in OTL, but this is less likely if he's managed to physically occupy territory on the mainland.

This could be a turning point. Sino-Soviet border conflict - Wikipedia en.wikipedia.org Between August and October 1969 both sides were VERY scared of possible nuclear escalation. The PRC feared a decapitation strike by the Soviets, perhaps on October 1, 1969: the PRC at 20. The Soviets were kinda affraid of the Cultural Revolution madness; that some kind of Red Guard nutcase influenced the PLA into dropping a nuke on USSR far east, say, Vladivostok. I think it might be possible possible to create an "October 27, 1962" situation between the PRC and USSR. That day a U-2 was shot down near Cuba killing its pilot; while the B-59 submarine almost torpedo-nuked a US carrier. And on top of that, Nixon was trying his hand at his "mad man theory". He was flexing nuclear muscles to try and scare North Vietnam into thinking he may use tactical nukes against them. Of course it was bluff, and what's more: while NV was not impressed nor took the bait, the Soviets on the contrary were a little aghast, wondering WDF Nixon was doing with his DEFCON and B-52 raised alerts. Joint Chiefs of Staff Readiness Test - Wikipedia en.wikipedia.org Operation Giant Lance - Wikipedia en.wikipedia.org Sino-Soviet split - Wikipedia en.wikipedia.org

AHC: Have a Full-Scale Sino-Soviet Nuclear War during the 1969 Border Conflict

Basically, have a realistic point of divergence, ideally 5 or less years before the start of the Sino-Soviet border conflict, but could be more time before then if need be, which would guarantee that the border conflict escalates into a nuclear war, but ideally without the US or other nuclear powers getting involved and turning the conflict into a global war. I'd imagine that a successful assassination of Leonid Brezhnev in January 1969 or Khrushchev somehow staying in power could be good PODs, but I want to ask here in case there are better ones. Also, this is my first AHC, so if this isn't formatted properly, my apologies in advance.

items.model_answer:
A full-scale Sino-Soviet nuclear war during the 1969 border conflict would have produced catastrophic and profoundly asymmetrical consequences, given the vast disparity in nuclear capabilities at that time.

In 1969, the Soviet Union possessed a mature nuclear arsenal with sophisticated delivery systems including ICBMs, while China had only begun its nuclear program—first testing a fission weapon in 1964 and a thermonuclear device in 1967, with limited and unreliable delivery capabilities consisting primarily of short-range missiles and bombers. A Soviet nuclear strike would have devastated China's nascent nuclear facilities, military infrastructure, major cities, and industrial centers, potentially killing tens of millions and effectively destroying the Chinese state as a functioning entity. China's limited retaliation could have inflicted significant damage on Soviet cities within reach of its early DF-2 and DF-3 missiles, but this would have been orders of magnitude less than the destruction China suffered.

The global consequences would have been enormous: massive radioactive fallout across East Asia and beyond, disruption of global agriculture and trade, and a shattered nuclear taboo that would have fundamentally altered international relations. The United States, already engaged in Vietnam, would have faced an agonizing strategic dilemma about whether to intervene against a Soviet Union that had just demonstrated willingness to use nuclear weapons annihilatively. The geopolitical landscape of Asia would have been irrevocably transformed, likely resulting in Soviet hegemony over a devastated China, massive humanitarian catastrophe requiring international response, and a world living under the precedent that nuclear war between major powers was not merely theoretical but actual.

edus.text: A full-scale Sino-Soviet nuclear war during the 1969 border conflict would have produced catastrophic and profoundly asymmetrical consequences,
given the vast disparity in nuclear capabilities at that time.
In 1969, the Soviet Union possessed a mature nuclear arsenal with sophisticated delivery systems including ICBMs,
while China had only begun its nuclear program—first testing a fission weapon in 1964 and a thermonuclear device in 1967,
with limited and unreliable delivery capabilities consisting primarily of short-range missiles and bombers.
A Soviet nuclear strike would have devastated China's nascent nuclear facilities, military infrastructure, major cities, and industrial centers,
potentially killing tens of millions
and effectively destroying the Chinese state as a functioning entity.
China's limited retaliation could have inflicted significant damage on Soviet cities within reach of its early DF-2 and DF-3 missiles,
but this would have been orders of magnitude less than the destruction China suffered.
The global consequences would have been enormous:
massive radioactive fallout across East Asia and beyond,
disruption of global agriculture and trade,
and a shattered nuclear taboo that would have fundamentally altered international relations.
The United States, already engaged in Vietnam, would have faced an agonizing strategic dilemma about whether to intervene against a Soviet Union
that had just demonstrated willingness to use nuclear weapons annihilatively.
The geopolitical landscape of Asia would have been irrevocably transformed,
likely resulting in Soviet hegemony over a devastated China,
massive humanitarian catastrophe requiring international response,
and a world living under the precedent that nuclear war between major powers was not merely theoretical but actual.

items.question: What If Female US Combat Pilots in WWII
human_answers: The opposition was intense. One of the reasons some individuals ceased opposition was in the expectation they would fail and prove the arguments against. One a lesser scale was opposition to recruiting significant numbers of Hispanics, Puerto Ricans, and so westerns from Arizona, New Mexico, Texas. Or Japanese Neisi, or Native Americans. Some even wrung their hands over the number of Catholics, and other non WASPS in the US military of 1944. Culturally I'd think the critical PoD needs to be far back in the 19th Century. More than one historian of US social development has noted that women acting as combatants, as business leaders, as manual laborers was much more acceptable in the 18th and early to mid 19th Century US. The cultural norm of the Feminine Home Maker and less capable protected sex grew with the expansion of the urban middle class in the latter half of the 19th Century. Reduce that in middle class culture of the US and you can continue with some fraction of the combatants in US wars as women. I'd approach it from the angle of accepting the most capable candidates. "She may be a girl, but dammint she can fly better than any man in the class." All female units are one route. The ultra capable specialist is the other, tho that one is a bit Hollywood. In the old Soviet and more modern Russian cinema the stories of women in combat units are a bit more common. The roles as the single female specialist or outlier appears, and the stories of all female combat units. Last year I watch part of a movie about individual women fighter aircraft regiment. It was a rather brutal and unvarnished narrative & it did not dodge around th deaths of the pilots, shoving those in the face of the audience. Underlying the story is the sense of desperation and emergency for the 1941-1943 segment of the Soviet-Axis part of the war.
items.original_question:
AHC: Female US Combat Pilots in WWII

USSR famously employed some female combat pilots, but the conditions that made this possible did not exist in the USA (not nearly so desperate a war, and no communist philosophy which held gender equality as an ideal). Of course women flew for the war effort in non-combat capacities (Jackie Cochran’s WASPs, etc.) How far back would a POD have to be to get at least a few American women flying fighters or bombers? Much worse opening to the Pacific War, more carriers sunk and experienced pilots killed, leading to an approval for female volunteers to serve as combat pilots in provisional capacity? A more developed feminist movement through the 20s and 30s, bringing such a possibility just barely into the Overton window?

items.model_answer:
If the United States had allowed women to serve as combat pilots during World War II, several significant changes would likely have occurred. The Soviet Union already demonstrated that women could be effective combat pilots with units like the "Night Witches," so capability was proven elsewhere.

With the severe pilot shortages the US faced during the war, integrating women would have expanded the available talent pool. The existing WASP program already showed that American women could fly military aircraft competently in non-combat roles, ferrying planes, testing aircraft, and towing targets for live ammunition practice—dangerous work that resulted in 38 WASP fatalities.

Combat integration would likely have accelerated post-war women's military inclusion. Instead of the WASPs being disbanded in 1944 and denied military status until 1977, female pilots might have established a permanent presence in military aviation. This could have hastened women's full integration into the armed forces, which didn't occur until the 1970s-90s.

Culturally, visible female combat heroes would have challenged gender norms earlier, potentially advancing the women's rights movement. However, significant resistance would have existed given 1940s social attitudes, possibly creating morale and discipline challenges that commanders would have needed to address.

The precedent might have influenced other military integration debates, including racial integration, which occurred in 1948. Aviation has often been a pathbreaker for military inclusion, so earlier gender integration in the skies could have catalyzed broader changes across the armed forces and American society.

edus.text: If the United States had allowed women to serve as combat pilots during World War II,
several significant changes would likely have occurred.
The Soviet Union already demonstrated that women could be effective combat pilots with units like the "Night Witches,"
so capability was proven elsewhere.
With the severe pilot shortages the US faced during the war,
integrating women would have expanded the available talent pool.
The existing WASP program already showed that American women could fly military aircraft competently in non-combat roles,
ferrying planes, testing aircraft, and towing targets for live ammunition practice
dangerous work that resulted in 38 WASP fatalities.
Combat integration would likely have accelerated post-war women's military inclusion.
Instead of the WASPs being disbanded in 1944 and denied military status until 1977,
female pilots might have established a permanent presence in military aviation.
This could have hastened women's full integration into the armed forces,
which didn't occur until the 1970s-90s.
Culturally, visible female combat heroes would have challenged gender norms earlier,
potentially advancing the women's rights movement.
However, significant resistance would have existed given 1940s social attitudes,
possibly creating morale and discipline challenges
that commanders would have needed to address.
The precedent might have influenced other military integration debates, including racial integration,
which occurred in 1948.
Aviation has often been a pathbreaker for military inclusion,
so earlier gender integration in the skies could have catalyzed broader changes across the armed forces and American society.

items.question: What If Tom Daschle wins re-election in 2004
human_answers: Another Daschle term would have been a real step down for Democrats in terms of leadership. Reid and Pelosi were the best Democratic floor leaders in generations and having them commanding the two chambers at the same time is a very big part of why Obama's first two years were so damn productive. Daschle rose through the ranks because he was really good on TV. Reid was terrible on camera, so Daschle is a plus for Democrats here, but I'm not sure it really matters. W was so badly screwing up his second term that Dems didn't really need to convince anyone that things were on the wrong track. The really interesting Qs are what Dems would do with an extra vote's breathing room in the Senate -- is it enough for Daschle to actually get things done even if he's less of a vote-counter than Reid? -- and what impact Daschle's somewhat more expansionist personal opinion on healthcare reform does to Obamacare. Daschle's tax fraud stemmed from income he earned from 2005-2007 -- i.e, after he lost re-election. He won't have that job or that income in ATL, so the whole scandal is butterflied away.

I don't see anyone mentioning the biggest butterfly: Ted Kennedy. Ted Kennedy died in August (I think?) taking Dems down to 59 seats. That's not going to happen if there's an extra seat. They're not going to have to bargain with Ben Nelson to get anything through. Dems are going to be at 60 seats through 2010. Also consequential, they're going to beat 60 seats before March of 2009 because of Al Franken. They had to do a run-off election which meant the Obama administration had to wait an extra 2-3 months to get their super majority. Daschle-Reid were effective. They got Jim Jeffords to switch. They'll be able to get something passed. Daschle wrote a book about how how single-payer is the ideal system but it's problematic in the states. I expect him to push for some Federal Health Board which will only increase death panel comparisons. I'd be interested in what others thing they can get passed through 2009-2010. More stimulus. More infrastructure. I'd love to hear thoughts. There's a small miracle that Daschle can survive in 2010 especially if he's up against a Tea Party lunatic. It's forgotten now but there was some talk after 2012 post-Sandy Hook that Obama might be the rare President who makes gains in the sixth year midterms. I think that's a stretch but it's not inconceivable. If Daschle can convince the retiring Senate Democrats to stay they certainly don't need to lose 9 seats.

Daschle loosing was a real bit of mud in the eye for Democrats in 2004. Him squeaking through would have been a help for sure; anything that gives Democrats an extra vote in the Senate in 2008-2010 will be a big help for Obama's agenda and the ACA. I don't remember how effective he was as a senate leader, Reid wasn't exactly a slouch though. He also had a corruption scandal in 2009 which might become a bigger deal if he's Senate majority leader. Big picture wise, the question is does the extra vote in the Senate and easier passage of a stronger ACA snowball into a more successful presidency for Obama? There's still going to be backlash in 2010, but if more gets done in 2008-2010 thanks to a less intransigent senate, then that momentum could carry forwards. Do they try to do immigration reform, or a stronger recovery package if less of the oxygen is sucked up by healthcare? Big picture the country would have all the same fundamental issues it currently does, but if the vibes are shifted enough in 2016 things could get very different, especially if a certain Orange man decides to stay out of the race.
items.original_question: What if Tom Daschle wins re-election in 2004 Tom Daschle was a Democratic senator from South Dakota who served as the Senate Democratic Caucus leader from 1995 to 2005. In 2004, Daschle was defeated by Republican John Thune by a narrow margin of only 4,508 votes. Daschle would be succeeded as the Senate Democratic leader by Harry Reid of Nevada, who would go on to serve as Senate Majority Leader during the last two years of George W. Bush’s second term and the first two years of Barack Obama’s first term. Democrats would achieve a supermajority during Obama’s first term, enabling the passage of the Affordable Care Act. However, the presence of Senator Joe Lieberman in the Democratic caucus would frustrate Obama’s agenda, axing the public option from the ACA. However, had Tom Daschle won re-election in 2004, perhaps Daschle would have been the 60th vote instead of Joe Lieberman. And unlike Lieberman, Daschle would very likely be for the public option. What would be the impact of a public option being passed as part of ObamaCare? What might change in the 2006, 2008, and 2010 elections if Daschle continued to lead the Democrats rather than Harry Reid? Would Democrats still win all of the seats they would win IOTL?

First, the Senate composition would have shifted slightly, with Democrats holding 45 seats rather than 44, potentially giving Daschle slightly more leverage as Minority Leader in negotiating with the Republican majority during Bush's second term.

Second, Daschle would have remained a prominent national Democratic figure and potential 2008 presidential contender. His continued presence in Senate leadership might have influenced Democratic strategy on key Bush-era policies, including judicial nominations, Social Security reform attempts, and Iraq War oversight.

Third, the Democratic Senate leadership structure would have been different—Harry Reid would not have ascended to Minority Leader in 2005, potentially altering his trajectory toward becoming Majority Leader in 2007.

Fourth, Daschle's relationship with Barack Obama might have evolved differently. Daschle was an early Obama supporter and advisor, but as a still-serving Senator rather than a former one, he might have been a more direct competitor for the 2008 nomination or a more powerful Senate ally.

Finally, South Dakota's political trajectory would have shifted, as Daschle's loss marked a significant moment in the decline of Democratic representation in rural Plains states.

edus.text: If Tom Daschle had won re-election to the Senate in 2004 instead of losing to Republican John Thune,
several significant consequences would likely have followed.
First, the Senate composition would have shifted slightly,
with Democrats holding 45 seats rather than 44,
potentially giving Daschle slightly more leverage as Minority Leader in negotiating with the Republican majority during Bush's second term.
Second, Daschle would have remained a prominent national Democratic figure and potential 2008 presidential contender.
His continued presence in Senate leadership might have influenced Democratic strategy on key Bush-era policies,
including judicial nominations, Social Security reform attempts, and Iraq War oversight.
Third, the Democratic Senate leadership structure would have been different—
Harry Reid would not have ascended to Minority Leader in 2005,
potentially altering his trajectory toward becoming Majority Leader in 2007.
Fourth, Daschle's relationship with Barack Obama might have evolved differently.
Daschle was an early Obama supporter and advisor,
but as a still-serving Senator rather than a former one,
he might have been a more direct competitor for the 2008 nomination
or a more powerful Senate ally.
Finally, South Dakota's political trajectory would have shifted,
as Daschle's loss marked a significant moment in the decline of Democratic representation in rural Plains states.

items.question: What If Equip the Best Possible Interwar Army From Scratch
human_answers: The problem is that what determines what hardware will be best ultimately depends a lot on geography If you are in the position of say Poland, where you are losing in three months no matter what and all that matters is doing as much damage as possible in that timeframe so as to maybe allow the Franco-British to liberate you in 1941, instead of the USSR "liberating" you in 1945, then you want the best raw performance, you don't really care much about logistics or manufacturing, what you have on day 1 is what you will fight the war with Now imagine you are in the position of Canada, you are basically safe and you are going to be fighting an expeditionary campaign in support of a greater power. In that case you would want compatibility with that great power even if that leads to overall inferior equipment, and the same with producibility IE for a service rifle if you are the first, you can pick whatever limited run prototype in whatever bespoke caliber is considered optimal for a service rifle by you. In the second you basically want a Springfield in .30-06 or an Enfield in .303 British depending on who you would be doing expeditionary operations with So basically if I am a safe country, I more or less copy either the US or UK exactly, because I expect to be doing expeditionary ops with them and the logistical benefits of using the same equipment will outweigh any real performance issues, and to be frank anything bought in 1930 is just going to be training stuff for the real fight. If I am not a safe country, then it gets interesting

Norway: With tight interwar budgets and a pacifistic government during the Interwar years, there wasn't much budget for the military. That was a common case for most Western Democracies during that time. However, the Norwegians were a a seafaring nation with a disproportionately long coastline, so the Navy would spread careful building of mostly destroyers and auxialliary craft, plus maintaining a couple of obsolete Coastal Defence ships. Have the Norwegians design and build their version of the German Schnellboats (1) , perhaps buying Italian or British torpedoes and 20-25mm or 3.7cm armament from Italy, Sweden, Poland, or ???. The Italians did do a barter of Caproni bombers for dried Norwegian cod in the late '30s (not kidding...), so there was a precedent for some form of dealing between those countries. Maybe even add in Isotta-Fraschini v-12 or V-16 boat engines to the barter, or British(RR?), or American(Packards?). Those Raske båter (fast boats) could have had general utility throughout their service life, patrolling up fjords and inside the myriad number of islands along the coast, with sufficient sea keeping ability to transit some lengths outside the islands too. As torpedo boats, they could have been very useful in April 1940, in the hands of bold commanders with clear orders of engagement (2) (1) I usually talk up the Italian MAS boats here, but I've come around to others suggestion that something more the size of an S-Boat would be a better option (2) Clear rules of engagement were historically lacking on April 9, 1940. The famous sinking of the Blucher was done by Oberst Birger Eriksen, sticking his neck out and ordering the big guns of the Oscarborg to fire and then the kill shots from the ancient shore based torpedoes. Elsewhere, the Germans got well inside the Norwegian defense before response came.

Medium field gun: (US) M1917/M1920 75mm (based on French Mle1897, with split trails for more traverse/elevation). HE, smoke, AP, canister ammo. Light tracked vehicle...basis for APC / gun tractor / field supply hauler / SP medium mortar: Carden-Loyd Mark VI. Heavy armored car: Landsverk S180 (with Bofors 37mm gun). Cavalry motorcycle (3 men): Norton Big 4 with sidecar. Sidecar front grab-bar at height to serve as gun-rest for LMG. Infantry light MG: Czechoslovak ZB vz. 30, chambered for 7.62 x 63 (.30-06). Infantry rifle: Garand, chambered for 7.62 x 63 (.30-06). (several-year POD from OTL development timeline) Rifle grenade system: VB. HE, smoke, WP ammo...WP is particularly for AT and anti-bunker use. Medium (81mm) infantry mortar: Brandt Mle 1927. HE, smoke, illumination ammo. Anti-personnel mine: German "S-mine". (~2 year POD from OTL patent date) Anti-tank mine: Tellermine 29. Medium-altitude anti-aircraft gun system: Bofors 40mm L/60. (2 year POD from first production.) Towed mount.
