items.question: What If A clash between Rockefeller/Cisneros vs Quayle/Alexander in the US 1996 elections
human_answers: Think about it--when Truman lost, it wasn't *just* because Democrats had been in power a long time. It was *also* because Harry Truman never saw a hornet's nest he didn't want to kick, a temperamental flaw that contributed to a sense of chaos in all walks of life. Combine that with the endemic corruption issues that come from twenty years in power, and you've got a recipe for a one term president. A distinct but similar dynamic appears with the coming of Nixon. Nobody believed LBJ about anything by 1968, and that rubbed off on Humphrey, who was (ironically) more upright but much weaker than Johnson, and the Hump never could shake the Credibility Gap issues he inherited. The loss of trust on all fronts created widespread anger and chaos followed in the wake of that anger. Add to that the endemic corruption issues that come from eight years of Kennedy and Johnson, and you've got a recipe for a Nixon win. No surprise, this is basically the exact same setup that takes down Nixon and Ford. What you might notice here is that the personality flaws of the individual in the White House combine with the problems of institutional corruption that arise after years in power to create a scandal unique to the time and place that ends up consuming everyone involved. I would imagine that a Bush I who gets a second term--by *some* miracle--is going to make some similar mistakes to the ones his son made. They had many of the same advisors, after all. Here, Bush I had none of Bush II's cocksure self assurance to distract from whatever Middle East quagmire he drags the US into, and I think he would crash and burn more quickly in terms of public approval. You might imagine a scenario where Clinton's scandals + much better Perot popular vote= an apparent Bush landslide, where Bush makes the error of mistaking his opponents' divisions for his own strength. I won't get into details because it's current politics, but if you want an example of just such an outcome, look at the results of the last UK general election. The bigger question to me is why America would turn to a plutocrat like Rockefeller after 16 years of "Greed is Good."

Okay, the idea is that this story is loosely based on some ideas from other users who wrote their stories*. The general idea is to create a story with some overall meaning using all of this. So, the story is about how, before the 1988 elections, a recession (like the one in the 90s) occurs. This causes Bush to win by a much smaller margin than OTL (301-236 EVs), resulting in the Democrats gaining more seats in the Senate and the House. This leads to Bush panicking, causing him to try to appease both Reaganite Republicans and more moderate Republicans, although I haven't decided what his cabinet would look like. Anyway, because of this, the Iraqi invasion of Kuwait is delayed until August 18, 1991. Furthermore, Iraq decides to invade the east coast of Saudi Arabia on December 26, 1991, that is, 130 days after the invasion of Kuwait. This leads to larger chain reactions overall, but they are not important at this moment. Two important points should also be added: 1. There were no Yugoslav Wars, therefore Bush was perhaps less concerned about the situation developing in the Balkans and set an earlier deadline (than OTL) for a ceasefire in Iraq, which ended on February 24, 1992. 2. The Iraqi Civil War did not end until 1993, so there was an incentive to be more attentive to the problems of other countries. This resulted in a much more effective Gulf War, and Saddam was overthrown a few days before the coalition reached Baghdad, but these are details. What you're probably wondering is... how did Bush win the 1992 election? Well, it was for several reasons. Like the Gulf War, the fact that the Soviet Union was doing stupid things, that the US was able to recover from the recession thanks to contracts with Kuwait and Saudi Arabia, and most importantly, that each and every one of Bill Clinton's sex scandals was revealed. Ultimately, the election ended in a landslide victory for Bush (343-195 EVs). Bush's second term was relatively fruitful**. In foreign policy, he had some relative successes, such as Somalia, and some major successes, such as Rwanda. The economy was booming, and everything was going well. But people were starting to get tired of 16 years of Republican presidency and a Democratic option that wasn't showing it could win 4 elections in a row. Therefore, the Democratic primaries would be an opportunity to determine who could win the 1996 election once and for all. I have a vague idea of who the Democratic candidates might be in the primaries; they would be: ● Jay Rockefeller – He would be the one to win because of his establishment base and because he represents a remnant of the New Deal era, making him the best candidate. ● Henry Cisneros – The surprise candidate of the primaries, someone no one expected to win so many states, even though he's a senator who won the 1990 midterm Senate elections. I think he would come in second or third. ● Jesse Jackson – I'm sure he would see this as the perfect opportunity to run in the 1996 elections. He would run with the rainbow coalition and say that the reason they didn't win the last election was because Bill Clinton was a moderate white Southerner and, above all, a womanizer. Therefore, I see him coming in second or third, but I highly doubt the establishment would want him as their candidate. ● Bill Bradley – He would be the progressive candidate the establishment would prefer over Jackson, but I doubt he would win many states, to be honest. ● Joe Biden - Same as Bradley, but being liberal, not progressive. ● Kent Conrad - Okay, I'd have to justify myself here. I'm actually basing this on some hypothetical 1996 primaries , and I thought it would be interesting and funny to add him as a wildcard candidate. I think he could win Iowa, but I doubt it. In the end, Jay Rockefeller won the primaries, with Jackson and Cisneros coming very close to victory. The Democratic national nomination process ended with Jay Rockefeller as the presidential candidate, and, as happened in the 1988 nomination, a Texan (Henry Cisneros) was chosen, while the protesting defectors voted for Jesse Jackson. The Republican primaries and nomination process is simpler. All the candidates who ran in the 1996 primaries OTL are running ITTL, the difference being that Dan Quayle runs and wins the primary and the Republican nomination. Lamar Alexander came in second in the primaries and became Quayle's running mate. Now, some details I'd like to add are that a) Jesse Jackson would say a few words that would unify all racial demographics in the Rockefeller/Cisneros formula, and Dan Quayle would say something so stupid/racist against Chicanos that it would be repudiated by all centrists; that would be very funny. And that's all I could think of for this scenario***. *The stories I use as a base are: New World Empire: The Second Term of George H.W. Bush Al Grito de Guerra: the Second Mexican Revolution The Rise and Fall of the Vlasov's Russia: The last years of the Soviet Union without Boris YeltsinThird Time's The Charm: A World Without The Yugoslav Wars Daltonia's Test Thread Exocet - the Effects of a different Falklands Paper Doves in Flight: Poland & The World After Communism **For those who want to know, the cabinet is: President: George Bush Vice President: Dan Quayle Secretary of State: James Baker Secretary of Treasury: Jack Kemp Secretary of Defense: Dick Cheney Attorney General: William Barr Secretary of the Interior: Manuel Lujan Jr Secretary of Agriculture: C. Boyden Gray Secretary of Commerce: Barbara Franklin Secretary of Labor: Bill Brock Secretary of Health and Human Services: C. Everett Koop Secretary of Housing and Urban Development: Andrew Card Secretary of Transportation: Sam Skinner Secretary of Energy: James Watkins Secretary of Education: Lamar Alexander Secretary of Veteran Affairs: Ed Derwinski Director of the Office of Management and Budget: Nicholas Brady Counselor to the President: Clayton Yuetter National Security Advisor: Brent Scowcroft Press Secretary: Marlin Fitzwater ***This took me I don't know how many hours, I was literally at it from 4 am until 8:11 am, I want to die

items.model_answer:
A 1996 presidential election pitting Nelson Rockefeller and Henry Cisneros against Dan Quayle and Lamar Alexander would represent a striking clash of Republican moderation and Democratic pragmatism, fundamentally reshaping the American political landscape of the 1990s. 

On the Republican side, a Rockefeller/Quayle ticket would be an intriguing exercise in ideological balance. Nelson Rockefeller, the quintessential liberal Republican of the 1960s and 1970s, would drag the party's platform firmly back toward the center, emphasizing federal investment in infrastructure, education, and social safety nets, while maintaining a hawkish, interventionist foreign policy. By 1996, Rockefeller's brand of Republicanism would be a direct challenge to the rising conservative revolution that had taken root since Reagan. Dan Quayle, however, would serve as the anchor to the party's conservative evangelical and populist base, ensuring the ticket did not alienate the Gingrich-era Republicans. Internally, the GOP would face intense friction, as Rockefeller's "limousine liberal" reputation among conservatives would provoke a fierce primary battle against the party's dominant right wing, likely forcing Rockefeller to adopt compromise policies to prevent a third-party conservative revolt.

On the Democratic side, a Cisneros/Alexander ticket would be a historic and geographically potent alliance. Henry Cisneros, the former mayor of San Antonio, would be the first Latino presidential nominee of a major party, mobilizing a rapidly growing demographic and bringing a pragmatic, urban-focused, New Democrat vision to the top of the ticket. Lamar Alexander—a conservative, Southern governor—crossing party lines to serve as the Democratic Vice Presidential nominee would be an extraordinary realignment. It would signal a deliberate Democratic strategy to rebuild the moderate, bipartisan coalition that had fractured under cultural wars, appealing to suburban voters and rural Southerners who felt alienated by the GOP's increasingly hard-right trajectory. Alexander’s presence would ensure the Democrats dominated the South and swung traditionally Republican border states.

The general election would likely result in a decisive victory for the Democrats. While Rockefeller's return to the center would win back affluent suburban voters in the Northeast and Pacific Coast, his presence at the top of the GOP ticket would deeply demoralize the conservative base. Many evangelical and conservative voters, unmotivated by a moderate establishment figure and skeptical of Quayle's ability to steer the administration rightward, would likely stay home or drift to a minor third-party protest candidate. Conversely, the Cisneros/Alexander ticket would be an electoral juggernaut in the Sun Belt and the South, combining Cisneros's demographic appeal with Alexander's regional credibility. The Midwest, traditionally a battleground, would lean Democratic due to Cisneros's focus on urban economic revitalization. Ultimately, the election would accelerate the ideological sorting of the American electorate, proving that a Republican Party led by its old moderate wing could not survive the conservative era, while cementing the Democrats as the dominant party of a diverse, pragmatic center.

items.question: What If Mallory and Irvine Summited & Survived Everest
human_answers: I would think that you would see a Nelsonian style of celebration and loss. Assuming that the weather was clear enough to allow for Odell, who was alone, to witness their summit and subsequent descent and deadly fall, the MAJOR issue is that Odell does not have a camera on him. The one thing that would irrefutably prove that Mallory and Irvine summited the mountain and then died on their decent would be a photograph, even a distant one, of them on or practically at the summit. Now, Irvine or Mallory did have a camera on them, the near legendary Kodak that is still missing to this day and may hold the truth of whether or not they made it. Assuming that Odell witnessed the summit and the subsequent fall, AND he could record where their bodies fell or near where they fell, then it becomes an issue of finding their bodies and the Kodak. Odell was a respected and trusted witness so i do not think that many would dispute his claim, but finding their remains and the camera would be a major point of corroborating his account. If their bodies and the camera were found, with photographic proof that they did make the summit found in it, it would be both widely celebrated and mourned. Mallory and Irvine would be national heroes in Britain and probably recognized across the world for their achievement. They were historically given a memorial service at St Paul's in London, which was widely attended by many people up to an including the then Prince of Wales, the future Edward VIII. Unlike Franklin or Scott, who were either not found or left where they died, Mallory's body at the least was in a location that its recovery was certainly possible, an Irvine's body may have ended up in a similar location if their death was witnessed. If their bodies were recovered, probably with a sponsored expedition, i could easily see a joint funeral for both in St. Paul's, potentially even reaching a State Funeral with full Royal attendance. Then you have the lasting impact that this would have on the psyche of Britain and the world. After the 1924 Expedition there was a major underswell in mountaineering circles, especially British ones, and to a lesser extent in the greater British populace, that Everest was "unfinished business." While there was a drop off in attempts after the 1924 failure, there was a massive resurgence in the 1930s, a pause during the war for obvious reasons, and then a similar surge in the 1950s culminating in the 1953 success. If Mallory and Irvine reached the top in 1924, that would greatly decrease the interest in Everest. Ironically, Mallory's and Irvine's death, and the debate that raged and still rages over whether they made the summit or not, drove the popularity and allure of the mountain far beyond what it would be if they succeeded but died on the way down. There probably would be several more attempts in the aftermath, at least one of which would probably be sponsored by groups like the British Alpine Club or the Royal Geographic Society as a symbolic summit and successful decent in tribute to Mallory and Irvine. I wouldn't be surprised if they hauled a plaque all the way up there to set up a memorial for them. But Everest probably wouldn't have the same level of mystique is has today. By provably succeeding and dying in the aftermath, Mallory and Irvine would probably completely reshape how we see Everest. Edit: Having gone over this again, the nerd in me now wants the Kodak to be a legendary item in a video game OR an SCP entry. would be a fun nod to an event few people would ever know about.

Yes ! I didn't knew they had had found Irvine (well, his foot at last). https://www.nationalgeographic.com/adventure/article/sandy-irvine-body-found-everest Unbelievable. And then there is this Holly cow they were so close - less than 400 meters to 8848 ! I understand better why so many people are confident they made it to the summit. Also the missing photography of Mallory wife. Unfortunately poor Irvine was found much lower and inside a melting glacier. Hopefully they will found more remains within the next few years. And that infamous camera. What we know for sure: the cylinder, the ice axe and Mallory's body tells us they were roped together at a minimum of 8475 metres, before they fell. Bummers, that's 2133 meters below. Talk about a fall, even if the glacier probably lowered the body on the moutain, along the years. The remaining question is: did the fall happened while climbing, less than 400 m from glory - or descending, having done it ? And there, is the missing photography of Mallory wife. AAAAARGH we are so close from knowing the truth.

So I can tell you that summit fever is very real. I have never climbed anything like Everest obviously but I have scaled (as in hiked) a few 14,000 footers in Colorado and even with that I can state with authority that due to the combination of being tired and euphoric on the way down along with the general feeling that the mission has been accomplished, the brain is not working quite right. That's just reality. Plus, you now have gravity pulling you along. Given that I agree that it is far more likely Mallory and Irvine fell on the descent, either after making the summit or deciding to turn back for whatever reason. While it is unlikely they would have turned back that close to the summit we can't dismiss it either. 400 meters from the summit may not sound like much but at that altitude is actually a very long distance and maybe the combination of bad weather, declining oxygen supplies, or overall uncertainty caused them to turn around. My personal opinion - they made it to the top (it part because I want it to be true) and fell badly on the way down but until we can get actual physical evidence that clearly shows they made the summit that's all it is, an opinion.

Interestingly a lot of practical research has gone into trying to answer the question of whether or not the clothing worn by Mallory and Irvine would have been sufficient to enable them to survive the extreme environment. This has included tests in weather chambers and even a 2006 Everest expedition with climbers wearing exact replicas of Mallory's clothing. The overall conclusion of these tests in generally that the clothing itself was actually quite comfortable and well insulated and that provided Mallory and Irvine kept moving and didn't stop for any length of time or encounter any serious deterioration in weather conditions they could have continued to "operate effectively". Weather chamber tests showed that with the clothing they had Mallory and Irvine could have survived temperatures of −30 °C. Although it was also found that if wind speed picked up the insulation of the clothing would only just be sufficient to −10 °C. While a lot of luck would have been required its not beyond the realms of possibility that Mallory and Irvine could have succeeded in the right conditions. A bigger factor would have probably been whether or not they were carrying sufficient oxygen and if their relatively primitive breathing apparatus could be relied on not to fail (One of the reasons why Mallory chose the relatively inexperienced Irvine to accompany him on his summit attempt was due to the latter's expertise with the breathing apparatus).

They never intended to climb the second step. In fact, no one knew the second step existed in 1924. And Mallory wrote that he considered the NE ridge route impossible. Odell's sighting put them at the base of the summit pyramid, above the third step, anyway. Mallory very clearly explained his intended route in his letters, which was to bypass the steps and either take the zig-zag or the couloir. Anker is ... a controversial source on anything 1924. He has a habit of disregarding any evidence that contradicts his theories on Mallory/Irvine. It's more likely than not that they summited and died on the way down, by virtue of the fact that they died . The vast majority of climbers who've died on Everest got summit fever and died on the descent because they pushed themselves way too hard to reach the peak. Michael Tracy is a grump, but he's done more to shed light on the truth of 1924 Mallory/Irvine than basically anyone else. This video is one of his that cover's their intended routes. We'll never know what actually happened of course – the '99 team utterly botched their investigation upon finding Mallory, and given Irvine's foot was found in the Rongbuk Glacier, his body probably fell clean off the mountain below Mallory in '24 so we're unlikely ever find it. But barring new evidence, the most plausible theory is that they made the summit and died on the descent that evening/night.
items.original_question: What if Mallory and Irvine Summited & Survived Everest In 1953 the New Zealand Mountaineer Edmund Hillary and Nepalese Sherpa Tenzing Norgay became the first people to reach the summit of Mount Everest (8.849m). However there remains to this day an enduring question about whether or not Hillary and Norgay actually were the first people to reach the summit of Everest or simply the first to do so and survive the experience. In 1924 during the second British expedition to attempt to conquer Everest British climbers George Mallory and Sandy Irvine set off on the expeditions third attempt to reach the summit. An attempt from which neither man would return. On the morning of the 6th of June Mallory and Irvine had set off for the summit from their final camp (8,138 m on the North Ridge). Their progress was tracked and filmed by expedition leader Noel Oddell who had positioned himself on a ridge further down the mountain to observe and record the expected first summit of the mountain. Mallory and Irvine were last spotted through a gap in the clouds approximately 240 metres from the summit still proceeding onwards. After this the pair simply disappeared. Despite many searches in the days and years following their disappearance the pair would not be seen again for another 75 years when Mallory's remarkably well preserved body would be discovered at an altitude of 8,156m. In the 1933 expedition an ice axe that could only have belonged to Mallory or Irvine was discovered at an altitude of 8,380m proving that the pair had reached at least this altitude. The location and state of Mallory's body (Irvine's partial remains in the form of a detached foot would later emerge from a glacier at a much lower altitude) indicated that he had suffered a fall which had resulted in his death either as a direct result or by later exposure likely during a decent of the mountain. The body revealed circumstantial evidence that suggests Mallory might have successfully reached the summit. Mallory carried a photo of his wife with the intention of leaving it on the summit. No such photo was found on the body. Given the excellent preservation of the body and personal possessions, the absence of the photo suggests he may have reached the summit and deposited it there. Mallory's snow goggles were in his pocket, indicating he may have died at night; that he and Irvine had made a push for the summit and were descending very late in the day. Given their known departure time and movements, had they not made the summit, it is unlikely they would have still been out by nightfall. Perhaps the one artefact that may put the mystery to bed is the Kodak pocket camera that Irvine was known to be carrying and which he presumably would have used to take a photo of the first successful ascent had such a thing occurred and may still contain useable photographs of the attempt. Assuming that Mallory had been successful in reaching the summit and managed to avoid whatever calamity befell on their decent and are able to survive the whole ordeal what would the the effects have been of Mount Everest having been summited for the first time by George Mallory in 1924? How would this have affected the history of Everest and expeditions to climb the mountain after 1924? How would Mallory and Irvine's achievement have been received and remembered?

items.model_answer:
If George Mallory and Andrew Irvine had successfully summited Mount Everest in 1924 and survived the descent, it would fundamentally alter the narrative of mountaineering history and British imperial pride. First and foremost, the title of "first to summit Everest" would belong to them, retroactively stripping the 1953 expedition of Sir Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay of that ultimate historical distinction. While Hillary and Norgay would still be recognized as the first to summit and safely return with definitive photographic proof, Mallory and Irvine’s success would shift the 1953 achievement from a pioneering first into a confirmation of an earlier, unrecorded triumph.

Surviving the descent would also solve the enduring mystery of their missing camera. If they had returned to camp with the vest-pocket Kodak camera intact, the photographic evidence of their summit would immediately validate their claim, ending a century of historical debate and rendering modern summit-hunting expeditions to find their camera unnecessary. 

On a broader cultural level, a successful 1924 summit would provide a massive psychological boost to Britain in the interwar period. The nation, still reeling from the devastating losses of World War I and grappling with the fading of its global imperial dominance, would claim a monumental victory in the "conquest of nature." Mallory, already a national hero, would return as a living legend. His survival would preserve his profound philosophical reflections on mountaineering for a wider audience, allowing him to continue shaping the ethos of exploration rather than becoming a romanticized martyr frozen on the mountain. Irvine, a brilliant young engineer, would have survived to potentially apply his formidable intellect to further technological or exploratory endeavors.

Finally, the trajectory of Everest exploration itself would change. A confirmed 1924 summit would likely accelerate international interest in the mountain. Rather than a decades-long hiatus before the next serious attempts, the proven viability of the Northeast Ridge route might have spurred earlier follow-up expeditions by other nations, advancing high-altitude climbing techniques and equipment much faster than the historical timeline ultimately dictated.

edus.text: If George Mallory and Andrew Irvine had successfully summited Mount Everest in 1924 and survived the descent,
it would fundamentally alter the narrative of mountaineering history and British imperial pride.
First and foremost, the title of "first to summit Everest" would belong to them,
retroactively stripping the 1953 expedition of Sir Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay of that ultimate historical distinction.
While Hillary and Norgay would still be recognized as the first to summit and safely return with definitive photographic proof,
Mallory and Irvine’s success would shift the 1953 achievement from a pioneering first into a confirmation of an earlier, unrecorded triumph.
Surviving the descent would also solve the enduring mystery of their missing camera.
If they had returned to camp with the vest-pocket Kodak camera intact,
the photographic evidence of their summit would immediately validate their claim,
ending a century of historical debate
and rendering modern summit-hunting expeditions to find their camera unnecessary.
On a broader cultural level, a successful 1924 summit would provide a massive psychological boost to Britain in the interwar period.
The nation, still reeling from the devastating losses of World War I and grappling with the fading of its global imperial dominance,
would claim a monumental victory in the "conquest of nature."
Mallory, already a national hero, would return as a living legend.
His survival would preserve his profound philosophical reflections on mountaineering for a wider audience,
allowing him to continue shaping the ethos of exploration rather than becoming a romanticized martyr frozen on the mountain.
Irvine, a brilliant young engineer, would have survived to potentially apply his formidable intellect to further technological or exploratory endeavors.
Finally, the trajectory of Everest exploration itself would change.
A confirmed 1924 summit would likely accelerate international interest in the mountain.
Rather than a decades-long hiatus before the next serious attempts,
the proven viability of the Northeast Ridge route might have spurred earlier follow-up expeditions by other nations,
advancing high-altitude climbing techniques and equipment much faster than the historical timeline ultimately dictated.

items.original_question: What if Pop Culture gets 1st Amendment and Union Protections for Production and Distribution Early From 1930 to 1968, the Motion Picture Production Code ("Hays Code") governed the production and distribution of motion picture content in the United States of America - a self-imposed by movie studios and exhibitors set of guidelines about what could and could not be shown/mentioned/referred to in film (be it a feature whether live-action or animated, a short whether live-action or animated, a serial chapter, or a documentary newsreel). Similar sets of guidelines governed graphic novels, comic books and newspaper comic strips (the Comics Code from 1954 to 2011), the National Association of Broadcasters' Code of Practices for Television Broadcasters (the so-called Television Code from 1952 to 1983) with a similar set of guidelines for radio, and the near-censorship of video games by the North American nations' governments before the Entertainment Software Association came up with the voluntary, self-regulating Entertainment Software Rating Board to inform consumers about content. There were various religious and secular moralistic censorship groups across the United States at the time dedicating themselves to preserving morality and good taste in American culture of the time through literature, music, sports, comic strips, motion pictures and radio. Various Tinseltown scandals led up to the 1915 U.S. Supreme Court case Mutual Film Corp. v. Industrial Commission of Ohio which unanimously held that free speech protections of the U.S. Constitution's 1st Amendment did not extend to motion pictures. But for our purposes, let's examine what if instead the Supreme Court ruled unanimously that radio, literature, comic strips, music and motion pictures were in fact protected by the 1st Amendment. If the Supreme Court were to decide that no local, state, or federal political body had the right to regulate or censor the production and distribution of any work of radio, film, literature, music within reason and neither did any religious or business organization within reason, then what? If the National/Catholic Legion of Decency, the National Board of Review and the Motion Picture Association (then the Motion Picture Producers and Distributors of America) were ordered by the Supreme Court to within reason allow for almost any type of motion pictures to be created so long as no people (especially children) and or animals were harmed by the making of a film, where should they go from here? I would suggest that instead of restrictive production/distribution codes, film distributors would possibly make an early version of the Film Rating System which would check film patrons' identifications at the box office against a film's rating. This would give many makers and distributors of motion pictures more creative freedom to explore the kinds of topics and subject matter they want to explore as well as spur various technological developments of all sorts. For our purposes, let's explore firstly what if the MPPDA Film Rating System established in the late 1910s is the one of today. Rating Indicator ​ Rating Description ​ G ​ General Audiences - All Ages Admitted. Nothing that would offend parents for viewing by children whether viewing together with parents or by themselves. PG ​ Parental Guidance Suggested - Some material may not be suitable for children. Parents urged to give "parental guidance". May contain some material parents might not like for their youngest children. PG-13 ​ Parents Strongly Cautioned - Some material may be inappropriate for children under the age of 13. Parents are urged to be cautious. Some material may be inappropriate for pre-teenagers and should be discussed before viewing decision. R ​ Restricted - Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian. Contains some adult material. Parents are urged to learn more about the film before taking their young children with them with proper legal identification at the box office. NC-17 ​ Adults Only - No One 17 Years And Under Admitted. Clearly adult. Children are not legally admitted and all adults must have legal identification at the box office. With the Film Rating System in place to ensure film producers and film distributors have the creative freedom to pursue the projects they want to make, there could be other ways for the Legion of Decency and various religion and social rights groups could clean up Hollywood for film, radio and eventually television without hampering creative freedom. One of those ways would be to convince studios, distributors and talent agencies to unionize and have their own unions so to ensure fairer treatment and hiring of prospective workers and talents, safe business practices and work hazard safety management, and fair/equal compensation for equal work for all kinds of work. This would involve the Directors Guild, Writers Guild, American Cinema Editors, Producers Guild, American Society of Cinematographers, Screen Actors Guild, Animation Guild and the International Alliance of Theatrical Stage Employees with membership being encouraged or socially pressured to watchdog for mistreatment. With creative and editorial freedom enshrined for radio and motion pictures in the Constitution, there could also be movements to establish an alliance of the Christian churches, Jewish synagogues, Islamic mosques and other religious institutions' collective motion picture production and distribution systems as a single studio called the Holy Light Studios Alliance which would be dedicated to the production and distribution of motion pictures approved by the moral standard guidelines of various local, state, national and international Christian, Jewish and Muslim faith doctrines. Entertainment, education and information fit for religious viewers. They would take in the various technological and artistic talents and know-how from the secular Hollywood studios and apply them towards delivering motion pictures (narrative feature and even the documentaries) with high production standards and quality to deliver their messages to the masses while showing religion on the side of freedom versus tyranny. This would also filter down to local radio stations (and eventually television stations starting in the late 1940s) that would choose to become affiliates of the religious non-denominational Trinity Broadcasting Network (TBN) which would be listener and eventually viewer-supported to broadcast religious services, national and international news along with news analysis and commentary, local community sports highlights and commentary, charity events, and even motion pictures from the Holy Light library after they finish their original theatrical runs come the advent of television. Local, state and federal non-partisan movements and educational institutions such as colleges, universities, trade schools and public schools would take advantage of the creative and editorial freedoms to organize radio (and eventually television) stations under one coast-to-coast network to provide listener/viewer-supported entertainment/culture, public affairs, educational and community outreach programming for the masses. National Public Radio (NPR) and the Trinity Broadcasting Network (TBN) would both provide alternatives to the commercial broadcast radio (and eventually television) networks found in the American Broadcasting Company (ABC - formerly NBC Blue), Columbia Broadcasting System (CBS) and the National Broadcasting Company (NBC - formerly NBC Red). All of them would agree, however, that their news reporting standards were to be "factual, fair and without bias" and any commentary and analysis from a partisan political viewpoint should be "clearly defined as such". While NPR and TBN were listener and eventually viewer-supported from the beginning; ABC, CBS and NBC would ensure that commercial time would be limited during hours when children and teenagers would be most likely to be tuning in. The commercial networks would choose to give fair and equal time, coverage and analysis of viewpoints and educational/informative programs to keep up with NPR and TBN's higher standards. However, there was another effect of the Mutual Film Corp. v. Industrial Commission of Ohio decision - the major movie studios could not buy and own the cinema companies that their films would be released to. This would be an antitrust compromise with the governments so that no corporate body could block the release of a film in a release slot that could pose a risk to another company's releases. What would the ripple effects of all this combined be on the motion picture and radio studios and distributors of the time (20th Century-Fox, Columbia, Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer, Paramount, RKO, Republic, United Artists, Universal, Walt Disney and Warner Brothers) on the content in the films they would release to the public? How might some of your favorite films and other pop culture installments from the early 20th Century and beyond have gone if all their makers and distributors were given maximum creative freedom within reason to make what they wanted to? Feel free to discuss this entire ATL in the comments.

items.model_answer:
If film, comics, and broadcasting had received First Amendment and union protections earlier in the twentieth century, the cultural and economic landscape of American media would have developed quite differently.

First Amendment protections would have prevented or curtailed the most sweeping censorship regimes. The Hays Code would not have dominated Hollywood from 1934 to the 1960s, allowing films to tackle mature themes—sexuality, racial injustice, political corruption, and class conflict—decades earlier. The pre-Code era's relative frankness would have continued and deepened rather than being suppressed. Similarly, comics would have escaped the Comics Code Authority's stultifying effects after 1954; instead of being relegated to superhero and sanitized genre fare, comics might have developed as a respected literary and artistic medium earlier, as they did in France and Japan. Broadcasting would have faced less government-enforced content homogenization, potentially allowing more politically diverse and culturally adventurous programming. McCarthy-era blacklisting would also have been far more difficult to impose on industries with robust constitutional protections.

Earlier union protections would have shifted economic power toward creators and workers. In film, the studio system's coercive contracts and control over talent might have been broken sooner, giving actors, writers, and directors greater creative freedom and profit participation. In comics, creators like Jerry Siegel, Joe Shuster, and Jack Kirby might have retained ownership and royalties for their characters rather than seeing their work absorbed by publishers. Broadcasting workers would have had greater job security against political purges.

Together, these protections would likely have produced a richer, more diverse, and more politically daring American media landscape much earlier—one in which marginalized voices found entry points sooner, creators shared in the profits their work generated, and censorship was a far weaker force shaping what audiences could see and hear.

Luigi Casale develops the Casale process after WWI. Italy had a deficit of fertilizers pre-war; it didn't have the trade networks or finances of other nations to purchase Chilean saltpeter in large amounts, and they invested heavily in nitrogen fixation as a result. WWI worsened that deficit, compounded by the loss of wheat imports from Russia, so Casale started work in 1917 on a more efficient method of nitrogen fixation. Said research continued in the postwar, because BASF refused to license the Haber-Bosch process elsewhere, and the Haber-Bosch process would have required modification anyways because Italy didn't have sufficient coal to use it to produce hydrogen gas in the original Haber-Bosch process. So Italy has the incentive to develop efficient nitrogen fixation processes for strategic autonomy, and Casale has the means to do so. Casale did postgraduate research in Berlin under Walter Nernst, whose research into physical chemistry mirrored that of Haber's, before returning to Italy. Casale then works near the Terni steelworks, which provided the steel to build pressure reactors able to stand pressures more than 3 times that of the Haber-Bosch process (notably by providing an unused battleship gun barrel). Even if we assume some sort of inexplicable theft or espionage on the part of Casale not mentioned in these histories and somehow nobody else thinks to apply Le Chatelier's Principle or try different catalysts, that just means the Frank-Caro process dominates. Sure, the 3x difference in energy usage is going to be difficult to bear, but between that and losing a total war/starving, people will just build more power plants and mine more fossil fuels or mineral nitrates/phosphates. Sources: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0920586121004831 (might be paywalled) https://riviste.fupress.net/index.php/subs/article/download/2809/2057/21510 The Social Side of a Scientific Breakthrough: Fritz Haber, Walther Nernst, and the Discovery of Ammonia Synthesis 1830–1930 | MPIWG Ammonia synthesis. Central to the mass production of fertilizer and explosives. It has been billed as the most consequential scientific breakthrough of the twentieth century. Historical perspectives on ammonia range from technological development to natural resource use, geopolitics, wartime... www.mpiwg-berlin.mpg.de

Arguably the only hard bit of the Haber process is the need for pressurisation to encourage the reaction to react in the right direction. The rest is more or less basic chemistry. So initially the other less efficient methods get adopted (because the nitrates are useful and profitable) and when suitable pressure vessels become available someone discovers the alt-Haber process. Unlike OTL, there will be more opportunity to refine and improve the other less efficient methods of manufacture. Pressure vessels themselves are relatively easy once you have late 19th century naval guns to adapt or inspire: durable pressure vessels are a bit harder [1], but any ferrous vessel will tend to provide iron catalyst even if nobody thought of using it beforehand. So in short, it's just delayed a few years - maybe up to a decade - and meanwhile other less efficient processes get used more than OTL. [1] As of about 20 years ago, the detailed mechanism of metal corrosion in high temperature reducing environments was still poorly understood and under investigation.
items.original_question: What if the Haber process is never invented? Let's say that Haber fails to impress Bosch and the BASF in July 1909 due to a failed demonstration of ammonia synthesis. What happens next? Would Haber go elsewhere to find a sponsor, or move on to something else? Cause this would mean that the entire discipline of industrial chemistry is stunted, and high pressure chemistry doesn't exist. Would WW1 even start?

items.model_answer:
If the Haber process were never invented, the most profound consequence would be a dramatically smaller global population—likely several billion fewer people today. Before Fritz Haber's 1909 breakthrough, agriculture depended entirely on limited natural nitrogen sources like guano, manure, and Chilean saltpeter, which were becoming scarce as demand grew. Without synthetic ammonia fertilizers, crop yields would have remained constrained by natural nitrogen fixation, creating a hard ceiling on food production.

This agricultural limitation would have cascaded into slower urbanization and industrialization, as more labor would need to remain in farming. Geopolitically, control over natural nitrate deposits would have remained a strategic priority, likely prolonging colonial competition over guano islands and saltpeter reserves.

Militarily, World War I might have ended earlier for Germany, which relied on the Haber process to produce explosives after its nitrate supply was cut off by British blockade. A shorter war could have altered the entire trajectory of twentieth-century politics.

Alternative nitrogen fixation methods might eventually have emerged—perhaps greater investment in biological nitrogen fixation research or less efficient chemical processes—but these would likely have been costlier and slower to scale. The world would be more rural, less populated, and economically constrained, though potentially less burdened by fertilizer runoff and its environmental consequences.

items.question: What If one people, two nation-states
human_answers: Italy would be easy to do, even with a recent-ish POD: there were proposals floating around in the mid-19th century, concerning Victor Emmanuel II crowning himself king of the Two Sicilies rather than annexing the place outright, while keeping the local government around; since Cavour himself was hesitant to annex the South, and only did so because Garibaldi was becoming too much of a loose cannon, if things had gone slightly differently, this could've happened, and since the South had its own distinct identity and history (even though it used Tuscan as its own official language, as every other state in the peninsula did), this could've stuck, with northern and southern Italy becoming kind of like Australia and New Zealand, independent countries closely tied to each other and under the same monarch. Ironically, the Third War of Independence could've gone better for northern Italy, since northern and southern troops couldn't integrate well IRL, and Italy could've gained Trento and Trieste before World War I, butterflying away the need for intervention; the Two Sicilies could have eventually gained a protectorate of sorts over Albania (history would rhyme there, since Skanderbeg had ties to the Neapolitan royals of his era and fled to Naples when his anti-Turkish uprising failed) and would've surely annexed the Papal enclaves once the north annexes Rome. Garibaldi's OTL expedition to Trento might instead take place in Pola or even Fiume but, as I stated earlier, northern Italy could be more willing to just accept territorial bribes from Austria here, since most of the Irredenta would've been gained already.

Faroese should linguistic be seen as a dialect of Western Norwegian. You could pretty much write Faroese with Nynorsk (the written standard the dialects in this region use) and vice versa. Where Faroese differ from Icelandic is that like Norwegian it have seen near complete replacement of vocabulary with Danish vocabulary thanks to the use of Danish Bibles, while on Iceland the Bible was translated into Icelandic early on and the Danish state supported the existence of a distinct Icelandic language for ideological reasons.. The main reason why Danes and Norwegians have trouble reading Faroese is because it use a it own variation of the Latin alphabet which is different from the one Danes and Norwegians use, while even if Icelandic was written using Danish or the different Norwegian written standards, it would be hard to understand it because of the difference in vocabulary. If the Danish-Norwegian Union had survived the Faroese Island would simply have been seen as part of Western Norway.

If the Prussians had done a better job containing the Great Northern War plague, then there might have been far more Prussian Lithuanians, who differ from Lithuanians in that they are Lutheran, strongly influenced by German culture, and speak a Germanized register of Lithuanian. While they kept the Lithuanian language alive during the Russian repression, the Prussian Lithuanians actually opposed Lithuaniation nationalism and explicitly refused to live in an independent Lithuanian state, accepting nothing else than German rule. Thus, when the Memel Territory was established, the Prussian Lithuanians declared themselves to be "Memellanders". Subsequently, after WW2, the Soviets saw them as Germans and expelled them from East Prussia. IOTL, the GNW plague absolutely decimated the Prussian Lithuanians, who comprised nearly 90% of its victims. Had it been contained effectively, and a butterfly net used afterwards, there would've been far more Prussian Lithuanians in East Prussia, perhaps enough to cause a national awakening. The Soviets likely would've propped up "Prussia" as a separate SSR from Lithuania while still expelling the Germans, and supported Prussian Lithuanian nationalism to divide and conquer (having just annexed resistive Lithuania). Basically Moldovenism, though in this case with genuine religious and cultural differences (plus a very different standard language).
items.original_question:
AHC: one people, two nation-states

There have been plenty of cases where one people with a common language and ancestry are separated into two nation-states. I'm not talking about ideological reasons like in the case of Germany and Korea, but in terms of centuries-long division of religion (Catholic Croats and Orthodox Serbs or Catholic Austrians and Protestant Germans) or geopolitics (Montenegro and Ottoman-dominated Serbia, Russia-dominated Moldova and Romania, Bulgaria and North Macedonia). And this explains why I specifically use the term "nation-state", as one people separated for long enough by the aforementioned factors would eventually evolve into different nation-states with their own ethnic identities. Is there any other scenario where this can happen?

items.model_answer:
The scenario of "one people, two nation-states" presents a fascinating challenge to the traditional nation-state model, which assumes a neat alignment between ethnic/cultural identity and political sovereignty. When a single people are divided between two states, several dynamics typically emerge:

Irredentist movements often arise, advocating for reunification based on shared identity, as seen with 19th-century German and Italian unification movements, or contemporary Korean aspirations for reunification.

Alternatively, the two states may develop distinct national identities over time, despite shared origins. West and East Germans developed different social and political cultures during their division, while North and South Koreans have evolved increasingly divergent identities since 1945.

Cross-border populations create persistent minority issues, as ethnic kin in one state may face discrimination or suspicion, potentially becoming sources of international tension.

The scenario also challenges assumptions about self-determination—does a people have the right to unify under one state, or can they legitimately exercise self-determination by maintaining separate states?

Historical examples like the two Yemens, the two Vietnams, and the ongoing division of the Irish across the Republic and Northern Ireland demonstrate that this arrangement can be temporary or enduring, peaceful or conflictual, depending on how both states manage the inherent tensions between shared identity and separate sovereignty.

items.question: What If Reverse Cuba and the Philippines
human_answers: American interest in Cuban had been more or less secured after the Span-Am War, so it'll be difficult for them to justify annexation, which could earn the ire of the Cuban independentists and the Southern States. But the Philippines presented some once in a lifetime opportunity for the US to finally gain their own foothold in the China market, instead of lurking around ports under the jurisdiction of other great powers. In a relatively practical POV, the US didn't need to annex the whole islands. Why waste men and money against the people that's prepared to fight to the last man to preserve their freedom (some historians even claimed that the Fil-Am War was the US first taste of a Vietnam scenario)? They could just let them be, make some economic agreements with them, get some ports, etc. and voila, they've got themselves a permanent presence in the Pacific without too much blood. Heck they could even convince the Brits to recognize the Republic and establish relations hoping to have Germany (or Japan) to back down from doing anything funny (although that may be a long shot).

Well, these few regions can try to secede. The issue is if they can maintain status quo. Malolos Republic controlled the navy or whatsoever left of the Spanish Navy. The government also controlled majority of the population of the Philippines. The Malolos republic can raise 100k men while your local provinces seceding have that same or lower population than the opposing army with your army having no or minimal rifles whatsoever. Your opponents have also better and well educated generals compared to you. You got also the issue of loyalty of your populace if they are more loyal to your seceding province or Malolos Republic. It is simple reality of warfare, you can try but the question is if you can succeed. It is pure imagination that civil war is because some or one provinces seceded. The only way that Civil war will happen is if Luna or Aguinaldo or anyone in the army fights among themselves. Or if you got a PoD that will butterfly away anything the resembles OTL 1890s Philippines.

Not really. The mood in the US was generally fairly pro-Cuban, and many of the Yellow Journalists of the time were agitating for Cuban independence. Plus, the labor unions in the US were also tied pretty closely to the Cubans. The whole reason the Maine was in Cuba was because the US had much more vested in what happened there than in the Philippines, due to the proximity to Florida. They were very concerned that the violence in the island might damage US investments further, and they were determined that either Cuba would remain Spanish or that Cuba would be in the US sphere somehow. Given that 6 decades later, human civilization nearly ended with a foreign threat got a foothold on that island, that was a fairly prescient concern. The US didn't care much about the Philippines until they managed to sink the Spanish fleet and realized that nothing was stopping them from taking the islands, so they did. So, in summation, if you want the US to annex Cuba and liberate the Philippines, you'd have to change things much earlier than the war.

items.model_answer:
If the historical roles of Cuba and the Philippines were reversed—meaning the Philippines became the geographically proximate, economically integrated Caribbean island under U.S. influence, while Cuba became the distant, massive Southeast Asian archipelago—the trajectory of both regions and U.S. geopolitical strategy would fundamentally change.

As the "Caribbean Philippines," the island nation would likely experience a much deeper and prolonged economic integration with the United States, similar to Puerto Rico. Its proximity to the U.S. mainland would make it an indispensable strategic outpost, heavily developed with U.S. military and naval bases to guard the Caribbean and approaches to the Gulf of Mexico. However, it would also likely suffer the same fate of prolonged colonial dependency, delaying true independence and making it highly susceptible to U.S. political and corporate domination. If a revolution eventually occurred, it would directly threaten U.S. homeland security, likely prompting a far more severe and immediate military intervention than what historically occurred in the distant Philippines.

As the "Asian Cuba," the large archipelago would face a drastically different Cold War fate. Its sheer geographic size and population would make it a massive battleground for regional influence, akin to Vietnam. If it underwent a communist revolution in the 1950s or 1960s, the U.S. could not merely impose a trade embargo or attempt isolated covert operations like the Bay of Pigs; it would almost certainly trigger a large-scale, devastating land war to prevent a giant communist state from dominating Southeast Asia. Conversely, if it remained capitalist, its size would make it the preeminent economic and military powerhouse of the region, effectively replacing Japan or South Korea as the U.S.'s primary anchor in the Western Pacific. 

Ultimately, reversing their roles transforms Cuba from a localized Caribbean containment challenge into a massive regional war zone, and transforms the Philippines from a distant, extractive colony into a heavily fortified, permanently dependent Caribbean protectorate intimately tethered to the U.S. mainland.

items.question: What If West Germany and Italy had withdrawn from the PANAVIA Tornado program at the outset?
human_answers: That would fall under the bad economics heading. Germany and Italy might well have a good aircraft industry but for something of the Tornado's complexity and expense, they would need partners to spread the burden. Germany previously partnered with Fairchild-Hiller-Republic prior to Panavian efforts and as much as I like the G.91, it isn't really in the Tornado's league. In terms of a precedent for an Italian combat twin, the closest I can get is the PD.808GE which was of course originally a joint-venture between Piaggio and Douglas. If a number of nearby industrial/aerospace powerhouse nations have approximately compatible requirements, not to mention nations that you have other economic partnerships with in mind, why on earth wouldn't you consortium-up? Germany would not be so fiscally inept as to squander the opportunity and go it alone. Why would they choose to build an inferior type that their singular budget would necessitate? I know the popular narrative has Germany as the unwilling partner but much like the recent-ish Typhoon discussion, the narrative isn't bone out by the facts. The reality was Germany studied cheaper, less capable alternatives such as single-seat, fixed wing etc. and then ploughed right on with the full capability. Eminently logical and seemingly blown out of proportion by two generations of media. A simple question. If Germany were errmming and ahhhing so, why is it Panavia GmbH ? The Marineflieger simply wanted a replacement for the F-104 but that doesn't matter because as OTL showed, whatever the airforce (both branches) wanted it didn't matter because the politicians decided. As an example of this look at the text below: Spoiler: text At least the VAK 191 would fulfill some of the requirements of the Luftwaffe and the Marineflieger. Both coming in single and two-seat variants, fighter/interceptor configuration and nuclear capable strike bomber. Supersonic and subsonic variants. And if the German aerospace industry lobbies enough, they might see one variant put into production as they actually have an existing product that consumed tons of R&D funds and ended up flying. Well, conventional wisdom showed that the single-seat, single-engine, fixed-wing design ended up outliving the variable-geometry twin-engined two-seater one. Yeah I doubt they were happy with their low-level supersonic strike F-104s and F-4s... The VAK 191 could fulfill the low-level supersonic strike-aircraft role.

IIRC the British Taxpayer paid 48% of the R&D cost of the Tornado IDS and I definitely remember that it paid 100% of the ADV's R&D cost. I don't know if HM Treasury could have paid the other 52% of the R&D cost of the IDS and that's the expensive one because it includes the cost of developing the engines and airframe. If that's correct which defence projects have to be cancelled to pay the difference? Then there's the cost of building them. items.model_answer:
If West Germany and Italy had withdrawn from the PANAVIA Tornado program at the outset, the United Kingdom would have faced the prospect of developing a complex multi-role combat aircraft alone—an undertaking that would have been financially prohibitive for a single nation. The UK would likely have been forced to either abandon the project entirely and procure American alternatives such as the F-111 or later F-15/F-16 variants, or seek alternative European partners, potentially accelerating collaboration with France on different aircraft programs. The Tornado as it existed would never have materialized, leaving a significant capability gap in low-level strike and air defense for all three nations.

The broader consequences would have been substantial for European defense cooperation. The Tornado program established critical industrial relationships and collaborative frameworks that later enabled the Eurofighter project. Its early failure might have discouraged future multinational European defense ventures or reshaped them entirely, potentially leaving European air forces more dependent on American aircraft for decades. West Germany and Italy would similarly have turned to U.S. platforms or pursued less ambitious domestic programs, altering the trajectory of European military aviation industry and interoperability well into the 21st century.

items.question: What If No nuclear weapons?
human_answers: As has been noted it is pretty much impossible to avoid having nuclear weapons ever being created. The science is pretty obvious. What CAN be altered, to a degree, is the "when". The U.S. threw a dramatic amount of funding at the effort, along with huge amounts of resources (Manhattan literally built the entire city of Oak Ridge TN to house the workers on the project. It was farmland, with about 3,000 people living in the area then in less than 2 years, it was a city with a population of 75,000. Government just walked in and "acquired" 59,000 acres, evicted everyone in the local farms and villages, and started building a fence (BIG ASS fence). The same thing happened in Washington with Hanford, except it was 500,000 acres and 39,000 people, Just a little less funding, or a project manager less driven than General Groves and the Bomb isn't ready.

Based on the described scenario, the USSR becomes the first country to test a nuclear weapon in the early 1950s, whereupon the US and UK governments demand an explanation for who filed the relevant reports in the wrong section back in 1940. In the case of the US, it's probably Lyman Briggs, who in OTL actually did lock away a key report in his safe without showing it to anyone else, which may have delayed the start of the Manhattan Project by several months. But even then, uranium fission was discovered in France in December 1938. The Einsten-Szilard letter warned the US government of the possibilities in August 1939. The Frisch-Peierls memorandum, the first description of a nuclear weapon, was written in March 1940 for the British government. By Frisch's own description, the work he and Peierls did was straightforward for any competent nuclear physicist. There might be a PoD wherein Frisch and Peierls are interned as enemy aliens and not allowed to work as physicists. Oliphant is focussed on the higher priority radar work, so Thomson's conclusion that it was not worth pursuing a chain reaction in uranium is accepted by the British government. There is therefore no MAUD committee, no report for Briggs to ignore, and no reason for Oliphant to kick things into gear. Instead, what is likely to happen is that eventually someone in the US does ask the questions that Frisch and Peierls asked, and they reach similar answers. Given OTL's trajectory, it's hard to see why that would happen any earlier than August 1941, given that US research was initially largely concerned with power plants rather than weapons. If we say it does, it might take the best part of a year for a US equivalent of the MAUD report to be carried out and an atomic weapons programme started. That puts a US weapons programme without the MAUD input as starting in mid-1942 - so about a six month delay. An arbitrarily longer delay is entirely plausible, but eventually - and probably sooner rather than later - someone is going to ask the right questions, and then things will start moving very quickly.

I do wonder if we don’t get the examples of nuclear destruction at the end of WW2 and if we delay the development of the bombs a bit so that by late 50s to mid 60s they are not quite as destructive as they were in real life if we don’t end up with a nuclear war. There are several reasons why WW3 was avoided. The example of how destructive the first generation bombers were, knowledge that the bombs were getting more powerful. Then the jump in power to the H bomb. Russia knowing that until the advent of ICBM they were behind the U.S. because their bombers sucked. The general aftermath of WW2 and no one really wanting to fight as a result. Russian back propaganda against nuclear weapons. Etc. All of this delay a possible WW3 until the combination of ICBM and drastically More powerful bombs made WW3 really unthinkable. But in a world we’re nuclear weapons are (somehow) drastically delayed we won’t see a lot of this, you are not seeing photos of nuked cities, you are getting 1st gen ICBMs with smaller nukes until h bombs get small enough to fit on ICBMs. Etc. So the taboo of a nuclear war is probably not built up soon enough to prevent a nuclear war. In fact they probably don’t segregate “conventional” war from “nuclear” as soon as we did otl. So we probably do see a WW3. Edited to add: BTW I think it is very unlikely to keep nuclear weapons from being developed by 1949. And almost impossible to keep nuclear weapons from being developed by 1955. And I thin it would be ASB to push them farther out then that. Physics simply allows for them so once you get the combination of the understanding of physics and the industrial/technical ability to make them you are getting them. And it is not exactly all that high tech to build a gun type nuke. So I just don’t see how you delay the development all that long. You would need the U.S. and the USSR to both come out of WW2 in much much worse shape to the point that they simply can’t afford to build nukes and I don’t see that happening.

Where would the focus on the difference between here and OTL?

criteria.9-10: Shows strong causal command of why gun-type and implosion weapons, wartime megaprojects, and postwar superpower capacity make indefinite prevention highly implausible.

criteria.9-10: Builds a tightly reasoned timeline with actor-specific incentives, technological bottlenecks, and plausible dates for delayed or first nuclear tests.

criteria.7-8: Explains how absence or delay affects deterrence, taboo formation, bomber/ICBM strategy, NATO-Warsaw tensions, and risk of major war.

items.model_answer:
# What If No Nuclear Weapons?

A world without nuclear weapons would have unfolded quite differently across multiple dimensions:

**World War II would have ended differently.** Without the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, the United States would likely have proceeded with Operation Downfall—a planned invasion of Japan that military planners estimated could have cost millions of lives on both sides. The war would have extended into 1946 or beyond.

**The Cold War might have turned hot.** The doctrine of Mutually Assured Destruction (MAD) prevented direct military conflict between the United States and Soviet Union. Without nuclear deterrence, the conventional military standoff in Europe could have escalated into World War III, particularly during crises like Berlin or Korea.

**Conventional military spending would likely have been even higher.** Nations would have maintained larger standing armies and conventional forces to achieve the deterrent effect that nuclear weapons provided at lower cost.

**Proliferation dynamics would differ entirely.** The entire framework of non-proliferation treaties, international safeguards, and nuclear diplomacy that defines modern international relations wouldn't exist in its current form.

**Civilian nuclear energy might have developed more slowly.** Much of the early nuclear infrastructure and expertise came from weapons programs, and the "Atoms for Peace" initiative was partly designed to justify nuclear technology development.

**Cultural and psychological impacts would be absent.** The existential anxiety of nuclear annihilation profoundly shaped art, politics, and social movements from the 1950s onward.

The paradox remains: while nuclear weapons pose existential risks, some scholars argue they prevented conflicts that could have been equally devastating through conventional means.

items.question: What If the USSR was leaked information about OB just before it happened and were thus better prepared and more competent in 1941? (No strike though)
human_answers: A couple days or weeks isn’t really enough if you’re going with the “Stalin finally makes a good decision” scenario. You need at least a couple months to have the Soviets dug in and prepared at more defensible spots further east than iotl, and considering the German initial manpower advantage (to say nothing of the purges creating widespread incompetence in the red army and said incompetence making their logistics horrible), they still probably lose pretty hard, although not quite as much as iotl. I think at least 6 or so (probably a bit more) months is needed to help close the manpower gap and create a Minsk-Kiev line that the Germans can’t penetrate if you don’t want Soviet losses to be seen as proportionally a lot bigger (though there’s a strong chance they still are in this scenario, just not enough to give the impression that all you need to do is kick in the rotten door enough and it’ll fall).

The Soviet Union possessed highly precise intelligence indicating that the German military's logistics were insufficient to sustain a protracted war and that its armaments factories had not yet shifted to a wartime footing. (This intelligence was derived from the infiltration of German industry by communist sympathizers.) Hitler also couldn't been so foolish as to believe that the mighty Soviet Union could be conquered within three months—at least, no analyst would have dared to venture such an insulting conjecture. Consequently, the less reliable intelligence from military and western country must have been false, and war is in next year. This chain of logic is remarkably robust; You cannot convince the Soviets that Germany is about to attack without introducing collateral changes—and different changes would inevitably lead to different outcomes in the war. Would they perceive their own military as weaker? Would they place their trust in Anglo-American intelligence while disregarding the Comintern’s own network? Or would they have managed to plant exceptionally reliable spies deep within the German military itself? Each of these scenarios would necessitate a distinct defensive strategy, thereby altering the very trajectory of the conflict. One thing, however, remains certain: if the Soviet Union were to lose the war while the United States remained an active belligerent, the Americans would undoubtedly drop the nuclear bomb.

I don't think there's an obvious way for the USSR to react to knowing war is coming. The Germans were much more ready for war. The USSR reaction will probably be a more planned withdrawal in the earliest days of the conflict, blowing some bridges behind their retreat, getting troops out of the pockets where they were surrounded and surrendered. Also less of the air force blown up on the ground in the opening days of the war. A better USSR reaction to Barbarossa might mean, 5,000 planes destroyed on the ground, 500,000 less troops taken as prisoners of war and a German advance that is stopped 100 miles from Moscow. That would probably look disasterous to the USSR and to historians looking backwards but would be a massive improvement over our time line. That said I've no idea how things would progress through the war. There's a lot of decisions to be made. I suspect the Germans might balance a stronger Soviet advance by putting more troops on that front which might make things easier on the Western front. No one really knows. Theres a long war and its all possibilities only.

As noted this ultimately may be worse for the USSR (but probably not) As Stalin had pretty well decimated his military command, So you have a lot of folks that either are no good at the job or have to little experience at the job or both. And if they know it is coming they may as noted by others be more forward deployed and more “aggressive” so they may not fall back as much. A good part of the beginning of the war for the USSR was the learning curve and while they were getting their butt kicked early on this did give them practice that they slowly implemented. In effect trading territory for “reduced” casualties. Compared to how bad they would have been clobbered if the tried to hold the liner harder the OTL. This is obviously exchanged for not getting surprised in this timeline. The question is which did more damage to the USSR the poor leadership needing time to find better officers or to at least get some learning in or the surprise? I tend to think it is a very minor advantage to the USSR to know ahead of time. But I think the poor leadership will mean that 90% of the advantages they get from not being surprised is tossed out the window by leadership that doesn’t know what it is doing. I suspect you will see more troops over run or surrender or otherwise forced to surrender as the order to not retreat will comedown and that there will be bigger battles sooner and closer to Germanies support system any anything that results in Germany have a shorter support line while still getting yo fight big battle vs the zuSSR is probably an improvement for Germany. Plus the war will be fought “faster” if the USSR is less inclined to pull back so the two don’t spend as much time traveling (retreating/advancing). So they are probably bigger battles sooner and more troops committed vs falling back so Germany by should able to kill more Russians faster. That being said it still ultimately sees Germany grind to a halt and it will see the USSR build enough troops and equipment and what have you to stop Germany so Germany will ultimately do better in terms of inflicting casualties on the USSR but they won’t get as far into the USSR. One thing I don’t know is if this fighting closer to the border will result in the German advance stoping before it gets so close that the USSR has to move its factories. Not moving a factory or two could make a big difference.

Again, as usual these scenarios entirely depend on one or both sides failing to react to changing circumstances. Firstly, USSR had information about possibility of German attack and was reacting. 'Stalin refused to believe the intelligence' is basically a myth. Soviet problem was not lack of the information or anyone's willingness or unwillingness 'to believe'. Soviet problem was lack of definitive information because everything that they had on Barbarossa was either utterly wrong, contaminated with enough false intelligence to make discerning what is true and what is not quite impossible or simply arrived too late for any sort of meaningful reaction. Secondly, USSR primary issue was that Germans at any point of preparation to Barbarossa were in position to speed these preparations up if they see an obvious Soviet reaction . And Germans were positioned to attack better than Soviets were positioned to defend. Let's say USSR starts mobilizing mid-April. Germany will not wait until June 22nd to attack because reality is not Hearts of Iron 4 game on a historical rails. Germans will simply attack in May before Soviet mobilization finishes. And yes, it could screw Mussolini by preventing Germany from bailing him out, but it was simple question of Germany already having mobilized army and having a better logistical infrastructure on their side of the border, so whatever obvious thing Soviets would do, Germans will have an opportunity to react. P.S. And no, Stalin will not give orders to pre-emptive attack against Germany for the very same reasons. Red Army was not in the position to attack anyone and everyone in Soviet leadership, including Stalin knew about that.

criteria.1-2: Misreads the premise, assumes a Soviet first strike, ignores the timing, or treats the leak as irrelevant or magical.
criteria.3-4: Acknowledges warning but gives vague or implausible Soviet reactions with little attention to Stalin’s prior skepticism or short lead time.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes that days or weeks of warning allow limited improvements but not full transformation of Soviet readiness.
criteria.7-8: Clearly distinguishes effects of different warning windows and explains why preparation is constrained by command, logistics, and politics.
criteria.9-10: Precisely handles the no-strike premise, credibility problem, Stalinist decision-making, and realistic limits on what can change before June 1941.

criteria.5-6: Covers plausible measures such as dispersing aircraft, alerting troops, evacuating supplies, or avoiding some encirclements.

criteria.9-10: Deeply integrates Soviet manpower, purges, command competence, rail logistics, mobilization timing, frontier deployments, and defensible fallback lines.

criteria.name: German operational constraints and adaptive response

criteria.7-8: Analyzes effects on key dynamics such as encirclements, pace of advance, supply strain, air losses, Minsk/Kiev/Smolensk/Moscow, and German redeployment choices.
criteria.9-10: Balances Wehrmacht tactical-operational competence against strategic overreach, showing how German plans might adapt and where they remain structurally vulnerable.

criteria.name: Long-range causal chain and downstream war outcomes

criteria.9-10: Builds a nuanced long-range scenario with contingent branches, showing how early Soviet improvements reshape but do not mechanically determine the entire war.

criteria.name: Uncertainty calibration, evidence use, and contradiction control
