criteria.9-10: Calibrates uncertainty exceptionally well, uses historically informed estimates, flags sensitive assumptions, and maintains causal consistency throughout.

items.model_answer:
If the USSR had received and acted on leaked intelligence about Operation Barbarossa just before the German invasion in June 1941, the Eastern Front would have unfolded quite differently. With Soviet forces on high alert, the catastrophic initial encirclements that saw millions of Red Army soldiers captured in the first months would likely have been reduced significantly. Soviet aircraft, dispersed and warned, would not have been destroyed en masse on the ground, preserving crucial air support. Defensive positions could have been prepared, and command structures activated rather than paralyzed by surprise.

The Wehrmacht's blitzkrieg, reliant on rapid breakthrough and encirclement, would have faced stiffer resistance from the outset. While Germany still held advantages in training and experience, the Soviet Union would have been able to conduct more organized fighting retreats rather than chaotic collapses. Moscow might never have been seriously threatened, and the front line might have stabilized further west, perhaps along the Dnieper River.

This better initial performance would have cascading effects: fewer Soviet casualties meant more experienced forces surviving to fight later, industrial evacuation would have proceeded under less desperate circumstances, and German losses would have mounted faster. The war in the East would likely have ended sooner, perhaps by 1943 or early 1944, with the Soviet Union emerging stronger and less devastated—potentially altering the postwar balance of power in Eastern Europe.

items.question: What If Modern Music without The Beatles and Elvis Presley.
human_answers: No Elvis will have minimal effect. Yes he was a popular Singer but he didn’t write anything. So the songs he is famous for will still exist. Will his lose have effects on music? Obviously. But it is not like music won’t more or less still evolve as it did. The lost of one singer is not going to have that drastic an effect there are simply to many of them. And as such someone else will slot in to become the “it” singer of that time. This is Not Like removing a given general from a given battle. In a battle the general has direct influence on the fighting. Swapping him out with someone else can have drastic effect. Who sings Hound Dog… not so much. Yes the song may or may not do worse at the charts and it may or may not have an impact on a company or a song writers career, But the removal of a singer is not effecting WW2. Singers and actors while obviously famous people in general are a dime a dozen! And pretty replaceable in most circumstances. Yes they have impact but is is hard to quantify. Yeah someone else singing a sang may mean that two people that loved that song and it formed the core of how they hooked up may not get it on in the back of a 1953 Chevy but… how the hell would anyone know that for certain? The impact of actors and singers and other people who are famous because they are famous has little impact if they are changed. You want an example of an impact from no Elvis? My uncle and his friend would not have had weekend gigs playing in the band of an Elvis impersonator. And I would have been able to stay home and avoid going to a really dull county fair that my folks dragged me to. And who knows I may have gotten farther with the pretty blonde next door sooner. But I doubt it. I know we have all heard of Elvis but he was simply not that important. I challenge you to tell me what he actually did that has a significance to history, or music. Yes a lot of folks imitated his style and his look and yes a lot of people bought his music. But if anything he had a negative knock on in music as his manager was an As$#@&*(. Of the first order and screwed many a song writers over big time. So there is a reasonable likelihood that some songwriters may have done better. Now the Beatles are a bit different. They wrote a LOT of music and some of that music had an impact on other writers. Once again the impact of them not being around has a knock on in pop culture in that you don’t get impersonator and it will effect in minor ways various individuals when they have to listen to different singers or whatever. But as with Elvis that has minimal influence on anything. And is almost impossible to document. But the lose of the songs that they wrote will have an effect on the evolution of music much more then not have an inspiration for singers shacking their hips. For example the Beach Boys will be effected as the album Pet Sounds was a direct response to some of the work the Beatles were doing. Writers have a more significant impact on music as they tend to influence each other a lot and it is simpler to replace the person singing any given song then the person that wrote it. Just look at how many people have success doing covers of songs. So the problem with this kind of post is twofold. One it is very very very hard to predict exactly what will change. For example will not having the song Dont Stop (thinking about tomorrow) influence the outcome one of the 1992 presidential election? Probably not. So you are dealing with things that are very nebulous. And if it just a singer that is even hard to say as it is possible that some unknown singer could get a break with the song instead. Elvis didn’t write his music so pretty much all his songs would be song by someone else if he disappeared. And the second problem with this kind of topic on this group is that there are a lot more people that know history and military stuff to a significant degree then know music. At least in the way that it will change. I probably know the words to 75% of the songs sung by Elvis and the Beatles but I don’t know who wrote most of Elvises songs nor who produced any songs for either of them. But I either know or have books that tell me who the major officers where at pretty much any major battle in the Civil War. And I know or can find out enough about most of them to have a good guess how swapping them will effect a given battle. But who can say what guy would have walked through the door and gotten the opportunity to perform if Elvis was gone. Frankly there are thousands of better singers in the world than Elvis that never got the chance. But the combination of his abilities and the opritunities he got made him a superstar. But it is impossible to know who would have gooten that chance if he was not there. But there are only a handful of people that may have been promoted if Montgomery got ran over by a tank.

I’m not saying that nothing would change. There absolutely would be changes from neither artist existing. It’s just that fundamentally: You still have popular music derived from Black American musical traditions. You still have a push away from large swing-style bands and towards smaller guitar-based bands - especially since before the digital era the guitar is the most accessible music instrument for young people wanting to make music. You still have the Baby Boom yielding a much larger youth cohort than before - thus yielding a significant generational divide by the early to mid 1960s as they’ve grown up having not known the struggles of their parents or older siblings - and have more room tackling lifestyle changes without worry for economic precarity. You still have big labels and radio stations wanting to play “different music” for “different races” so to speak. And with that you still have white singers becoming popular for their heavily sanitized covers of black R&B songs ( looks at Pat Boone ). You still have the post-WWII dominance and saturation of American pop culture - including music - in Europe and across the globe. And since the UK and the Commonwealth have virtually zero language barrier with the US - music that imitates American musical traditions (twice removed from Black American roots) has the potential to take off. You still have the advancements in recording technology that gave artists room to make more experimental and groundbreaking music than before. Plus the steady rise of FM radio later in the 1960s to provide a market for more ambitious music. You still have the Sexual Revolution to loosen norms around sex. On top of the various other drivers of the counterculture. You still have the payola scandal and the burnout of 1950s rock stars causing the 1959-64 dearth in the quality of pop music. But that’s just structurally speaking. Aesthetically speaking, things could be shifted around - with some new genre inspired by surf rock and garage rock (though realistically not actually either one of them) blowing up out of nowhere by 1964-65 - and Pat Boone is the King of Rock ‘n’ Roll all the artists of the 1960s are inspired by in terms of singing style and aura. While British rock bands are basically seen as a store brand that only gains later appreciation in the social media era decades later a la Japanese city pop. But it would still fundamentally fit the bigger variables that had been brewing years or even decades before the mid 1960s.

While the absence of the Beatles (and particularly Lennon and McCartney) would deprive us of some very good songs, there were vast numbers of competent bands in Britain that could have filled the niche if given the opportunity- whether together or singly. The bigger impact would probably have been on the penetration of British artists into the USA [1], but that's quite likely to happen eventually because there's money to be made from big crowds of relatively wealthy teenagers who happen to hit on a good enough band. The other impact might have been on the pressure to become singer-songwriters, rather than just singers/performers. Again, money is a big driver so it's likely to happen sooner or later. Otherwise, US innovation is likely to remain largely unchanged (Iggy and the Stooges will still form, and the drivers for hippy culture and rock bands is still there). Meanwhile, the Rolling Stones would still be experimenting with blues and quality musicians like Buddy Holly, Carl Perkins will be filling the niche that Elvis is no longer dominating. In short, different but still broadly recognisable. [1] The Monkees are unlikely to be formed, but songs like Day Dream Believer are too good not to end up being a success, even if it takes a few cover versions to become a real hit.

No Beatles or Elvis? Hmmm the amateur musicologist in me (that's what happens when you're a musician, who has also played in rock bands) says that rock 'n roll would still exist. The chances are also good that you would still have its superstar in the 50s - I read years ago that there were plans to push Carl Perkins (he of "Blue Suede Shoes" fame) towards superstardom by Sun Records. He might have actually become one if he hadn't suffered a major injury (he was in a car crash that kept him out of commission for a long time). Sam Phillips and even Elvis stated that Carl was doing rockabilly before Elvis, and unlike Elvis, Carl was also a songwriter. Most musicians will tell you that having that skill gives you much more staying power - you're not just a performer, you can make money off or songwriting royalties. By the time Carl recovered from the car crash it was too late, Elvis had overshadowed him. Jerry Lee Lewis, courtesy of his flamboyant personality might have become the 50s rock 'n roll superstar (how long he would have lasted would have depended upon whether or not he was still foolish enough to marry his underage cousin). The 60s? Hmmm that's not so certain - in the early 60s, rock 'n roll seemed to be on it's way out (or at least heading towards just being a niche genre of music). What rock 'n roll there was on Top 40 radio was mostly bland, and barely even qualified as rock 'n roll (Frankie Avalon anybody?). The Beach Boys were making songs with lame-o lyrics ("Be True to Your School", etc.). Even in Europe it was only doing so-so - I remember reading an interview of Jimmy Page (who along with playing guitar in Led Zeppelin, and the Yardbirds, was an in-demand session guitarist in the early and mid 60s), where he stated that in the early 60s, it was hard to even find rock 'n roll recording sessions to play on. Without the Beatles, rock'n roll might have just kept on being 50s-style teen hearthrob music performed by Cliff Richard, instrumental music played by bands like The Shadows (who also happened to be Cliff Richard's backing band), and possibly music played by 50s American rock 'n roll musicians, who were going nowhere in the USA with their careers (Bo Diddly, Eddie Cochran, etc. performed extensively in Europe in the early 60s when their careers fizzled out in the US). One of the big elements of the Beatles that helped to propel them to stardom IMO, was that for its time (the early 60s), the Beatles' music was considered HARD ROCK. As a result, it had more energy to it than your typical music of the period, and people liked it. The Stones? They were in their infancy, playing what is to me, watered down blues, that sounded nowhere near as intense. That hard rock edge the Beatles had is what kick started rock 'n roll again, and resulted in a million bands wanting to sound like them (even in the US, after they were on the Ed Sullivan Show). No Beatles and IMO, rock 'n roll continues its decline into a niche music genre, with the occasional Top 40 hit by bland groups like Gary Pucket and The Union Gap, Gary Lewis and The Playboys, etc. Not much in the way of edgy, interesting music. In the US, Link Wray never charts as high as he did with "Rumble" (which was actually banned by radio stations because it was "too threatening - it'll incite people to riot"), and Lonnie Mack at most has a few very modest hits like he had with "Wham".

Oh, for the love of Pete, not THIS again.... I just don't understand how some on this board can analyze military events down to the level of minutiae where they can argue that if a particular German general farted at a given moment in 1940, the entirety of World War II would come out differently, and yet at the same time assume that popular culture would remain essentially unaltered without the presence of two of its most important figures. Just as one example: before the Beatles, there was no such thing as a "British rock and roll group" in the eyes of Americans, and particularly American record companies, radio programmers, and concert promoters. Cliff Richard, who was Britain's biggest rock and roll superstar prior to the Beatles, went absolutely nowhere in America. Americans knew that rock and roll had originated in the U.S., and they were very parochial about it - the assumption, and it was not often wrong, before the Beatles was that anything coming from Britain would be a poor copy of records American teenagers already owned. (And it WAS teenagers almost exclusively who listened to rock and roll in 1963; projecting one's own current cultural dynamics into the past is part of the reason one gets lost). No British rock group - not one - had broken in the U.S. before 1964. The Beatles themselves at first were turned down by Capitol, the American division of EMI, who held their recording contract in the UK; Capitol refused to issue their first four singles in the U.S. It took the "Beatlemania" phenomenon to convince Capitol that it was worth giving the Beatles a shot, which enabled Beatlemania to cross the Atlantic. I'm sorry, but it's not as if "Holliemania" or "Dave Clark Fivemania" simply takes the place of that. There's a whole set of intangibles here. You can't just assume that you like the Rolling Stones better, so they automatically take the place of the Beatles. It would never have worked like that. What happens to the Rolling Stones becomes essentially undefinable. And that's just one example. I didn't even address the fact of no Elvis - which probably would have meant no Beatles AND virtually none of the other British Invasion acts either. Removing Elvis from the picture (which automatically would remove the Beatles as we know them) changes the ENTIRE trajectory of popular music from that day to this, in well-nigh unpredictable ways. Period.
items.original_question: What if Modern Music without The Beatles and Elvis Presley. American Singer and Actor Elvis Presley and British Rock Band The Beatles are the most Influential musicians in existence. With the former codifying Rockabilly and is credited for advancing the Feminist movement in America, and the Latter spearheaded the British Invasion, increased public interest in Psychedelic Drugs, Asian Spirituality and heralded the Album Era. Let's say both the musician and the Band never had any interest in music, preventing the codifying of Rockabilly and The British Invasion. How would this influence modern music?

rubrics.question_focus: What If Modern Music without The Beatles and Elvis Presley.

criteria.name: Counterfactual premise fidelity: removing Elvis and The Beatles without erasing broader preconditions
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer consistently reasons from the specific premise that Elvis Presley and The Beatles do not exist or do not become musical actors, while preserving the wider historical conditions that produced modern popular music.
criteria.1-2: Treats the premise inconsistently, erases unrelated history, or assumes modern music simply stops developing.
criteria.3-4: Acknowledges the absence of Elvis and The Beatles but makes broad unsupported changes to unrelated social, technological, or musical conditions.
criteria.5-6: Mostly preserves key background forces such as Black American musical roots, postwar youth culture, radio, labels, and recording technology, with some overreach.
criteria.7-8: Clearly separates the missing artists from continuing structural drivers and avoids most butterfly-effect exaggeration.
criteria.9-10: Precisely maintains the historical baseline except where causally affected, distinguishing performer loss, songwriter loss, market niches, and institutional continuity.

criteria.name: Mechanism coverage across musical, commercial, and social drivers
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer explains the main mechanisms by which Elvis and The Beatles did or did not shape modern music, including genre development, songwriting, performance, markets, technology, and youth culture.
criteria.1-2: Mentions only fame or personal taste with no causal mechanisms.
criteria.3-4: Covers one or two mechanisms, such as popularity or chart success, but neglects most music-industry and cultural drivers.
criteria.5-6: Discusses several relevant mechanisms, including rock and roll, British Invasion, singer-songwriters, or recording innovation, but unevenly.
criteria.7-8: Explains multiple interacting mechanisms: covers versus songwriting, Black R&B roots, guitar bands, labels, radio, youth markets, and studio experimentation.
criteria.9-10: Integrates performer, composer, producer, industry, technological, racial, transatlantic, and generational mechanisms into a coherent account of likely musical change.

criteria.name: Differentiation of Elvis’s and The Beatles’ causal roles
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer distinguishes Elvis Presley’s role as a performer and cultural popularizer from The Beatles’ role as songwriters, studio innovators, and catalysts for later rock and pop developments.
criteria.1-2: Treats Elvis and The Beatles as interchangeable celebrities or ignores one of them.
criteria.3-4: Notes that both were influential but gives little distinction between their types of influence.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes basic differences, such as Elvis popularizing rock and The Beatles writing songs, but does not trace implications far.
criteria.7-8: Explains why Elvis’s repertoire and image may be more replaceable while The Beatles’ compositions, albums, and British Invasion effects have deeper knock-on consequences.
criteria.9-10: Nuances both cases: Elvis’s racialized mainstreaming, performance style, and market role; The Beatles’ songwriting, album form, studio practice, peer competition, and global cultural signaling.

criteria.name: Long-range downstream coherence for modern music
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer plausibly traces consequences from the 1950s and 1960s through later genres, industry norms, and global pop without relying on disconnected speculation.
criteria.1-2: Provides scattered claims about later music with no causal chain.
criteria.3-4: Offers a simple linear story, such as one replacement artist changing everything, with weak links to later outcomes.
criteria.5-6: Identifies some plausible downstream effects, such as delayed British breakthrough, altered rock canon, or different singer-songwriter norms, but chains are incomplete.
criteria.7-8: Builds credible medium- and long-range chains linking substitute artists, genre niches, album culture, radio formats, counterculture, and later rock/pop evolution.
criteria.9-10: Presents a robust long-range scenario in which specific altered nodes are traced through later music while preserving broad continuity where structural forces dominate.

criteria.name: Uncertainty calibration and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer appropriately signals uncertainty in an open counterfactual, avoids overconfident exact predictions, and remains internally consistent.
criteria.1-2: Makes dogmatic predictions, contradicts itself, or invents precise outcomes without justification.
criteria.3-4: Uses some hedging but still asserts implausibly specific charts, elections, genres, or artists as certain.
criteria.5-6: Generally avoids certainty and acknowledges replacement effects, but contains some unsupported or inconsistent claims.
criteria.7-8: Clearly distinguishes likely structural continuities from speculative aesthetic changes and flags unknowable substitutions.
criteria.9-10: Carefully calibrates confidence throughout, presents alternatives where appropriate, and maintains strict consistency about what follows from the missing artists.

items.model_answer:
Without the Beatles and Elvis Presley, modern music would likely diverge into a landscape dominated by global folk traditions, jazz evolution, and regional electronic experimentation, largely missing the universal framework of rock and pop.

Elvis Presley served as the primary catalyst for rock and roll's cultural explosion, synthesizing rhythm and blues with country to create a mainstream phenomenon. Without him, Black rhythm and blues pioneers like Chuck Berry, Little Richard, and Fats Domino would still produce groundbreaking music, but their work would likely remain marginalized within segregated markets rather than breaking into mainstream white youth culture. The cultural bridge that ignited youth rebellion and the very concept of the "pop superstar" would be absent, delaying or entirely altering the cultural revolution of the 1950s and 1960s.

Without the Beatles, the evolution of recorded music and album-oriented rock would stall significantly. The Beatles transformed the LP from a commercial vessel for singles into a cohesive artistic statement, pioneered modern studio production techniques alongside producer George George Martin, and normalized the idea of a self-contained band writing its own material. In their absence, the 1960s musical landscape would likely be ruled by polished professional songwriters, session musicians, and solo vocalists. The concept of the "album" as an artistic journey would take decades to emerge, if it ever did at all.

The resulting musical world would be far more fragmented and genre-specific. Jazz and classical avant-garde movements would continue their intellectual trajectories, likely absorbing youth culture into more complex, improvisational forms rather than the accessible three-minute pop song. Synthesizer and electronic music development, freed from the guitar-centric paradigm of rock, might emerge earlier as the primary vehicle for sonic experimentation. Internationally, regional genres like Afrobeat, reggae, bossa nova, and various Asian folk-pop hybrids would develop without Western rock assimilation, creating a global music scene that is far less homogenized. Modern music would exist as a collection of distinct, localized traditions and intellectual art-music, lacking the shared global language of rock and roll that the Beatles and Elvis fundamentally built.

The cultural bridge that ignited youth rebellion and the very concept of the "pop superstar" would be absent,
delaying or entirely altering the cultural revolution of the 1950s and 1960s.
Without the Beatles, the evolution of recorded music and album-oriented rock would stall significantly.

pioneered modern studio production techniques alongside producer George George Martin,
and normalized the idea of a self-contained band writing its own material.
In their absence, the 1960s musical landscape would likely be ruled by polished professional songwriters, session musicians, and solo vocalists.
The concept of the "album" as an artistic journey would take decades to emerge,
if it ever did at all.
The resulting musical world would be far more fragmented and genre-specific.
Jazz and classical avant-garde movements would continue their intellectual trajectories,
likely absorbing youth culture into more complex, improvisational forms rather than the accessible three-minute pop song.
Synthesizer and electronic music development, freed from the guitar-centric paradigm of rock, might emerge earlier as the primary vehicle for sonic experimentation.
Internationally, regional genres like Afrobeat, reggae, bossa nova, and various Asian folk-pop hybrids would develop without Western rock assimilation,
creating a global music scene that is far less homogenized.
Modern music would exist as a collection of distinct, localized traditions and intellectual art-music,
lacking the shared global language of rock and roll that the Beatles and Elvis fundamentally built.

items.question: What If the Royal Navy had deployed carrier-capable Sea Beauforts and Sea Beaufighters from 1940 onward?
human_answers: Far too big Even with folding wings I don't think they would fit on the elevators and would take up too much room in the hanger even of they fit which again I suspect not Its landing on performance of he Beaufighter is about the same as an avenger (60 knots?) but its much heavier than the TBF so I am not sure the arrestor cables of the day could handle such a plane. Its a nice idea but its too much of a plane for the carriers of the day - might work on an Audacious class but not the carriers built in the late 30s. The Whispering Death is already doing sterling work as a land based anti shipping aircraft during the war and it has great range - not quite 'Rikko' (G3m and G4m Japanese bombers) range, but close too it, but still a scourge where ever it operated.

In the last thread on the subject I mentioned, given any wing-break would have to be somewhat outboard the engines*, that you could probably take one up and down on Implacable's forward lift but the hangar height would preclude you rolling it off. You could store one in Illustrious's hangar, if you made it from a kit of parts, as the lift is too narrow. So deck parks only. You could use some form of depressing oleos to lower the Beaufighter's resting angle. You might just scrape it into Implacable's hangar but clearances would be marginal. Any kind of seaway would make deck handling tricky to impossible. You could also only load a torpedo on the flight deck with the aircraft back up to full height. I also suggested an increased-chord rudder and handed props because the Beaufighter could be a handful with all the room in the world. Operating a Beau on/off of a carrier is an expensive way to give a pilot a coronary... ETA: The wing-breaks are going to be in the order of 25ft apart and Illustrious's elevators are only 22ft across. Folding the wings is also going to involve re-siting the cooling ducts from the outboard leading edge.
items.original_question: What if Sea Beaufort and Sea Beaufighters used on Royal Navy aircraft carriers? What if the Royal Navy used a possible Bristol Sea variant of both Beauforts and Beaufighters on their carriers starting in 1940 replacing Fairy Swordfish aircraft in the torpedo attack role for example? Would this be possible design wise? Would they be better than the bomb and torpedo attack aircraft available at the time? Would the aircraft actually be able to be used like this or would they be too large? How effective would they be if used on aircraft carriers? Regards

items.model_answer:
If the Royal Navy had deployed carrier-capable Sea Beauforts and Sea Beaufighters from 1940 onward, the Fleet Air Arm would have gained a dramatic leap in combat capability during the most critical years of the war.

The Sea Beaufort would have provided a modern, fast torpedo bomber to supplement and eventually replace the Fairey Swordfish, offering far greater speed, defensive armament, and survivability in strike roles against major warships. During the early war—particularly the Norwegian Campaign, the hunt for the Bismarck, and Mediterranean convoy operations—carrier air groups would have delivered far more lethal and resilient torpedo attacks rather than relying on slow, vulnerable biplanes.

The Sea Beaufighter would have been transformative as a carrier-based heavy fighter and strike aircraft. Its formidable armament of four 20mm cannon and six machine guns, combined with rugged construction and long range, would have given the FAA a genuine multi-role platform capable of fleet defense, anti-shipping strikes, and ground attack far earlier than historically possible. In the Mediterranean, Sea Beaufighters operating from carriers would have devastated Italian shipping and provided far superior air cover for Malta convoys. In the Indian Ocean and later the Pacific, they would have offered meaningful defense against Japanese land-based bombers and performed devastating anti-shipping sweeps.

Operationally, however, both aircraft were large twins, meaning carriers would carry fewer airframes and deck handling would be more cumbersome. The weight and size would have stressed escort carriers particularly, likely limiting deployment to fleet carriers. The engineering requirements for folding wings, arrester gear, and structural strengthening would also have diverted Bristol's design resources.

Strategically, a more capable FAA might have reduced British dependence on American carrier aircraft like the Corsair and Avenger later in the war, while potentially diminishing the urgency to develop dedicated naval designs like the Fairey Barracuda. The Royal Navy's carrier striking power would have been significantly enhanced during the war's leanest years, potentially altering outcomes in several naval campaigns where the FAA historically operated at a technological disadvantage.

edus.text: If the Royal Navy had deployed carrier-capable Sea Beauforts and Sea Beaufighters from 1940 onward,
the Fleet Air Arm would have gained a dramatic leap in combat capability during the most critical years of the war.
The Sea Beaufort would have provided a modern, fast torpedo bomber to supplement and eventually replace the Fairey Swordfish,
offering far greater speed, defensive armament, and survivability in strike roles against major warships.
During the early war—particularly the Norwegian Campaign, the hunt for the Bismarck, and Mediterranean convoy operations—
carrier air groups would have delivered far more lethal and resilient torpedo attacks
rather than relying on slow, vulnerable biplanes.
The Sea Beaufighter would have been transformative as a carrier-based heavy fighter and strike aircraft.
Its formidable armament of four 20mm cannon and six machine guns, combined with rugged construction and long range,
would have given the FAA a genuine multi-role platform capable of fleet defense, anti-shipping strikes, and ground attack
far earlier than historically possible.
In the Mediterranean,
Sea Beaufighters operating from carriers would have devastated Italian shipping
and provided far superior air cover for Malta convoys.
In the Indian Ocean and later the Pacific,
they would have offered meaningful defense against Japanese land-based bombers
and performed devastating anti-shipping sweeps.
Operationally, however, both aircraft were large twins,
meaning carriers would carry fewer airframes and deck handling would be more cumbersome.
The weight and size would have stressed escort carriers particularly,
likely limiting deployment to fleet carriers.
The engineering requirements for folding wings, arrester gear, and structural strengthening would also have diverted Bristol's design resources.
Strategically, a more capable FAA might have reduced British dependence on American carrier aircraft like the Corsair and Avenger later in the war,
while potentially diminishing the urgency to develop dedicated naval designs like the Fairey Barracuda.
The Royal Navy's carrier striking power would have been significantly enhanced during the war's leanest years,
potentially altering outcomes in several naval campaigns
where the FAA historically operated at a technological disadvantage.

items.question: What If : FDR picks a Segregationist VP in 1944
human_answers: The only Southerner who got any serious support at the DNC in 1944 was Alabama Senator John H. Bankhead II, who came in a distant third with 98 votes (8.33%) on the first ballot. The only other (non Alben W. Barkley) Southerners who got even one vote were: J. Melville Broughton (Governor of North Carolina), Prentice Cooper (Governor of Tennessee), Robert S. Kerr (Senator from Oklahoma), Herbert O'Conor (Governor of Maryland), Claude Pepper (Senator from Florida), Sam Rayburn (Speaker of the House), and Bascom N. Timmons (D.C. based newspaperman who grew up in Texas). Of these, only Bankhead II, Barkley, Broughton, Cooper, Kerr, and O’Conor got double digits. So your best case scenario is Roosevelt and/or the convention see a need to nominate a Southerner, and go with Bankhead II who IOTL died on June 12, 1946 following a stroke on May 24, 1946, which means you end up with three Presidents in little over a year. Based on the 1886 Succession Act, Bankhead II’s successor would be none other than… James F. Byrnes. IOTL, Truman appointed him in July of 1945, and it’s pretty likely Bankhead II does similarly, wanting to support a follow Southerner. (Prior to the Succession Act of 1947, neither the Speaker of the House nor the President pro tempore of the Senate were in the line of succession.) So in a roundabout way, you do end up with Byrnes as President…

Right. Byrnes thought he was Roosevelt's choice. Truman went to the DNC planning to make a nominating speech for Byrnes. If Byrnes does get the nod... FDR wins in 1944 anyway. But things diverge after that. IMO the Republicans sweep in 1946 as OTL. Byrnes was a very capable man and won't make any big missteps, so IMO he will be renominated in 1948. There may be a feeling that the 1948 nomination is a poisoned chalice, what with the 1946 GOP sweep and general public fatigue with 16 years of Democrat Presidents. The "Humphreyite" liberals may still try to push a civil rights plank at the DNC, but against Byrnes' at least tacit opposition will fail. They won't bolt to support Wallace overtly. Instead they may sit back to watch Byrnes crash and burn in November, while they regroup for 1952. Byrnes will lose a fair number of voters to Wallace outside the South. Also, AIUI, Dewey chose to soft-pedal civil rights OTL in the vain hope of winning some Upper South states with the Democrats divided. TTL that ignis fatuus isn't around, so Dewey probably emphasizes civil rights to draw the increasingly important black vote in the North and also some white liberals. This should be enough for Dewey to win. The next question is whether he has enough "coat tails" for Republicans to hold Congress. Another question is how the civil rights issue shapes across the next decade. OTL, leadership on the issue was taken by liberal non-Southern Democrats, with the low-key support of Republicans. The first cracks in the "Solid South" came in the 1950s, as a few white Southerners who could no longer rely on the national Democratic party to protect Jim Crow found they could vote Republican. If under Dewey, Republicans claim the leading role, that's not going to happen. The "Humphreyites" will gain control of the Democrats by 1952; there may be a Dixiecrat ticket that year. Dewey will be re-elected, barring some debacle in Korea or whatever. Warren won't be Chief Justice, but the Court will still be making rulings like Brown .
items.original_question: What if : FDR picks a Segregationist VP in 1944 In 1944, after intense pressure, President Franklin Delano Roosevelt would drop Vice President Henry Asgard Wallace from the ticket but due to his initial choice of James F. Byrnes being rejected due to his conversion from Catholicism, he would ultimately be convinced to go with Missouri Senator Harry S. Truman. Truman, as President, proved to be a liberal on racial issues and on labor rights, seeing as his SCOTUS Appointments sealed the deal on Brown v Board of Education being unanimous. However, what if ultimately, FDR went with a strict segregationist who was in favor of the New Deal at least early in their career? What happens when he becomes President and any ideas who this could be (one idea is Russell and another is Connally but both might say no to the offer)? Who do they appoint to SCOTUS instead of Burton and Vinson in 1945 and 1946 and Clark and Minton if they won a full term in 1948? What would 1948 look like in this TL? I suspect the southern president would probably appoint segregationist justices or lawyers to the court who make it through thanks to the Conservative Coalition being aligned on this one issue, though I admit I am unsure how they would handle the post war time frame, especially with 1945-1949. Furthermore, I could see a case for Dewey not being nominated ittl as in 1948 iotl, his nomination wasn't guaranteed but his wing of the party was able to get things to align with him by the convention. Here, with a more conservative leaning court and administration, the Republicans may pick a Conservative who can bring stability to both the party and the nation as long as it isn't Taft Sr. Also, I imagine the effects this has on American politics, specifically the civil rights movement, especially if Brown v Board goes the other way, if this has happened with perhaps more radical actions being taken and maybe an earlier Black Panther Party if things get really bad, but that's up in the air for the first decade of this period in time.

items.model_answer: If FDR had selected a segregationist running mate in 1944 instead of Harry Truman, the most immediate consequence would have been that this person would have become president upon FDR's death in April 1945, just months into his fourth term. A segregationist president would likely have opposed Truman's civil rights initiatives, including the desegregation of the armed forces in 1948 and the creation of the President's Committee on Civil Rights. The Democratic Party's internal divisions would have manifested differently—rather than Southern Dixiecrats bolting in 1948, Northern liberals might have fractured away or pushed for a third party. The civil rights movement would have faced a much less sympathetic federal government in its crucial early years, potentially delaying landmark developments by years or decades. Internationally, a segregationist president during the emerging Cold War would have provided the Soviet Union with potent propaganda about American hypocrisy on human rights, potentially undermining U.S. influence in decolonizing nations in Africa and Asia. The modern political realignment that saw African Americans shift firmly toward the Democratic Party and conservative whites eventually move toward the Republican Party would likely have been accelerated or altered significantly.

items.question: What If the Allies lose on the Salonica front?
human_answers: Alan Wakefield (IWM expert on Salonika, among other subjects) commented that most of the Bulgarian forces in September 1918 facing the British were well motivated, apart from the 1st Macedonian Bde that consisted of many men of Serbian origin. It was the collapse further west when the French & Serbian forces broke through three lines of defence, followed by the Greek breakthrough at Petit Couronne and Doiran Hill to the Bulgarian second line that unhinged the Bulgarian defences. Bulgarian C-in-C Todorov met with the German commanders von Steuben (German 11th Army) and von Reuter (Division Reuter) on 18 September, and agreed that Bulgarian 1st Army would be pulled back from positions east of the Vadar River, while the German 11th Army and Bulgarian 3rd Division would maintain contact. However the orders to 1st Army came as a severe blow to morale as the men were celebrating their stalling the British attacks, They started marching to Kosturino Pass but there was a serious shortage of draught animals, and of the survivors: " The majority of horses & oxen were absolutely unfit for work and they had need of at least six months rest in the interior, where they could be well nourished, Others had need of at least 45 days rest" - Major Nedeff, 9th Division, quoted in Under the Devil's Eye (Alan Wakefield & Simon Moody) from which much of the first three paragraphs are sourced. This was when the RAF caught the Bulgarian withdrawal through the passes, causing serious casualties & further delays. With foreign troops now on Bulgarian soil, political opposition to the war in the Sobranie was widespread. The PM, Malinov, was pro-western and had been appointed that June by Tsar Ferdinand with the purpose of proposing an armistice to the Allies, and on 26 September emissaries were sent through the lines to start discussions, although Franchet d'Esperey would only accept an unilateral unconditional armistice, which the Bugarian government then agreed to give, So it looks like the Bulgarian army was in generally good morale status until the final victories sparked by the French, Serbian & Greek forces, when the order of and losses taken on the retreat caused a final decline. But it looks like the home front collapsed first, if the Tsar was considering an armistice in June, so not sure what caused the domestic problems that drove the government to seek peace (I understand that a military rebelliion / mutiny at Radomir formulated by Bulgarian Agrarian National Union attempted to overthrow the government and establish a republic). Wiki suggests the following reasons: - Extreme war weariness, given Bulgaria had been at war since 1912 (short break 1914-15). Exhausted manpower (see #1 above) - I would add this resulted in dissatisfied minority groups supplying more troops, such as Macedonian Serbs & Greeks, diluting the Bulgar core. Both military & civilians suffering extreme food shortages (result of your point regarding harvests?). Troops poorly supplied - not only food but ammunition, clothing, boots, etc. Troops believing profiteers making hay at home at their expense. Feeling of betrayal by their allies, principally Germany, especialy regarding promised levels of supplies not being met, and lack of support for Bulgarian territorial ambitions at expense of Romania. Not sure how far the German troop levels had been reduced as you comment. The impact of the Russian Revolution. The impact of Woodrow Wilson's Fourteen Points (maybe a surrender would't be as bad as keep fighting) Recommended is 'The Enemy is Behind Us': The Morale Crisis in the Bulgarian Army during the Summer of 1918 - Richard C Hall, War in History Vol. 11 No. 4 which again refers to the collapse in morale starting by June 1918. Bulgarian C-in-C Nikola Zhekov reported to Tsar Ferdinand on 121 June that: "Today it is impossible ton have any illusions that the spirit of the soldiers is the same as at the beginning of the war, or even last year." I can't access as I don't have a school account! It does look like some units, such as the 9th (Pleven) Division, kept their high morale almost to the end. My main comment on demoralised forces would apply further north and primarily to the Austro-Hungarian troops who fell apart in October 1918, when I daresay no one suggests they were of high morale status. Earlier in the war that would not be the case, and I reckon me & a mountain goat could hold the Neretva Valley!

When you mentioned the Allies, I almost thought it was World War II. In reality, due to the division of Greece, neither the Entente nor the Central Powers could make any progress on the Thessaloniki front. Launching a large-scale offensive meant turning Greece into a battlefield, alienating more Greeks, and pushing more Greeks to the other side. The Entente was able to launch its offensive on the Macedonian front in 1917-1918 because the Entente countries had a large surplus of French reserves, willing to do everything except attack the Germans, such as conducting political work with the Greeks (Germany's reserves were smaller but more elite, and needed to do more important things; Bulgaria and the Ottomans were absolutely unacceptable to the Greeks). Ultimately, the deployment of hundreds of thousands of soldiers from the core countries of the Triple Entente only resulted in the defeat of one vassal state. The Central Powers could not accept this waste of reserves (unless Italy joined the Central Powers, providing some low ability soldiers). Even so, the problem of resource shortages must be taken into account.

It's my impression that it's something of a convention on this post 1900 forum to use "Entente" instead of "Allies", presumably to avoid confusion with the Allies of WW2. IMVHO I do prefer "Allies" for the WW1 military coalition because "Entente" is a derivation of the "Triple Entente" which applies to France/Russia/Britain, but by the end of WW1 the key great powers were Britain/France/Italy/America (and Russia was out) and there were multiple smaller allied powers. Why couldn't the Central Powers advance? Like, I thought Gallipoli ultimately failed because it was a trench-warfare stalemate; the Allies couldn't overcome a German client state. IIRC the proximal reason for the Gallipoli evacuation was that Bulgaria had joined the Central Powers, providing a route for German war material (not merely advisor personnel) like heavy siege artillery to be delivered to Turkey, which the Allies thought would be decisive. Was that assessment correct? Are you saying the Ottomans (with German support) could do something (push an Allied army into the sea) the Bulgarians (with their German support) could not? Or do you think that if the Allies had dug in on the Gallipoli peninsula in 1916, they might have obtained a stalemate which lasted until 1917/1918 when further offensives could be launched? I read that because of the potential futility of the front, Britain (and France) contemplated withdrawing their troops from mainland Greece before lines were solidified. Surely the Central Powers could have conquered Greece under those circumstances, no? I suppose in a grand strategy sense I recognize Germany was trying to fight a multi-front conflict against [the entire rest of the world] and was ultimately all but certain to lose the war. But in the narrower sense of "could the Balkan theater have played out differently", isn't it possible that the Central Powers could have achieved more success? Like, what if some resources from a different offensive (which surely would see less success than in OTL) devoted towards breaking through on the Macedonian front?

The allies couldn't overcome a German ally with more than 50 divisions and more than a million men on the field you mean, which in 1915 were about as well armed as their own troops. This is not 1942 in the Eastern front. But to get to the actual question in the fall of 1915 Greece was fully mobilized with 16 divisions and 325,000 troops in Macedonia and the Germans were doing their level best to keep Constantine in control and Greece out of the war. If they invade Greek territory you can kiss that neutrality goodbye and these 16 divisions just come into play added to the British and French divisions already landed in Salonica. And you'd better time it after the Serbs have been pushed into retreating into Albania, if your invasion comes before you just saved the lives of a couple hundred thousand Serbs. No. You essentially suggest Berlin says "to hell with the shenanigans to keep the Greeks neutral, let's invade them too. " So you just about gave numerical parity to the defenders... who don't have to move everything but food and fodder for the Macedonian and Turkish fronts though a single track railway going all the way back to Vienna. Before Dobro Polie and Desperate Frankie advancing all the way to Hungary and Austria putting the final nail in the Austro-Hungarian empire's coffin the actual front looked a pretty good deal to Berlin. Over 400,000 allied troops before the Greeks joined, that could be fighting elsewhere contained through mostly Bulgarian manpower... which could not be used elsewhere. Biggest POW camp in the world jokes and all that.

Well, Alternate History Challenge: An equivalent of Dobro Polie and subsequent desperate Frankie advances happen six months to a year earlier than OTL, *before* the Germans start getting pushed back on the western front, not after, and perhaps as a consequence, we get to see see the desperate Frankie international force *keep advancing* through the territory of capitulated Austria-Hungary, and over onto German territory from its southern and eastern borders (to Munich, Passau, Dresden, Gorlitz, Liegnitz or further to Cottbus or Berlin) before the Germans actually capitulate. Could this have ever happened in the right combination of circumstances? Could an earlier resolution of the Greek political divide in favor of the Venizelist side, committing the full Greek Army to the Entente side earlier, have helped with this? What might it take, faster French seduction? Or, going the opposite direction, more in line with what the OP wants, is there any way the Venizelist side could have been so marginalized that the Royalist side in Greece became willing to openly side with the Central Powers and openly welcomed/sought CP support in expelling Allied forces from Salonica and any other parts of Greece at any point during the war?
items.original_question: What if the Allies lose on the Salonica front? As I loosely understand it, the Salonica front was established after the Serbian army was routed. What if the Central Powers were able to continue advancing into Greece and expelled the Allies from the mainland Balkans? The Salonica front in some ways seems to resemble Gallipoli (an Allied lodgment supplied by sea) and the Central powers were able to prevail at Gallipoli, so it seems possible. The Allies also had to deal with the fact that the Greek government was divided - if the Central powers were more successful it seems possible Greece would have “switched sides”, or at least had a compliant government installed.

criteria.name: Counterfactual premise definition and historical anchoring
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer clearly defines what it means for the Allies/Entente to lose on the Salonica/Macedonian front and anchors the divergence in the real military, political, and logistical conditions of 1917-1918.
criteria.1-2: Treats the premise vaguely or anachronistically; confuses WWI with WWII or ignores the Salonica/Macedonian context.
criteria.3-4: Identifies the front but gives an unclear or implausible Allied defeat with little reference to real 1918 conditions.
criteria.5-6: Defines a plausible defeat, such as failed Entente offensive or withdrawal, with some correct historical anchors.
criteria.7-8: Specifies a credible point of divergence tied to Doiran, Vardar, Bulgarian morale, Greek participation, or Entente logistics.
criteria.9-10: Precisely frames the counterfactual, distinguishes limited tactical defeat from strategic collapse, and grounds it in documented constraints of the Macedonian front.

criteria.name: Causal fidelity to Balkan military mechanisms
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates how well the answer explains the military mechanisms by which an Allied loss could occur and what immediate effects it would have on Bulgaria, Greece, Serbia, and Central Powers operations.
criteria.1-2: Relies on unsupported claims of easy conquest or collapse; ignores terrain, supply, morale, and force composition.
criteria.3-4: Mentions military outcomes but with weak or inaccurate causal links, such as assuming Salonica alone decides the war instantly.
criteria.5-6: Addresses some relevant mechanisms, including defensive terrain, Bulgarian forces, Entente reserves, or Greek involvement.
criteria.7-8: Connects battlefield outcomes to Bulgarian morale, Serbian recovery, Greek politics, supply bottlenecks, and Central Powers priorities.
criteria.9-10: Provides a robust operational chain showing how Allied defeat affects withdrawals, lines of communication, Balkan armies, and feasibility of further Central Powers advances.

criteria.name: Integration of Bulgarian domestic collapse and alliance constraints
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer accounts for Bulgaria’s internal war weariness, food shortages, manpower exhaustion, mutiny risk, relations with Germany, and the limits these imposed even after an Allied defeat.
criteria.1-2: Portrays Bulgaria as either effortlessly triumphant or inevitably collapsing without explaining domestic conditions.
criteria.3-4: Mentions Bulgarian morale or politics only superficially and misses why Bulgaria sought an armistice historically.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes some domestic pressures such as shortages, war weariness, or agrarian unrest but underdevelops their implications.
criteria.7-8: Explains how an Allied defeat could delay or alter, but not automatically remove, Bulgaria’s morale and political crisis.
criteria.9-10: Carefully weighs military success against structural exhaustion, minority troop issues, Radomir-style unrest, Malinov’s policy, and German failure to meet Bulgarian expectations.

criteria.name: Long-range strategic consequences for World War I
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates the coherence and plausibility of the answer’s downstream chain from an Allied loss at Salonica to wider outcomes for the Central Powers, Austria-Hungary, the Ottoman Empire, Italy, Germany, and the 1918 armistices.
criteria.1-2: Jumps directly to sweeping conclusions such as Central Powers victory or unchanged history with no causal chain.
criteria.3-4: Gives a broad outcome but neglects key theaters or timing, especially the Western Front and Austria-Hungary’s collapse.
criteria.5-6: Discusses several downstream effects, such as delayed Bulgarian surrender or altered pressure on Austria-Hungary, with partial coherence.
criteria.7-8: Builds a plausible sequence linking the Balkan result to Serbia, Greece, Ottoman communications, Danube/Balkan security, and Germany’s worsening overall position.
criteria.9-10: Balances local Central Powers gains against decisive global constraints, showing how Salonica might delay or reshape armistices without overclaiming reversal of Germany’s strategic defeat.

criteria.name: Uncertainty calibration and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer distinguishes likely, possible, and unlikely outcomes, avoids internal contradictions, and handles ambiguous terms such as 'Allies lose' with appropriate caveats.
criteria.1-2: States speculative outcomes as certain, contradicts itself, or ignores the ambiguity of the premise.
criteria.3-4: Uses some caveats but still makes deterministic or mutually inconsistent claims.
criteria.5-6: Shows moderate uncertainty awareness and mostly avoids contradictions, though some assumptions remain unstated.
criteria.7-8: Clearly separates immediate, medium-term, and long-term probabilities and flags dependencies such as scale of defeat or German reinforcement levels.
criteria.9-10: Maintains consistent assumptions throughout, compares multiple plausible branches, and calibrates confidence in each major causal claim.

items.model_answer:
If the Allies had lost on the Salonica Front during World War I, the consequences would have been significant for the Balkans and potentially the broader war. Bulgaria would have remained in the conflict rather than becoming the first Central Power to surrender in September 1918, maintaining the southern flank of the Central Powers' alliance. The reconstituted Serbian Army would have suffered a second devastating defeat, effectively ending organized Serbian resistance and eliminating a key Allied partner in the region.

A Central Powers victory would likely have endangered Greece, potentially toppling Prime Minister Eleftherios Venizelos's pro-Allied government and bringing Greece under Central Powers influence. This would have given the Central Powers control of the Aegean coast and key ports, threatening Allied naval operations in the eastern Mediterranean and potentially providing supply routes to the Ottoman Empire.

items.question: What If the Curtiss P-40 had been designed around the Rolls-Royce Merlin engine?
human_answers: 1 - as noted by the fellow member, the P-40F and L used the Merlin 2 - it was a pretty simple upgrade 3 - engine itself does not require a laminar flow wing; a laminar flow wing will cut some drag, however, and thus allow for some speed increase 4 - historically, it offered some 30 mph over the P-40E at 18000 ft and above, IOW it was an improvement the P-40 badly needed 5 - P-51s used the better Merlins, these with 2-stage supercharger; a P-40 with such an engine would've probably be as fast as the Spitfire IX, but not as fast as the Merlin Mustang, nor as rangy - and thus the answer is 'no' 6 - as-is, the performance was better on the P-40F than on the ubiquitous P-40E; with 2-stage Merlin, it would've probably been good for 400+ mph, and much better rate of climb (the XP-40Q did 420+ mph with a 2-stage supercharged V-1710)

I'll have to take your word for it as I'm forbidden from your links but that sounds about right. A more advanced Merlin won't really help the P-40 though. There are availability issues with the Merlin, as ever, which historically forced Curtiss to revert to the V-1710-81 for the P-40M, despite more than half the production run going to the RAF. Not even every P-40F/L received a Merlin as some were completed as V-1710-81 engined P-40Rs. More though, there is the tale of the XP-60, which was a P-40D fuselage with a new laminar-flow wing. It was an improvement, with 387mph at 22,000ft. Modified as the XP-60D with an enlarged tail, it may or may not have received the V-1650-3 slated for it by the time of it's destruction in a crash on 6th May 1943. It certainly didn't perform any substantive testing with it. By that time the Merlin Mustang was established as superior in performance and was already entering production. The XP-60A with 1425hp V-1710-75, good for 420mph at 29,000ft, was part-cancelled in January 1942 (with the remainder following in June 1943) in favour of P-40Ks, Ls and P-47Gs. I think that is going to be the fate of any advanced or improved P-40 variant. Cancelled in favour of sustained production of known quantities.

items.model_answer:
If the Curtiss P-40 had been designed around the Rolls-Royce Merlin engine from the outset, the most transformative impact would have been dramatically improved high-altitude performance. The Allison V-1710's single-stage supercharger left the P-40 struggling above 15,000 feet, confining it largely to low- and medium-altitude roles. The Merlin's two-stage supercharger would have maintained power at altitude, giving the P-40 competitive performance against Luftwaffe fighters at heights where the actual aircraft was hopelessly outclassed.

This would have made the P-40 a far more effective fighter in the European theater, where air combat frequently occurred above 20,000 feet. The RAF, which operated P-40s as Tomahawks and Kittyhawks, would have received a genuinely competitive air superiority fighter rather than a stopgap best suited for ground attack and low-level combat. In North Africa and the Mediterranean, Merlin-equipped P-40s would have been more evenly matched against Bf 109s and Fiat G.55s across the altitude envelope.

The additional power at altitude—potentially 1,500+ horsepower in later Merlin variants versus the Allison's roughly 1,040 to 1,200 horsepower—would have improved climb rate and service ceiling, addressing two of the P-40's most critical deficiencies. However, the airframe's aerodynamics, particularly its relatively thick wing and drag-producing radiator scoop, would still have limited top speed compared to cleaner designs like the P-51 Mustang. The P-40 would have remained somewhat slower than a Merlin Mustang, as the P-51's laminar flow wing gave it lower drag.

Strategically, a Merlin-P-40 might have reduced the urgency to develop subsequent fighter designs, potentially slowing American fighter development. Curtiss might have continued refining the airframe rather than losing market position to North American and Republic. The aircraft would likely have remained in frontline service longer and in more demanding roles, though its fundamental airframe limitations would eventually have required replacement by more advanced designs regardless of engine.

edus.text: If the Curtiss P-40 had been designed around the Rolls-Royce Merlin engine from the outset,
the most transformative impact would have been dramatically improved high-altitude performance.
The Allison V-1710's single-stage supercharger left the P-40 struggling above 15,000 feet,
confining it largely to low- and medium-altitude roles.
The Merlin's two-stage supercharger would have maintained power at altitude,
giving the P-40 competitive performance against Luftwaffe fighters at heights
where the actual aircraft was hopelessly outclassed.
This would have made the P-40 a far more effective fighter in the European theater,
where air combat frequently occurred above 20,000 feet.
The RAF, which operated P-40s as Tomahawks and Kittyhawks,
would have received a genuinely competitive air superiority fighter
rather than a stopgap best suited for ground attack and low-level combat.
In North Africa and the Mediterranean,
Merlin-equipped P-40s would have been more evenly matched against Bf 109s and Fiat G.55s across the altitude envelope.
The additional power at altitude—potentially 1,500+ horsepower in later Merlin variants versus the Allison's roughly 1,040 to 1,200 horsepower—
would have improved climb rate and service ceiling,
addressing two of the P-40's most critical deficiencies.
However, the airframe's aerodynamics, particularly its relatively thick wing and drag-producing radiator scoop,
would still have limited top speed compared to cleaner designs like the P-51 Mustang.
The P-40 would have remained somewhat slower than a Merlin Mustang,
as the P-51's laminar flow wing gave it lower drag.
Strategically, a Merlin-P-40 might have reduced the urgency to develop subsequent fighter designs,
potentially slowing American fighter development.
Curtiss might have continued refining the airframe
rather than losing market position to North American and Republic.
The aircraft would likely have remained in frontline service longer and in more demanding roles,
though its fundamental airframe limitations would eventually have required replacement by more advanced designs regardless of engine.

items.question: PT-109: What If JFK Died on 7/2/43?
human_answers: It seems plausible to me that if Jack were to die in the Pacific, Sr would use connections to ensure that Jr would come home in one piece so that grooming for public office could begin. That said, I've read several accounts that suggest/indicate Jr was not as approachable/astute/able to think on his feet as well as Jack. That might make a political career more challenging: still feasible, but more challenging and quite possibly more costly (Sr might have had to write more and/or larger checks to make things happen?). I could see Jr with a House, and later a Senate seat. Then the question becomes: could he work his way into such a position that Adlai Stevenson might consider him as a running mate in 1956? Arguably, that propelled Jack into the limelight enough to become a presidential contender in 1960. My sense is that Jr would not get the same consideration ITTL that Jack did IOTL. Rather, he would plausibly have tried a presidential run having something like 8-10 years of Senate experience under his belt in 1960. We're talking a crowded field for the Dems in 1960: Lyndon Johnson, Hubert Humphrey, Jr, and the usual cast of favorite sons. Johnson might be the favorite, but not a prohibitive favorite: coming from Texas would assure that. Too manybut Lodge won northerners would be skeptical. On the other hand, Humphrey would definitely not play well in the south. Could Jr emerge as a compromise candidate? Maybe, but he'd be a tough sell in the south given his Catholic faith. My sense is that a protracted, multiple ballot convention would ultimately result in a Johnson nomination, with a middle of the road midwesterner (I'll yield to someone else here) as a VP candidate. Nixon will still be the GOP nominee, but Lodge won't be his running mate: don't need to counter a Kennedy. I suggest it would be MD governor Theodore McKeldin, a man who knew how to work with both sides (he was the last GOP mayor of Baltimore). McKeldin would bring a great deal more to the ticket than Lodge, but that's a pretty low bar. While we're at it, look for the 1960 campaign to be nasty. Lyndon Johnson had few scruples if any as far as that went, so I wouldn't be surprised if he started it. Then all Nixon has to do is take the high road and point out how well things have gone during Ike's tenure, and pump up his role (maybe this time Ike wouldn't make his famous "...if you give me a week..." remark?). And I don't see Richard Daley doing much to help Lyndon Johnson in Chicago, so IL might well flip to the GOP. Long story short: Nixon wins in '60. That leaves 1968 as Jr's next shot at the White House: he wouldn't try to unseat Nixon unless something totally unforeseen happened.

I once posted on another thread about a different pathway that Joe Jr's career would look like. IOTL JFK had the choice of running for Congress or for Lt. Governor of Massachusetts, and he chose to run for Congress in 1946. My alternate path for Joe Jr. had him running for Lt. Governor in 1946 and getting Statewide exposure, IOTL the Democratic ticket lost, but with Joe Sr's money the Democrats win. Joe Jr. runs for US Senate against Republican incumbent Leverett Saltonstall in 1948 and wins in a Democratic year. The main character flaw of Joe Jr. was his fierce loyalty to his father. There is a story about how Joe Sr. was on the Harvard baseball team and by playing on the Harvard-Yale game he would get a letter, but due to anti-Catholic bigotry, he was left on the bench and didn't get a letter. When Joe Jr. as a senior on the team, he was the first baseman and made the final put out of the Harvard-Yale game, and by tradition the ball is given to the team captain and Joe Jr. kept it himself and gave the ball to his father. How this would play out is uncertain, how far would he go in defending Joe Sr.'s isolation? JFK was able use his service to separate himself against any criticism against his father, but could Joe Jr. do that?

Both are possible, but I do think that Jor Sr trying to pull some strings would be more plausible (at least to me). But if Joe Jr still does his mission (maybe the dates between Jack's death and Joe's mission are too close), it could be that Robert gets chosen as the next. That being said... This was something I didn't think about, but from what I read it would make sense. Robert was always known as the black sheep of the family. If Ted was chosen by Joe Sr, he may very well have been thrown into Korea. The only question would be where Ted's future would go: He would have been far too young to run for President in 1960, but he could have won a seat as Senator in Massachusetts (although it would have been difficult). Maybe eight years later (say 1968), Ted might try to make his move, although 1972 might be more plausible.
items.original_question: PT-109: What if JFK Died on 7/2/43? In 1943, John F Kennedy's patrol boat PT-109 was rammed by the battleship Amagiri. After PT-109 exploded, JFK was able to survive, swimming from the wreck to a nearby island to stay alive while also saving his fellow soldiers. The moment cemented Jack as a war hero, and after his brother Joe died in a special mission, Jack was seen as next in line to join the Senate, before finally becoming President (which we all know how it ended). But what if things went slightly differently? Maybe Jack is closer to the blast and dies in the initial explosion. What next? What would happen to Joe Jr, and by extension, the Kennedy family? In our timeline, Joe Jr was killed in a special mission, but could the death of JFK stopped Joe Jr from going on the mission, and continue to stay alive to be the frontrunner of the family? Joe Jr had approved of Hitler, but his ideals could have easily morphed over time. Could Joe have done what Jack did and become President, and how would his presidency have looked? And if Joe Jr did in fact die anyway, who would replace him? Robert would have been far too young, along with Ted. Would the Kennedy family fade out of the limelight? What would become of the 1960 elections? The more obvious question, with Jack dead, who would be the man to lead the Democrats against Nixon? The most likely options are Hubert Humphrey, Lyndon Baines Johnson, and (although less likely), Adali Stevenson. Who would have been able to win the primaries, and could they have dealt with Nixon? With whoever becomes President, how would their Presidency look, and what could happen to them if they were also assassinated? For me personally, the most likely ticket would have been Johnson, causing him to be President.

items.model_answer:
If John F. Kennedy had died when PT-109 was rammed by a Japanese destroyer on August 2, 1943, the consequences would have rippled across decades of American history.

The most immediate impact would have been on the Kennedy family. Joseph P. Kennedy Sr. had already lost his eldest son Joe Jr. in 1944, and with Jack gone, the family's political ambitions would have shifted to Robert Kennedy as the likely standard-bearer, though Bobby was only 17 at the time and would have developed under very different circumstances.

The 1960 presidential election would have proceeded without Kennedy. The Democratic nomination likely would have gone to Lyndon Johnson, Stuart Symington, or Hubert Humphrey, with Richard Nixon potentially winning the general election against a different opponent.

The Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962 might have ended very differently under another president—possibly escalating to nuclear war if handled less cautiously, or being avoided entirely through different Cold War policies.

Civil rights legislation would likely have followed a different timeline without JFK's moral framing of the issue and the political momentum generated by his assassination.

The space program might not have received JFK's famous moon landing commitment, potentially slowing America's space achievements.

Robert Kennedy's political career would have unfolded without the shadow of his brother's martyrdom—he might never have become attorney general, senator, or presidential candidate, and his 1968 assassination might not have occurred.

The entire "Camelot" mythology that shaped American political culture and generational attitudes would simply not exist.
