edus.text: If a human continued to grow at the absolute linear rate of a one-month-old baby
gaining about 1 kilogram (2.2 pounds) and adding 4 to 5 centimeters (1.5 to 2 inches) in height every month
they would reach a staggering height of over 40 meters (130 feet) and weigh roughly 960 kilograms (2,100 pounds) by the age of 80
However, surviving this growth would be biologically impossible due to the square-cube law
which dictates that as a shape scales up, its volume increases at a much faster rate than its surface area
If you maintained the linear growth rate
your weight would not scale proportionately with your height
a 130-foot-tall person weighing only 2,100 pounds would be impossibly emaciated
lacking the structural mass to hold themselves together
On the other hand, if you maintained the infant's physical proportions as you grew to that height
your weight would scale by the cube of your height
resulting in a mass of nearly 2,000 metric tons
At that scale, your bones would instantly shatter under your own weight
and your muscles would be entirely unable to move your mass
Beyond structural collapse, your internal systems would fail almost immediately
The human heart relies on relatively short distances to pump blood
extending the circulatory system to 130 feet would require a heart capable of generating immense pressure to push blood all the way up to the brain against gravity
A normal human heart would fail instantly
resulting in blood pooling in the lower extremities and the brain starving of oxygen
Additionally, a proportionally scaled human would generate so much internal metabolic heat
that the relatively smaller surface area of the skin could not dissipate it fast enough
causing the body to literally cook from the inside out
If you interpret the growth rate as the compounding percentage of a one-month-old
where a baby gains roughly 25 to 30 percent of its body weight in a single month
the outcome is even more catastrophic
A 30 percent monthly compounding increase would cause your mass to multiply by a factor of over 10 billion within a decade
You would quickly become an immobile, collapsing sphere of flesh
eventually generating enough gravity to crush your own internal organs
In any interpretation, keeping the rapid growth rate of a one-month-old would result in swift structural failure, cardiovascular collapse, and fatal overheating long before reaching adulthood

items.question: What If a Tyrannosaurus Rex Were Released in New York City?
human_answers: About half of an adult, or one ten-year old child: [Image: image] Tyrannosaurus rex weighed about as much as an elephant.[1]This always seemed a little off to me; my mental image of elephants is that they're in the same size range as cars or trucks, whereas T-rex, as Jurassic Park showed, is big enough to stomp on cars. But a Google image search for car+elephant (https://www.google.com/search?tbm=isch&q=elephant+car) shows elephants looming over cars just like the T-rex in Jurassic Park. So, great, now I'm also afraid of elephants. [Image: image] No one is totally sure what dinosaur metabolism looked like, but the best guesses for how much food T-rex ate seem to cluster around 40,000 calories per day.[2]Food calories (kcal). Sources: This (http://www.pnas.org/content/106/29/12184.full) and this (http://palaeo-electronica.org/1999_2/gigan/issue2_99.htm), and this (http://www.jstor.org/discover/10.2307/2666002) with some notes from this (http://www.plosone.org/article/info%3Adoi%2F10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0026037) and distraction from this (http://regex.alf.nu/). If we assume dinosaurs had metabolisms similar to today's mammals, they'd eat a lot more than 40,000 calories each day. But the current thinking is that while dinosaurs were more active (loosely speaking, "warm-blooded") than modern snakes and lizards, very large dinosaurs probably had metabolisms that more closely resembled komodo dragons than elephants and tigers.[3]For big sauropods, we know this must be the case, because otherwise they would overheat. However, there's a lot of uncertainty surrounding T-rex-sized dinosaurs. Next, we need to know how many calories are in a human. This number is helpfully provided, by Dinosaur Comics author Ryan North, on this wonderful t-shirt (http://www.topatoco.com/merchant.mvc?Screen=PROD&Store_Code=TO&Product_Code=QW-PERSON&Category_Code=QW). Ryan's shirt tells us that an 80-kg human contains about 110,000 calories of energy. Therefore, a T-rex would need to consume a human every two days or so.[4]Although a T-rex would likely be willing to eat several days to weeks worth of food in one meal, so if it has the option, it might eat a bunch of people at a time, then go for a while without eating. The city of New York had 239,736 births in 2011, which could support a population of about 1,000 tyrannosaurs. However, this ignores immigration—and, more importantly, emigration, which would probably increase substantially in this scenario. [Image: image] The 33,000 McDonald's restaurants worldwide sell something like 15 billion hamburger patties per year,[5]They stopped reporting the "x billions served" number on their signs, but this website (http://overhowmanybillionserved.blogspot.com/) has some extrapolations. for an average of 1,245 burgers per restaurant per day. 1,245 burgers is about 600,000 calories, which means that each T-rex only needs about 80 hamburgers per day to survive, and one McDonald's could support over a dozen tyrannosaurs on hamburgers alone. [Image: image] Ands if you live in New York, and you see a T-rex, don't worry. You don't have to choose a friend to sacrifice; just order 80 burgers instead. And then if the T-rex goes for your friend anyway, hey, you have 80 burgers. [Image: image]

criteria.3-4: Uses the premise but relies on cinematic assumptions; includes several inaccurate claims about size, speed, diet, or behavior.
criteria.5-6: Mostly plausible biology and setting; some oversimplifications or unsupported assumptions remain.
criteria.7-8: Grounds the scenario in reasonable estimates of mass, food needs, movement, predation, and stress responses.
criteria.9-10: Carefully applies uncertain but evidence-based T. rex biology to the exact NYC release scenario without sensationalism.

criteria.name: Mechanism Coverage of Immediate Urban Interactions
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates coverage of the direct mechanisms by which a T. rex would interact with New York City: streets, crowds, vehicles, buildings, transit systems, noise, barriers, police response, and animal-control logistics.
criteria.1-2: Gives only vague destruction or panic with no concrete urban mechanisms.
criteria.3-4: Mentions a few effects such as traffic or panic but lacks causal detail.
criteria.5-6: Covers several immediate interactions, including people, vehicles, and emergency services, with moderate detail.
criteria.7-8: Explains how NYC infrastructure, congestion, visibility, barriers, and responders would shape the event.
criteria.9-10: Provides a rich, mechanically coherent account of the first minutes to hours across crowds, transport, buildings, and containment.

criteria.name: Long-Range Causal Chain Coherence
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer traces coherent downstream effects beyond the initial release, including containment, casualties, public behavior, institutional response, media, legal consequences, scientific interest, and city recovery.
criteria.1-2: Stops at the initial encounter or gives disconnected consequences.
criteria.3-4: Includes some later effects but with weak sequencing or missing causes.
criteria.5-6: Presents a plausible short-to-medium-term chain but omits major downstream domains.
criteria.7-8: Links immediate events to longer-term emergency, political, economic, scientific, and social consequences.
criteria.9-10: Builds a well-sequenced long-range scenario from release through containment and aftermath with minimal causal gaps.

criteria.name: Food, Energy, and Survival Reasoning
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer plausibly estimates or qualitatively reasons about the T. rex's caloric needs, feeding opportunities, prey availability, scavenging, zoo/livestock/human food sources, and whether it could survive in NYC.
criteria.1-2: Ignores food needs or makes absurd claims about constant mass killing or starvation.
criteria.3-4: Mentions eating people or animals but gives little metabolic or availability reasoning.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes large but finite food requirements and identifies plausible food sources.
criteria.7-8: Uses reasonable quantitative or comparative estimates and connects them to NYC food systems and human behavior.
criteria.9-10: Carefully analyzes survival using calibrated caloric needs, feeding intervals, available food, and containment timescale.

criteria.name: Uncertainty Calibration and Contradiction Control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer distinguishes knowns from uncertainties, avoids internal contradictions, and resists overconfident claims about extinct-animal behavior, emergency outcomes, or exact casualty counts.
criteria.1-2: Highly overconfident, contradictory, or internally inconsistent.
criteria.3-4: Some uncertainty is acknowledged, but key claims conflict or are asserted without support.
criteria.5-6: Mostly consistent; notes a few uncertainties but still overstates some outcomes.
criteria.7-8: Clearly flags uncertain areas such as T. rex behavior, response time, and casualties while keeping the scenario consistent.
criteria.9-10: Maintains tight internal consistency and well-calibrated uncertainty across biological, logistical, and social consequences.

items.model_answer:
If a Tyrannosaurus Rex were released in New York City, the immediate aftermath would be chaos and panic. A T. Rex stood roughly 12-13 feet tall at the hip, measured about 40 feet long, and weighed 6-9 tons—an enormous animal that could easily crush vehicles, knock down streetlights, and batter through storefronts. Its presence on crowded streets or in areas like Times Square or Central Park would trigger mass stampedes, likely causing more immediate injuries from human panic than from the animal itself.

The dinosaur would be profoundly disoriented. Modern noise, smells, and concrete surfaces would be alien to a creature adapted to Cretaceous floodplains and forests. It might initially freeze, flee, or lash out defensively. Hunger could eventually drive it to hunt, but modern humans are far smaller than its typical prey, and urban environments offer little that would satisfy its dietary needs.

Authorities would respond rapidly. NYPD and emergency services would evacuate nearby zones, while National Guard or military units would likely be mobilized. Modern firearms, including high-caliber rifles and tactical weapons, would be effective against even a large animal. A T. Rex has no experience with projectiles or coordinated human threats, making it highly vulnerable. Animal control experts and veterinarians might advocate for sedation if containment were feasible, but given the extreme danger, lethal force would probably be authorized quickly.

Within hours to a day, the animal would almost certainly be killed or sedated. Its survival prospects in a modern metropolis are essentially zero—between armed response, lack of appropriate food, stress, and the sheer incompatibility of a Cretaceous predator with 21st-century infrastructure, the episode would be brief, terrifying, and tragic for both the city and the dinosaur.

human_answers: Weak, bordering on homeopathic. The standard cup of tea, as described by the International Organization for Standardization in ISO 3103 (http://www.iso.org/iso/catalogue_detail.htm?csnumber=8250), contains two grams of tea per 100 mL of water.[1]Further ISO standards concerning tea include ISO 3720 (http://www.iso.org/iso/catalogue_detail.htm?csnumber=51541) (black tea), ISO 11287 (http://www.iso.org/iso/catalogue_detail.htm?csnumber=51540) (green tea), and ISO 14502-2 (http://www.iso.org/iso/iso_catalogue/catalogue_tc/catalogue_detail.htm?csnumber=31357) (the difference between black tea and green tea). The Great Lakes have a volume of about 22,600 cubic kilometers, which means we would need about 450 billion tons of tea to reach proper strength. According to the Tea Board of India, one year's global tea harvest totals only about 4.8 million tons,[2]Using figures from this report (http://www.teaboard.gov.in/pdf/Tea%20Statistics%20Global%20Scenario.pdf) extrapolated forward to 2014. only 1/100,000th of what we'd require to make Great Lake Tea. If we dumped those 4.8 million tons into the lakes, the resulting tea would be about as strong as if we'd dripped two drops of tea in a bathtub.[3]Technically, calling this kind of tea "homeopathic" is an exaggeration, since substances in homeopathy are diluted way more than this. Proper bathtub tea, of course, requires one 3-kg bag. [Image: image] For better lake tea, we should find a lake with a volume of 240 million cubic meters (0.24 cubic kilometers). Wular Lake in Kashmir is one candidate. Its volume varies with the seasons, but during the winter it's just about exactly the right size.[4]Unfortunately, it's shrinking (http://www.ramsar.org/pdf/wurc/wurc_mgtplan_india_wular.pdf). (For winter volume, see the chart on page 18 of that report.) India is the world's second-largest tea producer, so it's also conveniently located. Ullswater, in the UK's Lake District, is another great candidate. With a relatively stable year-round volume of about 0.23 cubic kilometers, it would be an excellent site for brewing a global cup of tea. Of course, while neither Wular Lake or Ullswater has ever been used as a giant teakettle, something like this was—famously—attempted in my own backyard in Boston. In 1773, a group of colonists disguised as American Indians[5]They dressed up as American Indians to align themselves politically with the Americas—against Britain—invoking the popular European stereotype of the free and noble savage. The Mohawk people, the actual Indians who the protesters were mimicking, mistrusted the settlers encroaching on their land, sided with the British during the subsequent war, and afterward were driven from their homes by the Americans and fled to Canada. boarded three British ships and threw the cargo of tea—around 44 tons of it—into Boston Harbor to protest British-run tax policy. Boston Harbor has a volume of about 0.44 cubic kilometers, which means that the "tea" brewed in 1773 would have been even more dilute than our Great Lakes tea. The harbor is also somewhat larger[6]The tidal range in Boston is so large (over three meters) that the harbor's volume at high tide is nearly double what it is at low. than Wular Lake or Ullswater, so all the tea in the world would still make Boston Harbor slightly too weak. [Image: image] There's another problem: Heat. If you wanted to make tea from a lake, such as Ullswater or Wular Lake, you'd have to heat the water up. Is that even possible? There's clearly enough stored energy in the world to do it. After all, we presumably heat that amount of water for tea every year already; we just do it in small batches around the world. To heat up Ullswater to 80°C[7]Lots of people have very strong opinions on what this temperature should be. Please direct any corrections on this matter to What-If Tea-Related Complaints Dep't, c/o Her Majesty The Queen, Buckingham Palace, London SW1A 1AA. would take \(6.6 \times 10^{16}\) joules of energy—about 20 days worth of British electricity consumption. which is roughly what would be released if you dropped a water bottle full of antimatter in the lake. [Image: image] Asking Britain to go without electricity for 20 days just to fill one of their lakes with tea seems like it might be a hard sell. Fortunately, there's an easier solution. Boiling Lake in Dominica is a volcanic lake about 60 meters across. Its temperature varies, but it's often near boiling at the edges and vigorously boiling in the center. Measuring the depth of the lake is difficult, so it's hard to get an estimate of the total volume. [Image: image] Frying Pan Lake in New Zealand, on the other hand, is the largest hot lake in the world. It has a volume of about 200,000 m3, and an average temperature of around 50°C—not quite hot enough for tea, but much closer than Ullswater or Wular Lake. New Zealanders consume about 600 grams of tea per person,[8]Kerryn Pollock. 'Tea, coffee and soft drinks (http://www.teara.govt.nz/en/tea-coffee-and-soft-drinks)', Te Ara - the Encyclopedia of New Zealand, updated 15-Jul-13 for a total of 2,700 tons of tea. If they waited until Frying Pan Lake got particularly hot, then dunked it all in at once ... [Image: image] ... they could brew a year's worth of tea in minutes.

criteria.name: Dilution and Scale Quantification
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer correctly estimates how dilute the Great Lakes tea would be by comparing world tea production to the volume of the Great Lakes and to normal tea-brewing concentrations.
criteria.1-2: Gives no meaningful quantitative comparison or falsely implies the lakes would become strong drinkable tea.
criteria.3-4: Mentions dilution but with missing, vague, or severely incorrect scale estimates.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes extreme dilution and gives some plausible numbers, but omits either lake volume, tea mass, or normal tea concentration.
criteria.7-8: Uses reasonable estimates for Great Lakes volume, global tea production, and tea strength to show the result is extremely weak.
criteria.9-10: Accurately connects all key scales, including about 22,600 km³ of water, millions of tons of annual tea versus hundreds of billions of tons needed, and a near-homeopathic-strength conclusion.

criteria.name: Physical and Chemical Mechanism Coverage
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer explains the physical processes involved in dumping tea into the Great Lakes, including extraction, mixing, temperature, solubility, and particulate behavior.
criteria.1-2: Treats the event as magical or instantaneous without relevant physical mechanisms.
criteria.3-4: Mentions one mechanism such as mixing or weak flavor but ignores most physical constraints.
criteria.5-6: Covers dilution and some mixing or extraction issues, but gives limited treatment of heat, steeping efficiency, or solids.
criteria.7-8: Explains that cold lake water would extract poorly, tea would disperse unevenly at first, and solids would float, sink, or wash ashore.
criteria.9-10: Integrates dilution, cold extraction limits, lake circulation timescales, suspended organic matter, tannins/caffeine release, sedimentation, and shoreline accumulation into a coherent mechanism.

criteria.name: Ecological and Environmental Downstream Effects
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer plausibly reasons through biological and environmental consequences of adding all global tea to the Great Lakes.
criteria.1-2: Ignores environmental consequences or makes unsupported catastrophic claims.
criteria.3-4: Mentions pollution or harm in generic terms without connecting to tea composition or lake ecology.
criteria.5-6: Identifies some plausible impacts, such as organic loading or caffeine, but lacks depth or scale calibration.
criteria.7-8: Discusses likely localized or temporary effects from organic matter, decomposition, oxygen demand, tannins, nutrients, and cleanup burden while noting dilution limits.
criteria.9-10: Carefully distinguishes chemical dilution from solid biomass impacts, addresses oxygen depletion risks, microbial decomposition, shoreline smothering, invasive/pathogen concerns, water treatment effects, and spatial heterogeneity.

criteria.name: Long-Range Causal Chain Coherence
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer follows consequences over time from the initial dump through mixing, ecological response, human response, and eventual dissipation without skipping or reversing causal steps.
criteria.1-2: Presents disconnected claims with no temporal or causal structure.
criteria.3-4: Has a basic sequence but includes major causal gaps or implausible jumps.
criteria.5-6: Provides a mostly sensible short-term chain but weakly handles medium- or long-term consequences.
criteria.7-8: Tracks immediate dumping, partial extraction, dispersal, environmental response, cleanup, water-use disruptions, and gradual degradation/flushing.
criteria.9-10: Builds a robust multi-timescale chain from hours to years, including uneven initial concentrations, basin circulation, biological decay, sediment burial, outflow through the St. Lawrence, monitoring, and policy/public health responses.

criteria.name: Uncertainty Calibration and Contradiction Control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer states assumptions, handles uncertainty in estimates, and avoids contradictions with the counterfactual premise and known facts.
criteria.1-2: Contains major contradictions, impossible claims, or overconfident unsupported assertions.
criteria.3-4: Shows some awareness of uncertainty but relies on inconsistent numbers or conflicting conclusions.
criteria.5-6: States a few assumptions and avoids obvious contradictions, but confidence and estimates are uneven.
criteria.7-8: Clearly distinguishes annual world tea production versus all existing tea if relevant, notes estimate sensitivity, and keeps conclusions consistent with extreme dilution.
criteria.9-10: Explicitly calibrates uncertainties in tea mass, lake volume, extraction temperature, mixing, and ecological thresholds while maintaining internally consistent quantitative and causal reasoning throughout.

items.model_answer:
If you dumped all the world's tea into the Great Lakes, you would not get a giant basin of iced tea. The global annual tea production is roughly 7 million metric tons, while the Great Lakes hold about 22,671 cubic kilometers of water. When distributed across that massive volume, the concentration of tea would be roughly 0.3 milligrams per liter. A standard cup of tea requires about 2 to 3 grams of tea per 250 milliliters, meaning the lakes would be about 30,000 times weaker than a properly brewed cup. The water would not change color, and you would not be able to taste it. 

However, the ecological impact would be significant. Dumping 7 million tons of dry organic matter into the lakes would create massive floating mats of soggy leaves that would block sunlight from reaching aquatic plants and clog municipal water intake systems. The real danger would come from decomposition. As bacteria and fungi broke down the tea leaves, they would consume vast amounts of dissolved oxygen in the water. While the sheer volume of the Great Lakes means the entire system would not be depleted of oxygen, the localized areas where the tea was dumped would suffer severe hypoxia. These suffocating dead zones would kill off fish and other aquatic life. Additionally, the tannins released from the tea, while too dilute to be toxic on a lake-wide scale, would concentrate in these rotting mats, further altering the local water chemistry. Ultimately, the world's entire tea supply is simply too small to brew the Great Lakes, but it is more than enough organic matter to cause a localized ecological disaster through decomposition.

items.question: What If All the World's Viruses Were Gathered in One Place?
human_answers: It would be a huge pile, but human viruses would make up only a tiny fraction of it. HIV, the virus that causes AIDS, has killed tens of millions of people worldwide, and over 30 million people are currently living with HIV. The number of copies of the virus carried in someone's blood can vary dramatically,[1]Data on viral load—the number of copies of the virus per mL of blood—can be found in this paper (http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23196933). but across all the people in the world, there probably exists about a spoonful worth of HIV. [Image: image] The typical healthy human body contains about \(3 \times 10^{12}\) viruses. This is actually not as many as you might expect; by volume, humans are apparently a less friendly environment for viruses than, say, soil.[2]An area of wetlands in Delaware (http://www.rcn.montana.edu/pubs/pdf/2008/Srinivasiah%20Res%20%20Micro%202008.pdf) contains something like four billion viruses per mL of soil, in case you were looking for a fun vacation destination. If you gathered together all the viruses in all the humans in the world, they would fill about ten oil drums: [Image: image] These 10 barrels only represent a tiny portion of the global virus community. Most of the world's viruses aren't found in humans. They're found in the sea. Seawater is full of microorganisms, and we've recently learned that those microorganisms are preyed on by viruses in a big way. Every day, about one in five living cells in the ocean is killed by a virus.[3]Marine viruses—major players in the global ecosystem (https://www.uni-due.de/imperia/md/content/water-science/ws0910/2031b_02z_ws0910_suttle_marine_viruses.pdf) These viruses are found from the surface of the ocean down to the depths.[4]Oddly, as you go further offshore and further down, the concentration of viruses doesn't decrease as much as the concentration of bacteria, so the virus-to-bacteria ratio is higher in the deep oceans than near the shore. Because the sea is so big,[5]Citation: Go and look at the sea. It's big. it contains a staggering number of viruses. If you piled up all these viruses—more than 1030 of them—in one place, they would be the size of a small mountain. [Image: image] It's hard to say exactly what the virus mountain would look like, but it would probably resemble something in between pus and meat slurry.[6]Blame Dave—he's the one who asked. Regardless of its exact appearance, it would almost certainly be disgusting. [Image: image] The pile wouldn't stay mountain-shaped for long, any more than a mountain of any organic secretion would.[7]If you don't believe me, try building a mountain of earwax or snot. You'll find you can't make it higher than a few inches before your friends and family show up and sit you down for a talk. To avoid a gigantic flood, it might be better to collect them into some kind of container. MetLife Stadium, host of Super Bowl XLVIII, has a volume of about 1.5 million cubic meters. Earth's viruses could fill the stadium about 150 times over. So if you watch the Super Bowl, take a moment to picture all the players floating, suspended, in a sea of yellowish-white secretions. [Image: image] Enjoy the game!

criteria.name: Scale and Source Attribution of the Virus Pile
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer correctly reasons about the quantity, volume, and dominant sources of all viruses on Earth under the gathering premise.
criteria.1-2: Gives wildly incorrect scale claims, such as saying the pile is microscopic, planet-sized, or mostly human viruses.
criteria.3-4: Recognizes viruses are numerous but gives vague or materially wrong estimates and misses that humans contribute only a tiny fraction.
criteria.5-6: Identifies that most viruses are environmental, especially marine, and gives a broadly large but imprecise pile size.
criteria.7-8: Uses reasonable order-of-magnitude reasoning, noting around 10^30 viruses and a pile comparable to a small mountain or many stadium volumes.
criteria.9-10: Clearly distinguishes human, soil, and ocean contributions, keeps estimates order-of-magnitude plausible, and avoids false precision.

criteria.name: Physical Consequences of Gathering Viruses in One Place
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer plausibly models what the gathered viruses would physically be like and how the mass would behave.
criteria.1-2: Treats viruses as magical, gaseous, glowing, or self-organizing matter with no physical constraints.
criteria.3-4: Mentions a pile but gives implausible physical behavior, such as a stable sharp mountain or a solid block without justification.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes the gathered material would be a large biological slurry and would not retain a tall pile shape for long.
criteria.7-8: Explains that water, organic material, capsids, and host-associated residues would form a disgusting fluid or paste needing containment.
criteria.9-10: Connects volume, density, fluid collapse, containment needs, decomposition, and environmental exposure in a physically coherent way.

criteria.name: Virology and Infectious-Risk Mechanisms
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer accurately reasons about infectivity, host specificity, and disease risk from concentrating all viruses.
criteria.1-2: Claims all viruses would instantly merge, become one supervirus, or infect every organism indiscriminately.
criteria.3-4: Overstates pandemic risk while ignoring host specificity, viability limits, and the need for susceptible hosts.
criteria.5-6: Notes that many viruses would not infect humans, though some concentrated pathogens would pose local hazards.
criteria.7-8: Explains host range, environmental decay, dose, exposure routes, and the difference between virions being present and causing infection.
criteria.9-10: Balances severe local biosafety danger with rejection of universal-contagion claims, including bacteriophages, plant viruses, animal viruses, and human pathogens.

criteria.name: Long-Range Ecological and Biological Downstream Effects
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer traces plausible longer-term consequences of removing and relocating Earth's viruses.
criteria.1-2: Ignores downstream effects or gives unrelated apocalyptic claims with no mechanism.
criteria.3-4: Mentions ecosystem disruption but only in generic terms and without linking to viral ecological roles.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes that removing viruses would affect oceans, microbes, and disease dynamics, but with limited causal detail.
criteria.7-8: Connects viral removal to microbial population changes, nutrient cycling, marine food webs, phage control of bacteria, and microbiome disruption.
criteria.9-10: Develops a coherent multi-step chain from viral disappearance to microbial blooms/crashes, altered carbon and nutrient fluxes, ecosystem instability, and possible recovery or replacement dynamics.

criteria.name: Counterfactual Consistency, Uncertainty, and Contradiction Control
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer maintains a clear interpretation of the counterfactual and calibrates uncertainty without contradicting itself.
criteria.1-2: Contradicts the premise, shifts scenarios repeatedly, or presents impossible outcomes as certain.
criteria.3-4: Uses an unclear version of the premise and mixes incompatible assumptions, such as viruses both remaining everywhere and being fully gathered.
criteria.5-6: Mostly follows the gathering premise but leaves key assumptions ambiguous and makes some overconfident claims.
criteria.7-8: States reasonable assumptions, distinguishes immediate from long-term effects, and flags uncertain estimates or biological responses.
criteria.9-10: Maintains one consistent counterfactual, separates physical aggregation from ecological removal effects, and uses uncertainty ranges without undermining causal reasoning.

items.model_answer:
If all the world's viruses were gathered in one place, the result would be surprisingly underwhelming visually but catastrophic ecologically.

**The Pile Itself**

There are an estimated 10³¹ viruses on Earth—roughly 10 million times more than all the stars in the observable universe. Yet because viruses are minuscule (most range from 20 to 300 nanometers), their combined mass totals only about 0.2 gigatons of carbon. Gathered together, they would form a pile roughly the size of a small mountain or large building—impressive, but not planet-sized. The material would appear as a viscous, organic sludge since most viruses are simply protein shells containing genetic material, and outside their hosts they're inert.

**The Real Catastrophe: Removal**

The devastating consequences would come from their absence. Viruses, particularly bacteriophages, kill an estimated 20-40% of all ocean bacteria daily, keeping microbial populations in check. Without this "viral shunt," bacterial populations would explode, disrupting marine food webs and altering global carbon and nutrient cycles. Algal blooms would run unchecked, potentially creating massive dead zones.

Viruses also drive evolution through horizontal gene transfer, moving genetic material between organisms. Roughly 8% of human DNA originated from ancient viral infections, including genes critical for placenta development. Long-term, evolution would slow significantly without this genetic mixing.

**If Released Back**

Releasing the concentrated viral mass would create a brief, chaotic exposure event, though most viruses are host-specific and harmless to most life. The ecological disruption from their temporary absence, however, might already be irreversible.

items.question: What If You Tried to Catch a Bullet after It Slowed Down?
human_answers: Yes. The "bullet catch" is a common magic trick in which a magician appears to catch a fired bullet in mid-flight—often between their teeth. This an illusion, of course; it's not possible to catch a bullet like that.[1]This was confirmed (http://www.discovery.com/tv-shows/mythbusters/mythbusters-database/catch-bullet-teeth.htm) by Mythbusters in episode 4 of Season 4. But under the right conditions, you could catch a bullet. It would just take a lot of patience.[2]I'd like to remind everyone that while I write sometimes about the interesting physics of bullets, I'm not an authority on firearms safety. I was raised Quaker (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quakers); I've never held a gun, much less fired one. A bullet fired straight up would eventually reach a maximum height.[3]Don't do this. In neighborhoods where people fire guns upward in celebration, bystanders are routinely killed (http://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/PDF/wk/mm5350.pdf) by falling bullets. It probably wouldn't stop completely; more likely, it would be drifting sideways at a couple meters per second. At that speed, as long as you were in the right place at the right time, you could snatch it out of the air. If someone fired a bullet upward ... [Image: image] ... and you were hanging out in a hot-air balloon directly above the firing range ... [Image: image] ... it's possible that you could reach out and snag the bullet at the apex of its flight. If you succeeded, you might notice something odd: In addition to being hot, the bullet would be spinning. It would have lost its upward momentum, but not its rotational momentum; it would still have the spin given to it by the barrel of the gun. [Image: image] This effect can be seen, dramatically, when a bullet is fired at ice.[4]Floor water. As confirmed by dozens of YouTube videos (https://www.youtube.com/results?search_query=bullet%20spinning%20ice) (and Mythbusters), bullets fired into ice are often found still spinning rapidly. You'd have to grab the bullet firmly; otherwise, it might jump out of your hand. If you don't have a balloon, you could potentially make this work from a mountain peak. Mount Thor, which you may remember from question #51 (http://what-if.xkcd.com/51/), features a vertical drop of 1,250 meters. According to ballistics lab Close Focus Research, this is almost exactly how high a .22 Long Rifle bullet will fly if fired directly upward.[5]Close Focus Research, Maximum Altitude For Bullets Fired Vertically (http://www.closefocusresearch.com/maximum-altitude-bullets-fired-vertically) [Image: image] If you want to use larger bullets, you'll need a much larger drop; an AK-47's bullet can go over two kilometers upward. There are no purely vertical cliffs that are that tall, so you'd need to fire the bullet at an angle, and it would have significant sideways speed at the top of its arc. However, a suitably tough baseball glove might be able to snag it.[6]In fact, according to Rifle Magazine, a gun writer once claimed (https://www.riflemagazine.com/magazine/article.cfm?magid=78&tocid=1094) that at a thousand yards, he could catch ordinary rifle bullets with a baseball glove. Of course, he was being figurative—you wouldn't see the bullet coming, so you'd be just as likely to catch it with your face as with your glove. In any of these scenarios, you'd have to get extraordinarily lucky. Given the uncertainty in the bullet's exact arc, you'd probably have to fire thousands of shots before catching one at exactly the right spot. And by that point, you may find you've attracted some attention. [Image: image]

items.model_answer: If you tried to catch a bullet after it slowed down, the outcome would depend entirely on its remaining velocity, but assuming it has decelerated to a safe speed, it would feel like catching a small, warm rock. When a bullet is fired straight up into the air, gravity and air resistance slow it to a complete stop at its peak altitude. As it falls back down, it reaches a terminal velocity typically between 100 and 200 miles per hour, depending on the bullet's mass and whether it is tumbling or falling base-first. At this reduced speed, a lighter, tumbling bullet might lack the kinetic energy to break human skin, meaning you could theoretically catch it, though it would deliver a sharp sting and feel noticeably hot due to the initial gunpowder ignition and air friction. However, a heavier bullet falling aerodynamically can retain enough velocity to penetrate skin and bone, making an attempt to catch it severely injurious or lethal. Furthermore, if the bullet were fired at an angle rather than straight up, it would maintain a lethal ballistic trajectory and much of its horizontal velocity, rendering it impossible to catch safely. Ultimately, successfully catching a sufficiently slowed bullet is physically possible, but misjudging its residual energy would result in catastrophic injury.

nodes.text: If you tried to catch a bullet after it slowed down,
the outcome would depend entirely on its remaining velocity,
but assuming it has decelerated to a safe speed,
it would feel like catching a small, warm rock.
When a bullet is fired straight up into the air,
gravity and air resistance slow it to a complete stop at its peak altitude.
As it falls back down,
it reaches a terminal velocity typically between 100 and 200 miles per hour,
depending on the bullet's mass and whether it is tumbling or falling base-first.
At this reduced speed,
a lighter, tumbling bullet might lack the kinetic energy to break human skin,
meaning you could theoretically catch it,
though it would deliver a sharp sting
and feel noticeably hot due to the initial gunpowder ignition and air friction.
However, a heavier bullet falling aerodynamically can retain enough velocity to penetrate skin and bone,
making an attempt to catch it severely injurious or lethal.
Furthermore, if the bullet were fired at an angle rather than straight up,
it would maintain a lethal ballistic trajectory and much of its horizontal velocity,
rendering it impossible to catch safely.
Ultimately, successfully catching a sufficiently slowed bullet is physically possible,
but misjudging its residual energy would result in catastrophic injury.

items.question: What If Astronauts Tried to Reach the Moon by Hitting Golf Balls in Orbit?
human_answers: It depends how good your swing is. That sounds glib, but it's sort of true. The answer to this question hinges on exactly how fast you can hit a golf ball. Sometimes, exact numbers don't matter that much. If my baseball, car, dog, or Zamboni goes a little faster than yours,[1]$20 says they will! it will go a little farther. But that's not how it works in rocket golf. The design of our spaceship turns out to involve an equation where the speed of the golf ball is in the exponent. That means a small change in speed can make a big difference. The equation in question—which might be my favorite in all of physics—the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation: \[ \Delta v = v_\text{exhaust} \ln \frac{m_\text{initial}}{m_\text{final}} \] This equation comes up a lot in What If calculations. I like it both because it says something fundamental about our ability to explore the universe, and because you can use it to get really good at Kerbal Space Program. With some rearranging, the equation can help us figure out how much of our ship's weight has to be golf balls: \[ \frac{\text{Mass of ship plus golf balls}}{\text{Mass of ship alone}} = e ^ \left ( \frac{\text{Ship's change in speed}}{\text{Speed of golf ball}} \right ) \] Someone who, like me, has never been golfing before, might—after swinging and missing a few times—manage to hit the ball at 120 mph (50 m/s).[2]See Trackman's page on ball speed (http://mytrackman.com/explore/trackman-data/trackman-ball-data/ball-speed) To get to the Moon from low Earth orbit, you would need enough fuel to add 5,300 m/s to your ship's speed. By putting those numbers into the rocket equation, we can find out how large a sack of golf balls would have to be for the average golfer to reach the Moon. If we plug it in to Wolfram|Alpha (http://www.wolframalpha.com/input/?i=please+calculate+2*%28%283%2F%284*pi%29%29*%28%28e%5E%285300+m%2Fs+%2F+120mph%29%29*200+kg%29+%2F+%2865%25*1.15+kg%2FL%29%29%5E%281%2F3%29+thank+you) ... [Image: image] ... we find that the bag of golf balls will have to be just about exactly 100 billion miles in diameter. That's much, much bigger than our Solar System.[3]As a Fermi rule of thumb, planets in the inner Solar System are 100 million kilometers away and planets in the outer Solar System are a billion kilometers away. Or miles; either one works. [Image: image] It would also promptly and violently collapse into a black hole. Fortunately, we should be able to avert that disaster by making relatively small changes to the "120" in that equation. If we increase the golf ball's speed from 120 mph to 150, it shrinks the answer dramatically, and the required number of golf balls would fit snugly between the Sun and Mars. Still too big to avoid a catastrophic collapse, but we're getting somewhere. [Image: image] Tiger Woods can hit a golf ball at about 180 mph, which means that if he were powering our spaceship, the bag of golf balls would be only twice the diameter of the Sun! [Image: image] According (http://www.guinnessworldrecords.com/records-10000/fastest-golf-drive/) to the Guinness Book of World Records, the record for fastest golf drive is 211 mph, set by Maurice Allen in 2012. This corresponds to a bag of golf balls only 100,000 kilometers across—smaller than Jupiter, but still (obviously) not practical. However, golfer Ryan Winther claims (http://www.ryanwinther.com/about_records.htm) to have beaten this record, though without Guinness observers there.[4]And, obviously, it doesn't count unless it's overseen by people from a beer company. If you want to set a world record, hit a golf ball at a radar gun and get it certified by the Mike's Hard Lemonade people. His ball speed was measured by something called the "Titleist Performance Institute" to be 226.7 mph, and he claims a personal best of 237 mph. If he could consistently hit 237 mph, we could shrink our fuel container down to the size of Earth[5]Although it would still be large enough to partially collapse under its own gravity, similar to what happened to the mole of moles (http://what-if.xkcd.com/4/). [Image: image] This still wouldn't work; even in a high orbit, the massive tides from your ship—which is much more massive than the Moon—would be highly disruptive. We could probably shrink the fuel tank further by using "illegal" equipment. There are Superball-style balls and "trampoline face" clubs which can hit much farther, and which would not be permitted in tournament play.[6]On the other hand, we're talking about a sport that brought whites-only clubs with it into the 21st century (http://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2010/06/01/AR2010060103918.html), and Agusta, host of the Masters, admitted its first woman in 2012 (http://www.reuters.com/article/2012/08/20/us-golf-augusta-idUSBRE87J0IE20120820). So maybe we shouldn't worry too much about their traditional rules. A hypothetical 270 mph drive would allow a fuel tank the size of the Moon. At this point, why are we even using a club? According (http://arxiv.org/abs/1305.0966) to research from the US Air Force Academy and BTG Research,[7]Oddly, both researchers have the name "Courtney". There are probably about 200,000 people in the US named Courtney (first or last); maybe we should recruit them to all build potato cannons. a potato cannon fueled by acetylene can launch a potato at 140 m/s (310 mph). If it were capable of launching golf balls at that speed,[8]We're not factoring in the weight of the acetylene—but then again, we also weren't factoring in the weight of the hamburgers the golfer would need to eat to keep hitting those drives. our ship would have a diameter of only 150 miles! [Image: image] There's the small problem that manufacturing that many golf balls would cost quintillions of dollars. You could bring the size down further by making the potato cannon more and more powerful and efficient, but at that point you're simply building a rocket. And the potato cannon scenario has an extra perk. If you somehow made the balls durable enough to survive atmospheric entry, and you set up your maneuver so the ejected golf balls covered the middle latitudes evenly, then over the course of this maneuver you would be statistically likely to hit a hole-in-one ... at every golf course in the world. [Image: image]

criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer gives plausible orders of magnitude for the required delta-v, ball speeds, and resulting impossible propellant/fuel-container sizes.

criteria.9-10: Captures the key scale: ordinary golf speeds imply a container vastly larger than the Solar System, while record/potato-cannon speeds still leave impractically astronomical or planetary-scale requirements.

criteria.name: Long-range feasibility and downstream physical consequences
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer follows the counterfactual beyond launch mechanics to major consequences such as gravitational collapse, tides, orbital hazards, and impractical manufacturing.
criteria.1-2: Stops at 'yes' or 'no' without considering downstream effects of the required mass or ejected balls.
criteria.3-4: Mentions impracticality generally but misses the dominant consequences of astronomical propellant mass.
criteria.5-6: Identifies at least one major downstream issue, such as huge mass, cost, or danger from ejected balls.
criteria.7-8: Explains multiple consequences, including self-gravity/collapse, tidal disruption, and the impracticality of storing or producing the balls.
criteria.9-10: Coherently traces the full causal chain from required mass to black-hole/gravitational collapse risks, lunar/Earth tidal effects, manufacturing impossibility, and possible atmospheric reentry impacts.

criteria.name: Counterfactual coherence, uncertainty calibration, and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer maintains the premise while clearly distinguishing assumptions, approximations, jokes, and impossible extensions without internal contradictions.
criteria.1-2: Contradicts itself or rejects the premise without analyzing it.
criteria.3-4: Partly engages the premise but mixes incompatible assumptions, such as treating the balls as both massless and massive.
criteria.5-6: Maintains a mostly consistent scenario but leaves assumptions about orbit, ball velocity, or spacecraft mass vague.

criteria.9-10: Provides a tightly coherent counterfactual analysis with calibrated approximations, consistent units and directions, and clear boundaries where the scenario becomes equivalent to building a conventional rocket.

items.model_answer:
It would be completely impossible for astronauts to reach the Moon by hitting golf balls from orbit. The fundamental problem is one of velocity.

To travel from low Earth orbit to the Moon requires a trans-lunar injection velocity change (delta-v) of approximately 3.1 km/s. The fastest golf ball ever hit on Earth travels at about 90 m/s (324 km/h). Even from orbit, where the ball would already have the station's orbital velocity (~7.8 km/s), the additional velocity a human can impart with a golf club is only about 0.08 km/s—roughly 40 times too little to reach the Moon.

A golf ball hit from orbit would simply enter a slightly different Earth orbit with a marginally higher apogee, eventually decaying and burning up in the atmosphere due to orbital drag. It would never come close to escaping Earth's gravitational influence.

Even if we imagined the astronaut using the recoil from hitting golf balls as propulsion (conservation of momentum), each hit would change the astronaut's velocity by only about 0.02 m/s. To accumulate the necessary 3.1 km/s, they would need to hit approximately 150,000 golf balls—while somehow carrying them all along.

The gap between human athletic capability and the energy requirements of space travel is simply too vast for this approach to work.

items.question: How Powerful Would Radar Have to Be to Stop a Speeding Car?
human_answers: Radio waves exert force on things. Not a lot of force. The average cell phone transmitter exerts about a billionth of a newton of pressure on its surroundings. That means that it would take several trillion cell phones to collectively levitate a snowflake; the pressure from one phone wouldn't even measurably slow it down. [Image: image] If the phone did put out enough energy to levitate a snowflake by radiation pressure, the power flowing through the snowflake (a few kilowatts) would quickly cause the snowflake to become a raindrop, which would quickly become water vapor, which would quickly become the least of your problems. [Image: image] The fate of the snowflake hints at what kinds of problems our car will encounter. If you want to slow down a one-ton car by radiation pressure, your radar gun would need to deliver about two trillion joules worth of radiation—the energy of a small nuclear weapon.[1]The formula for figuring out that amount out is simple: The energy required is equal to the desired change in speed (say, 20 mph) times the mass of the car times the speed of light. The radar gun would need to emit even more energy than that, since not all of the radiation will be absorbed (or reflected) by the car.[2]The fact that some of it is reflected makes things easier, since that doubles the momentum delivered by the radiation. This is why simple solar sails are white and not black. For more on radar reflectivity of materials, you can check out one of the worst scanned PDFs I've ever seen (http://www.dtic.mil/dtic/tr/fulltext/u2/601365.pdf). Your radar gun would also vaporize the car. This is a problem, in one sense, but it's also a solution. Even if most of the energy is reflected, the portion that was absorbed would convert the materials in the car into gas or plasma. The expanding cloud would exert a lot more pressure on the car than the radiation itself.[3]This process, called ablation (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laser_ablation), is also what got rid of the Moon in the What If #13 (http://what-if.xkcd.com/13/). This is convenient—it means that we wouldn't need nearly as much energy to stop the car as we would using radiation pressure alone. There are even simpler ways to slow down a car with radiation. For example, you could aim a radiation beam at the tires and melt them, or use the electromagnetic radiation to knock out the car's electrical systems. Or just use a laser pointer to blind the driver and hope they reflexively slow down. Of course, you don't need any of those things. If your goal is to slow down the car—rather than to catch speeders—your radar gun doesn't need any power. You can just stand by the side of the road next to a police car holding a fake radar gun. [Image: image] In the end, a radar gun capable of slowing cars through radiation pressure would be roughly equivalent to a nuclear weapon, and using nuclear strikes in response to traffic violations is probably overkill. It would work, in the literal sense, but it would also destroy the offender, car, police officer, road, and all other traffic for miles around.[4]It would also cause fragments of the driver to violate the speed limit in all directions at once. Of course, maybe using the apocalyptic radar gun wouldn't be necessary; just the threat of a nuclear strike against drivers would probably deter speeding. Come to think of it, maybe that's what those other signs you sometimes see are hinting at. [Image: image]

items.model_answer: To stop a speeding car using radar, the required power depends entirely on whether you mean physically halting the car's momentum through the force of the radiation itself, or electronically disabling the vehicle's computer systems. If you mean physically pushing the car to a stop using radiation pressure, the radar would need to output roughly 1 terawatt of continuous power—equivalent to the total electrical output of hundreds of nuclear power plants combined and focused into a single beam. Because electromagnetic waves carry very little momentum relative to their energy, applying enough radiation pressure to decelerate a 3,000-pound car would require an astronomical amount of power. At this intensity, the radar wouldn't just push the car; the sheer thermal energy would instantly vaporize the vehicle and its occupants into plasma long before it rolled to a stop. However, if you mean stopping the car by using radar frequencies to disrupt its electronics, the required power is surprisingly modest. Real-world military and law enforcement high-power microwave (HPM) systems—often referred to as car-stopping radars—operate on pulsed power levels of just a few hundred kilowatts to a few megawatts. These systems use directed radar pulses to induce massive voltage spikes in the car's electronic control unit, instantly frying the microchips and stalling the engine, allowing the vehicle to coast to a halt without applying any physical force.

items.question: What If All the CO2 in Bottled Soda Were Released into the Atmosphere?
human_answers: For most of the history of civilization, there were about 270 parts per million of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere. In the last hundred years, industrial activity has pushed that number up (http://www.skepticalscience.com/print.php?r=45) to 400 parts per million. One "part per million" of CO2 weighs about 7.8 billion tons. A can of soda contains in the neighborhood of 2.2 grams of CO2, so you would need about 450 quadrillion cans of soda. That's enough to cover the Earth's land with ten layers of cans. [Image: image] There's clearly not enough room to do this. Even if we stacked the cans up to the edge of space,[1]I don't have any hard numbers, but my guess would be that you could probably stack supermarket soda six-pack crates a few hundred meters high before the bottom layer ruptures. they'd still take up an area the size of Rhode Island.[2]We shouldn't actually try it, given what happened last time (http://what-if.xkcd.com/8/). We'd need to add even more cans to keep up with ongoing emissions. We're currently increasing the atmosphere's CO2 concentration by an average of 2 parts per million each year: [Image: image] At that rate, we'd need to add one can of soda per person every 30 seconds, which is about 10,000 times the current consumption rate.[3]The global average (http://what-if.xkcd.com/74/) is one can per person every 5 days. In the US, the average is one every 18 hours. That would add a new layer of cans to the ground every 6[4]I originally had the wrong number here; thank you to Paulina for catching it! years or so. This layer of cans would get pretty annoying. [Image: image] Are there any ways out of this predicament? In some areas, you can turn in soda cans for recycling and receive a small amount of money; in Massachusetts, where I live, it's 5 cents. If you collected one year's worth of soda cans—instead of layering them across the Earth's surface—and emptied them out, you could redeem them for $372 trillion. With that much money, you could simply buy the world's current reserves[5]Source: xkcd.com/980 (http://xkcd.com/980), bottom right. of coal, oil, and natural gas—the source of the whole problem. Then, you put it all back in the ground and leave it there. [Image: image] Problem solved.

items.model_answer:
If all the CO2 dissolved in the world's bottled soda were released into the atmosphere at once, the impact on global climate change would be virtually imperceptible, though there would be a few interesting physical and chemical consequences along the way.

The total volume of carbonated beverages produced globally each year is roughly 200 billion liters. A typical soda contains about 3 to 8 grams of dissolved CO2 per liter. Even taking the higher end of that range, this amounts to only about 1.6 million metric tons of CO2. For context, human activities—primarily fossil fuel burning—emit over 37 billion metric tons of CO2 annually. The soda industry's entire yearly carbonation output represents less than 0.05% of a single year's global emissions. Releasing it would add a negligible fraction to the atmosphere's existing burden of roughly 3,000 gigatons of CO2, having no measurable effect on global warming or ocean acidification.

However, the immediate physical consequences of releasing all that gas simultaneously would be quite dramatic. If the CO2 were liberated from its liquid suspension all at once, it would expand massively. Dissolved CO2 occupies far less volume than gaseous CO2; at standard atmospheric pressure, those 1.6 million tons would expand to roughly 800 billion cubic meters of gas. This sudden, massive expansion of gas inside billions of sealed containers would trigger a worldwide explosive chain reaction. Every soda bottle and can on Earth would violently burst, creating a global hail of aluminum shrapnel, glass shards, and plastic fragments that would cause widespread injury and property damage.

If we imagine the CO2 simply evaporating harmlessly into the air without the explosive containers, the immediate environmental effect would still be minimal. In a localized, confined space—like a sealed warehouse storing millions of bottles—releasing that gas could temporarily displace oxygen, creating a localized asphyxiation hazard for humans and animals, as CO2 is heavier than air and pools at ground level. But dispersed across the entire global atmosphere, it would be instantly diluted to background levels. 

Ultimately, the CO2 trapped inside the world's fizzy drinks is a tiny, highly concentrated fraction of the Earth's natural carbon cycle. Releasing it would not shift the planet's climate balance, though the exploding packaging would certainly make for a memorable day.

nodes.text: If all the CO2 dissolved in the world's bottled soda were released into the atmosphere at once,
the impact on global climate change would be virtually imperceptible,
though there would be a few interesting physical and chemical consequences along the way.
The total volume of carbonated beverages produced globally each year is roughly 200 billion liters.
A typical soda contains about 3 to 8 grams of dissolved CO2 per liter.
Even taking the higher end of that range,
this amounts to only about 1.6 million metric tons of CO2.
For context, human activities—primarily fossil fuel burning—emit over 37 billion metric tons of CO2 annually.
The soda industry's entire yearly carbonation output represents less than 0.05% of a single year's global emissions.
Releasing it would add a negligible fraction to the atmosphere's existing burden of roughly 3,000 gigatons of CO2,
having no measurable effect on global warming or ocean acidification.
However, the immediate physical consequences of releasing all that gas simultaneously would be quite dramatic.
If the CO2 were liberated from its liquid suspension all at once,
it would expand massively.
Dissolved CO2 occupies far less volume than gaseous CO2;
at standard atmospheric pressure, those 1.6 million tons would expand to roughly 800 billion cubic meters of gas.
This sudden, massive expansion of gas inside billions of sealed containers would trigger a worldwide explosive chain reaction.
Every soda bottle and can on Earth would violently burst,
creating a global hail of aluminum shrapnel, glass shards, and plastic fragments
that would cause widespread injury and property damage.
If we imagine the CO2 simply evaporating harmlessly into the air without the explosive containers,
the immediate environmental effect would still be minimal.
In a localized, confined space—like a sealed warehouse storing millions of bottles—
releasing that gas could temporarily displace oxygen,
creating a localized asphyxiation hazard for humans and animals,
as CO2 is heavier than air and pools at ground level.
But dispersed across the entire global atmosphere,
it would be instantly diluted to background levels.
Ultimately, the CO2 trapped inside the world's fizzy drinks is a tiny, highly concentrated fraction of the Earth's natural carbon cycle.
Releasing it would not shift the planet's climate balance,
though the exploding packaging would certainly make for a memorable day.

items.question: What If I Threw a Tungsten Countertop into the Sun?
human_answers: Not very far. With its high melting point, tungsten is a good[1]Except that the word "good" implies that you have some kind of goal you're working toward, which—given how strange the thing you're doing is—I'm not sure about. choice for a sundiving countertop. The first problem would be sunlight. As the countertop approached the Sun, it would heat up. Tungsten has the highest melting point of any element, but the Sun is one of the meltiest things in the Solar System. When the countertop got within a couple of solar radii, it would liquify. [Image: image] If you protected it with a heat shield of some kind, or dropped it from a sundiving spaceship, it could enter the Sun's atmosphere relatively intact. In this case, some interesting physical effects would destroy it.[2]"Some interesting physical effects would destroy it" summarizes the answers to a large percentage of the questions submitted to this blog. Because the Sun is so heavy, anything that falls to its surface will be accelerated to a tremendous speed by its gravity. A falling countertop would reach speeds of over 600 km/s—0.2% of the speed of light. (Our rockets can only accelerate spacecraft to 10-20 km/s.) From the countertop's point of view, particles from the Sun's atmosphere would be slamming into it at 600 km/s. These particles would pack quite a punch.[3]From a particle physics point of view, the individual protons would have energy of about 2 keV. When the countertop got within about a few thousand kilometers[4]I don't want another unit-related word to mentally keep track of, but it's always seemed a little weird that we don't call thousands of kilometers "megameters". of the Sun's surface, these collisions would start delivering more energy to the countertop than the sunlight. The collisions would fling individual tungsten atoms away from the surface—a process called sputtering (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sputtering). Between the sputtering and ordinary heating from the impacts, the countertop would start to absorb a lot of energy very quickly. If the countertop were larger, it could penetrate into the Sun's photosphere—the first layer beneath the "surface"—and potentially trigger a solar flare.[5]For a scientific discussion of this, see the article Impacts of comets onto the Sun and coronal mass ejections (http://meetings.copernicus.org/www.cosis.net/abstracts/EGU05/04384/EGU05-J-04384.pdf). For a science fiction discussion of this, see Stephen Baxter and Arthur C. Clarke's 2005 novel Sunstorm. But as it is, it wouldn't even make it through the Sun's atmosphere—it would be vaporized somewhere in the Sun's chromosphere. [Image: image] This brings us around to a key question: Who the hell has tungsten countertops? Sure, it has good heat tolerance. But I'd be nervous about using tungsten as a food-preparation surface. In September of 1994 (http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8874460), a French soldier drank wine from a rifle barrel. Fifteen minutes later, he started having seizures. He was rushed to the hospital and treated for "acute tungsten intoxication"—the first known case in medical history. He reportedly made a full recovery, although concentrations of tungsten were present in all his body tissues for weeks. The lesson here is to use normal materials. Michael, just make your countertops out of granite and don't drop them in the Sun. And if you're a French soldier, please just drink wine like a normal person. [Image: image]

items.model_answer: If you threw a tungsten countertop into the Sun, its fate would be determined by the star's extreme temperature gradient and the remarkable heat resistance of tungsten. Tungsten boasts the highest melting point of any metal at 3,422 degrees Celsius, but the Sun's visible surface, the photosphere, is roughly 5,500 degrees Celsius. As the countertop approached the Sun, the intense radiation would heat it to a glowing white, and upon hitting the photosphere, the metal would finally melt into a liquid blob. However, the countertop would not simply float at the surface; the Sun's immense gravity would pull the incredibly dense mass downward into the interior. As it sinks into the convective and radiative zones, temperatures skyrocket into the hundreds of thousands and eventually millions of degrees. At these depths, the temperature far exceeds tungsten's boiling point of 5,930 degrees Celsius, causing the molten metal to rapidly vaporize. Almost immediately after vaporizing, the extreme heat would strip the electrons from the tungsten atoms, turning the metal into a highly ionized plasma. Because tungsten is a heavy element, it would briefly radiate energy highly efficiently as it absorbs heat to transition through its phases, creating a microscopic and fleeting cool spot in the solar plasma. Ultimately, however, the mass of a countertop is infinitesimally small compared to the Sun, so the tungsten would simply dissolve into the star as an unnoticeable trace element, having absolutely no measurable impact on the Sun's structure, lifespan, or fusion processes.

nodes.text: If you threw a tungsten countertop into the Sun, its fate would be determined by the star's extreme temperature gradient and the remarkable heat resistance of tungsten.
Tungsten boasts the highest melting point of any metal at 3,422 degrees Celsius,
but the Sun's visible surface, the photosphere, is roughly 5,500 degrees Celsius.
As the countertop approached the Sun, the intense radiation would heat it to a glowing white,
and upon hitting the photosphere, the metal would finally melt into a liquid blob.
However, the countertop would not simply float at the surface;
the Sun's immense gravity would pull the incredibly dense mass downward into the interior.
As it sinks into the convective and radiative zones, temperatures skyrocket into the hundreds of thousands and eventually millions of degrees.
At these depths, the temperature far exceeds tungsten's boiling point of 5,930 degrees Celsius,
causing the molten metal to rapidly vaporize.
Almost immediately after vaporizing, the extreme heat would strip the electrons from the tungsten atoms,
turning the metal into a highly ionized plasma.
Because tungsten is a heavy element, it would briefly radiate energy highly efficiently as it absorbs heat to transition through its phases,
creating a microscopic and fleeting cool spot in the solar plasma.
Ultimately, however, the mass of a countertop is infinitesimally small compared to the Sun,
so the tungsten would simply dissolve into the star as an unnoticeable trace element,
having absolutely no measurable impact on the Sun's structure, lifespan, or fusion processes.

items.question: What If Earth Spun Fast Enough for a Day to Last One Second?
human_answers: If this is going to happen, I hope it doesn't happen late in the afternoon next Friday. The Earth rotates,[citation needed (https://web.archive.org/web/20151210155028/http://www.timecube.com/)] which means its midsection is being flung outward by centrifugal force.[1]Which is still a real thing (http://xkcd.com/123/). This centrifugal force isn't strong enough to overcome gravity and tear the Earth apart, but it's enough to flatten the Earth slightly and make it so you weigh almost a pound less at the Equator than you do at the poles.[2]This is due to several effects, including centrifugal force, the flattened shape of the Earth, and the fact that if you go far enough toward the pole in North America people start offering you poutine. If the Earth (and everything on it) were suddenly sped up so that a day only lasted one second, the Earth wouldn't even last a single day.[3]Either kind. The Equator would be moving at over 10% of the speed of light. Centrifugal force would become much stronger than gravity, and the material that makes up the Earth would be flung outward. [Image: image] You wouldn't die instantly—you might survive for a few milliseconds or even seconds. That might not seem like much, but compared to the speed at which you'd die in other What If articles (http://what-if.xkcd.com/1/) involving relativistic speeds, it's pretty long. The Earth's crust and mantle would break apart into building-sized chunks. By the time a second[4]I mean, a day. had passed, the atmosphere would have spread out too thin to breathe—although even at the relatively stationary poles, you probably wouldn't survive long enough to asphyxiate. [Image: image] In the first few seconds, the expansion would shatter the crust into spinning fragments and kill just about everyone on the planet, but that's relatively peaceful compared to what would happen next. Everything would be moving at relativistic speeds, but each piece of the crust would be moving at close to the same speed at its neighbors. This means things would be relatively calm ... until the disk hit something. The first obstacle would be the belt of satellites around the Earth. After 40 milliseconds, the ISS would be struck by the edge of the expanding atmosphere and would be vaporized instantly. More satellites would follow. After a second and a half, the disc would reach the belt of geostationary satellites orbiting above the Equator. Each one would release a violent burst of gamma rays as the Earth consumed it. [Image: image] The debris from the Earth would slice outward like an expanding buzzsaw. The disk would take about ten seconds to pass the Moon, another hour to spread past the Sun, and would span the Solar System within a day or two. Each time the disc engulfed an asteroid, it would spray a flood of energy in all directions, eventually sterilizing every surface in the Solar System. Since the Earth is tilted, the Sun and the planets aren't usually lined up with the plane of the Earth's equator. They'd have a good chance of avoiding the buzzsaw[5]I keep reading this as "Buzzfeed". directly. However, Next Friday, April 25th, the Moon will cross the plane of the Earth's equator (as it does every two weeks). If Dylan sped up the Earth at this moment, the Moon would be right in the path of the resulting planetary buzzsaw. The impact would turn the moon into a comet, sending it rocketing from the Solar System in a spray of debris. The flash of light and heat would be so bright that if you were standing at the surface of the Sun, it would be brighter above you than below. Every surface in the Solar System—Europa's ice, Saturn's rings, and Mercury's rocky crust—would be scoured clean ... [Image: image] ... by moonlight.

items.model_answer: If Earth spun fast enough for a day to last one second, the planet would instantly tear itself apart. Completing a full rotation in one second means the Earth would be spinning 86,400 times faster than it does now. At the equator, the surface would be moving at roughly 40,000 kilometers per second, which is about 13% the speed of light. This extreme velocity would generate a centrifugal force millions of times stronger than Earth's gravity. The atmosphere and oceans would be flung into space immediately, followed by the crust, mantle, and core. Because rock and metal lack the tensile strength to hold together under such immense rotational stress, the Earth would flatten into an oblate disk before completely disintegrating into a rapidly expanding cloud of superheated debris. Additionally, because the equator would be moving at a significant fraction of the speed of light, relativistic effects like time dilation would occur, though the complete destruction of the planet would make this impossible to observe.

items.question: What If Rain Broke a Windshield before Speed Did?
human_answers: Fast. [Image: image] Raindrops are tiny. Even in the heaviest rainstorms, the water in the air weighs less than the air itself (which is one of several reasons you can't swim upward in a rainstorm). Even at very high speeds, they can't break a windshield via their momentum alone. Under ordinary circumstances, raindrops don't damage car windshields at all. However, they can destroy the windows of supersonic aircraft. Here's what happens when a raindrop hits a glass surface at high speed: When the droplet makes contact with the surface, a shockwave travels back up through the droplet. [Image: image] Normally, this shockwave would move at the speed of sound within the liquid—about 1300 m/s, four times faster than in air. However, at high impact speeds, this shockwave actually moves substantially faster than the speed of sound in water. The water is squeezed between the incoming drop and the glass surface, which makes it squirt sideways in all directions. These jets of water can move even faster than the original (already supersonic) droplet, and even faster than the shockwaves we mentioned. [Image: image] One paper (http://e-collection.library.ethz.ch/eserv/eth:26251/eth-26251-02.pdf) ran a simulation of water droplets hitting a surface at 500 m/s (about Mach 1.5), and found that the water sprayed out from the point of contact at over 6000 m/s—Mach 18.[1]That's a pretty simple way to expel material at 6 km/s. I wonder if anyone's ever tried to come up with a spacecraft propulsion system using it ... The sharp pulse from the shockwave can crack glass. The highest pressures are found in the ring around the edge of the droplet, and only exist for a tiny fraction of the impact. [Image: image] In addition to the direct downward pressure, the water jetting sideways can cause damage, too. If the material has any microscopic holes, cracks, or bumps, those jets can strike them and create new cracks or widen existing ones. Even at high speeds, a raindrop won't create a bullet hole on its own—but a long series of supersonic droplets would start to eat away at the glass, cracking and pitting it like sand.[2]This type of "erosion" can also cause damage to steam turbine blades (http://www.technicaljournalsonline.com/ijeat/VOL%20II/IJAET%20VOL%20II%20ISSUE%20II%20APRIL%20JUNE%202011/ARTICLE%2014%20IJAET%20VOLII%20ISSUE%20II%20APRIL-%20JUNE%202011.pdf). Eventually, the windshield could fail catastrophically. Luckily, cars can't drive at Mach 1 (http://what-if.xkcd.com/61/) without lifting off, so your windshield is safe from ordinary rain. On the other hand, if you're driving under a thunderstorm with strong updrafts ... [Image: image] ... the precipitation can smash your windshield at any speed.

items.model_answer: If rain could break a windshield before speed-related forces did, it would fundamentally change vehicle design and driving behavior. Windshields would need to be engineered primarily for impact resistance against water droplets rather than aerodynamic stress, likely requiring much thicker, heavier glass or alternative materials like polycarbonate composites. The physics of rain impact would become a critical safety concern—during heavy downpours, the cumulative percussive force of thousands of drops striking glass at terminal velocity (9-10 m/s for large raindrops) could cause catastrophic failure. This would make driving in rain extremely hazardous, potentially requiring vehicles to have deployable protective shields or making rain travel inadvisable altogether. Insurance, infrastructure, and transportation patterns would shift dramatically, with weather-based driving restrictions becoming commonplace and vehicle design prioritizing hydrodynamic deflection alongside traditional aerodynamics.
