items.question: What If You Drank the Blood of a Drunk Person?
human_answers: You would have to drink a lot of blood. A person contains about 5 liters of blood, or 14 glasses. [Image: image] If your blood is more than about half a percent alcohol, you stand a pretty good chance of dying. There have been a handful of cases of people surviving with a blood alcohol level of above 1%, but the LD50—the level at which 50% of people will die—is 0.40 (http://www.nellis.af.mil/shared/media/document/AFD-110211-015.pdf) (0.4%). If someone had a BAC of 0.40, and you drank all 14 glasses of their blood in a short amount of time,[1]Hey, there's a 50% chance they were going to die anyway. you would throw up: [Image: image] You wouldn't throw up because because of the alcohol; you'd just throw up because you're drinking blood. If you somehow avoided vomiting, you would have ingested a total of 20[2]Thank you to Conor Braman, among others, for correcting a missing zero in the original version of this calculation. grams of ethanol, which is the amount you'd get from a pint of beer. [Image: image] Depending on your weight, drinking that much blood could raise your own blood alcohol level to about 0.05. This is low enough that you could legally drive in many jurisdictions, but high enough to double your risk of an accident if you did. If your BAC is 0.05, it means only 1/8th of the alcohol from the other person's blood made it into yours. Supposing that after you drank all this blood, someone killed you and drank your blood,[3]It's only fair. they would then have a BAC of 0.006. If this process were repeated about 25 times, there would be fewer than 8 molecules of ethanol left in the last person's blood. After a few more cycles, there would likely be none;[4]By homeopathic standards, this is still quite concentrated. they'd just be drinking regular blood.[5]Like a loser. Whether there's any alcohol in it or not, drinking 14 glasses of blood wouldn't be fun. There's not a huge amount of medical literature on the subject, but anecdotal evidence from online forum posts suggests that any normal person who tries to drink more than about a pint of blood will vomit: [Image: image] If you drink blood regularly, over a long period of time the buildup of iron in your system can cause iron overload (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_overload). This syndrome, which sometimes affects people who have repeated blood transfusions, is one of the few conditions for which the correct treatment is bloodletting (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloodletting).[6]Others include PCV (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polycythemia_vera) and PCT (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porphyria_cutanea_tarda). Drinking one person's blood probably wouldn't cause iron overload. What it could give you is a blood-borne disease. Most such diseases are caused by viruses that can't survive in the stomach, but they could easily get into your blood through scratches in your mouth or throat as you drank. Diseases you could get from drinking an infected person's blood include hepatitis B and C, HIV, Hantaviruses, and Ebola. I'm not a doctor, and I try not to give medical advice in these articles. However, I will confidently say that you shouldn't drink the blood of someone with Ebola. That said, drinking or eating blood is not unheard of. It's a taboo in many cultures, but the British eat "black pudding", which is largely blood, and there are similar dishes all around the world. Maasai pastoralists in east Africa once lived mainly on milk, but also sometimes drank blood (http://digitalcommons.calpoly.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1005&context=honors), drawing it from their cattle and mixing it with the milk to form a sort of extreme protein shake. So the bottom line is that drinking enough of someone's blood to get drunk would be very difficult, probably quite unpleasant, and might give you some serious diseases. In the end, the blood itself would do awful things to your body long before the booze ever could. [Image: image]

items.model_answer:
If you drank the blood of a drunk person, you would not get drunk yourself. The alcohol concentration in human blood, even in a highly intoxicated person, is extremely low—typically measured in parts per thousand (a BAC of 0.08% means 0.08 grams of alcohol per 100 mL of blood). By comparison, a typical beer contains about 5% alcohol by volume.

To equal the alcohol in even one standard drink, you would need to consume an impractical and dangerous volume of blood—several liters at minimum. Long before you could ingest enough blood to feel any alcohol effects, you would face serious medical issues from the blood consumption itself, including iron toxicity, vomiting, and risk of infection from bloodborne pathogens.

Any tiny amount of alcohol present would be metabolized by your liver normally, just as it processes the minute amounts of alcohol naturally produced by gut bacteria during digestion. The more significant concerns would be the health risks of consuming blood itself, not the alcohol content.

items.question: How Many Birds Would It Take to Collapse into a Giant Bird Ball?
human_answers: The video shows starlings, birds which ... • gather in giant flocks of sometimes more than a million animals • can talk (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1VZYG00_qvE) • sound like R2-D2, though not as much as bobolinks (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9ABjBldAtPQ#t=9) do The gravitational force between adjacent starlings is small. If two birds were flying half a meter apart and tried to go perfectly straight, they would fly for over a thousand kilometers before the gravitational force between them finally steered them into colliding. [Image: image] Side note: The following is the first sentence from a journal article (http://jeb.biologists.org/content/204/19/3311) on starling metabolism:We trained two starlings (Sturnus vulgaris) to fly in a wind tunnel whilst wearing respirometry masks. I really think the paper should have stopped there; no matter what their results were, they can't possibly improve on the achievement they opened with. [Image: image] Anyway, back to gravity. To calculate the gravitational force from a whole flock of starlings, we need to know the flock's density. Conveniently, a 2008 paper (http://arxiv.org/abs/0802.1667) in Animal Behavior gathered some detailed statistics on starling flocks. The highest density they saw was about half a starling per cubic meter.[1]0.54 (•)>m-3 If the birds weigh about 85 grams each, that means the air in a starling flock weighs 25 times more than the starlings themselves.[2]This makes a certain intuitive sense. If they were that much heavier than the air between them, it's hard to imagine how they'd be able to stay airborne by pushing off of it with their wings. This means that the air's gravity is 25 times stronger than the starling cloud's gravity, and it's the air's gravity that will dominate the collapse. The collapse of giant clouds of gas or birds is governed by the equation for the Jeans instability (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeans_instability). It suggests that in order to undergo collapse, a cloud of uniform room-temperature air full of starlings would have to be much larger than the Earth to collapse. [Image: image] The gas cloud's gravity would be very weak, so the starlings would probably have a hard time flying until they got used to it. (Birds can fly (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=w4sZ3qe6PiI&feature=kp) in zero g—or, at least, they flap around in confusion. But, to be fair, that's how I'd react if I were abruptly and without warning yanked from my bed and tossed into the air in a zero g airplane cabin.) Such a cloud wouldn't form in the first place without some extra compression. To collapse naturally under its own gravity, the starling cloud would need to be so large that it would engulf the Solar System. When it did collapse, it would heat up, and the starlings ... [Image: image] ... would become a star.

items.model_answer: It would take approximately 10 quintillion to 100 quintillion average-sized birds (around 10^19 to 10^20 birds) to collapse into a giant spherical ball under their own gravity. For a mass of birds to "collapse into a ball," their collective gravitational pull must become strong enough to overcome the structural integrity of their bones and tissues, crushing them into a round shape in a state known as hydrostatic equilibrium. Because birds have a density roughly equal to water (about 1,000 kilograms per cubic meter) and their flesh and bone are relatively soft compared to rock, we can calculate the threshold where gravity takes over. The central pressure of a spherical body scales with the square of its radius, and once that pressure exceeds the yield strength of biological material (roughly a few megapascals), the birds will crush themselves into a smooth sphere. This happens at a mass of roughly 10^19 to 10^20 kilograms. Assuming an average bird weighs about 1 kilogram, this directly translates to 10^19 to 10^20 birds. A "bird ball" of this mass would have a diameter of roughly 200 to 500 kilometers, making it comparable in size to medium-sized moons in our solar system, like Saturn's moon Mimas. If you meant collapse into a black hole rather than just a round ball, the number skyrockets; you would need roughly 10^33 birds—a mass greater than our Sun—at which point their gravity would be so immense that not even light could escape the resulting avian singularity.

edus.text: It would take approximately 10 quintillion to 100 quintillion average-sized birds (around 10^19 to 10^20 birds) to collapse into a giant spherical ball under their own gravity.
For a mass of birds to "collapse into a ball," their collective gravitational pull must become strong enough to overcome the structural integrity of their bones and tissues,
crushing them into a round shape in a state known as hydrostatic equilibrium.
Because birds have a density roughly equal to water (about 1,000 kilograms per cubic meter) and their flesh and bone are relatively soft compared to rock,
we can calculate the threshold where gravity takes over.
The central pressure of a spherical body scales with the square of its radius,
and once that pressure exceeds the yield strength of biological material (roughly a few megapascals), the birds will crush themselves into a smooth sphere.
This happens at a mass of roughly 10^19 to 10^20 kilograms.
Assuming an average bird weighs about 1 kilogram,
this directly translates to 10^19 to 10^20 birds.
A "bird ball" of this mass would have a diameter of roughly 200 to 500 kilometers,
making it comparable in size to medium-sized moons in our solar system, like Saturn's moon Mimas.
If you meant collapse into a black hole rather than just a round ball,
the number skyrockets;
you would need roughly 10^33 birds—a mass greater than our Sun—
at which point their gravity would be so immense that not even light could escape the resulting avian singularity.

items.question: What If All the Water on Earth Vanished?
human_answers: As is often the case with these questions, everyone would die. The first people to notice would be swimmers and boaters, for obvious reasons. [Image: image] To avoid a glass half empty (http://what-if.xkcd.com/6/) scenario, we'll assume the water is replaced by air. Most people swim in water which is relatively shallow, so most of them would survive the fall to the bottom, albeit with a few broken bones.[1]Those swimming in quarries and glacial lakes, on the other hand, could easily fall to their deaths a few feet from shore. People out on the ocean, on the other hand, would be in trouble. The ones in shallow water would hit bottom first, since they wouldn't have as far to fall. Within the first second, a large fraction of the boats in lakes, rivers, and harbors would crash into the bottom, and many of those on board would survive. [Image: image] Boats out on the ocean would take longer to fall. Over the next five seconds, a wave of crashes would spread outward from the continents, as boats struck the continental shelf farther and farther from shore. These boats would be smashed to tiny fragments, killing everyone on board. After the first six or seven seconds, there would be a brief lull in the ship destruction rate. Continental shelves drop off steeply, and most of the ships out over the deep sea would take a little longer to fall. The Titanic sank in about two miles of water. After it disappeared beneath the surface, the two halves of the ship took between 5 and 15 minutes to reach the bottom.[2]When the Titanic bow hit the sea floor, it was moving at almost exactly the same speed as when it struck the iceberg three hours earlier. (This is not quite a coincidence.) Without the ocean there, it would have reached the bottom in about 30 seconds, striking it at airliner cruising speed.[3]Although no one has ever dropped a cruise ship from a high altitude,[citation needed] their terminal velocity at the surface is probably a little below the speed of sound. Because the air in the ocean basins would be compressed, the terminal velocity of ships near the bottom would be lower than at the surface. This compression also means that to magically replace the water, you'd need more air than you'd expect from the ocean's volume alone, since it would need a varying density profile. In other words, your water-replacement spells will need to have some calculations behind them. Sufficiently advanced magic is indistinguishable from technology. Within the first minute, just about every large ship would be on the bottom. The final boat to reach the bottom would probably be a small sailboat or life raft that was crossing an ocean trench when the water vanished. Thanks to low weight and/or drag from the sails, one of these vessels could take many minutes to reach the bottom. [Image: image] If there were a seaplane floating on the deep ocean, it could conceivably survive, although it would take some luck and quick thinking by the pilot. The plane would initially drop, but as it gained speed it would tend to pull into a glide. After the initial shock, the pilot would have a reasonable amount of time to try to start the engine. Thanks in part to the thicker air, it's possible a seaplane could successfully land (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YZx6wa6zHAc) on a smooth patch of seabed. If the engine got started, the pilot could also try to fly to shore and land on a runway. Fish, whales, and dolphins, and nearly all marine life would die immediately. Those near the bottom would suffocate or dessicate, while those near the surface in deeper water would suffer the same fate as boats. [Image: image] Then the really weird stuff starts. Without evaporation from lakes and oceans feeding the water cycle, it would stop raining. Without pools of water to drink from, people and most animals would dehydrate and die in a matter of days. Within a few weeks, plants would start withering in the ever-drier air. Within months, mass forest die-offs would begin.[4]Some drought-resistant trees could survive for years, but others wouldn't (http://treephys.oxfordjournals.org/content/33/3/252.full). Huge amounts of dry, dead vegetation lead inevitably to fire, and within a few years, most of the world's forests would have burned. Forests store huge amounts of CO2, and this burning would roughly double the amount of greenhouse gas in the atmosphere, accelerating global warming. All in all, Joanna's scenario would result in virtually all life dying out pretty fast. But then things would get even worse. [Image: image] Without a water cycle to weather rocks, the carbon-silicate feedback system which acts as a long-term thermostat to stabilize climate[5]CO2 is added to the atmosphere by volcanoes (although at the moment, it's being added about ten times faster by people.) When water flows over certain rocks, chemical reactions suck CO2 from the air and eventually bury it in seafloor sediments. With less CO2, the planet gets colder. A colder planet means less evaporation, which means less weathering, which means CO2 removal slows down. This feedback loop—which operates over much longer timescales than human-caused climate change—is probably what's kept the Earth's temperature relatively stable over the last few billion years (give or take a few snowball Earths (http://www.snowballearth.org/overview.html)) even though the Sun has gotten hotter (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faint_young_Sun_paradox). would shut down. Without this feedback, volcanic CO2 would build up in our atmosphere, leading—in the long term—to scorching temperatures similar to what's happened on Venus.[6]Interestingly, because of Venus's lighter color (and thus higher reflectivity), it only absorbs about half the solar radiation that Earth does despite being substantially closer to the Sun. The thick blanket of CO2 in its atmosphere is what keeps it hot (http://www.skepticalscience.com/Venus-runaway-greenhouse-effect.htm). We were going to lose our oceans anyway. As the Sun gets hotter, eventually water will start escaping through evaporation, and—one way or another—the planet will dry out and heat up. However, the loss of the oceans never seemed like something worth worrying too much about, since it's a billion years in the future. The oceans will be here long after our species is gone. [Image: image] Unless Joanna ruins everything.

items.model_answer:
If all the water on Earth vanished, the planet would rapidly transform into a desolate, lifeless desert, fundamentally altering its geology, atmosphere, and climate.

Biologically, the extinction of all life would be almost immediate. Every organism, from humans and animals to plants and microbes, relies on water as a solvent for biochemical reactions. Without it, cellular processes would cease within days. Plants would wither and die almost instantly, halting photosynthesis and stopping the production of atmospheric oxygen. The global food web would collapse, and terrestrial life would perish from dehydration within a few weeks. Marine life would die even faster, leaving behind vast, empty basins.

Geologically, the disappearance of oceans—which currently cover over 70% of the planet—would expose a massive, continuous landscape of oceanic crust. The extreme weight of the world's oceans currently presses down on the tectonic plates beneath them. Removing trillions of tons of water would cause the oceanic crust to buoyantly rebound and rise, while the continental crust, now lacking the counterweight of the oceans, could subtly sink or shift. This massive redistribution of planetary mass would trigger unprecedented, catastrophic earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, and tsunamis (of rock, not water) as tectonic plates violently adjusted to the new pressures. 

The climate and atmosphere would undergo radical shifts. Without water vapor—the most abundant and potent greenhouse gas on Earth—the planet's ability to trap heat would plummet. Global temperatures would swing to extremes: searing, uninhabitable heat in areas exposed to the sun, and freezing, sub-zero temperatures at night or in the shade. The lack of moisture would completely halt the water cycle, meaning no evaporation, no clouds, and no rain. Without clouds to reflect sunlight, the Earth's albedo would change, further exacerbating the temperature extremes. 

Additionally, the exposed seabeds, rich in hydrated minerals and salts, would dry out and be swept up by intense, unobstructed global winds. This would create colossal, toxic dust storms that would choke the remaining atmosphere with salt and mineral particles, eroding what little organic matter remained. Ultimately, Earth would become a barren, sterilized rock bearing only the fossilized remnants of a biosphere, resembling a harsh, extreme version of Mars or Venus.

edus.text: If all the water on Earth vanished,
the planet would rapidly transform into a desolate, lifeless desert,
fundamentally altering its geology, atmosphere, and climate.
Biologically, the extinction of all life would be almost immediate.
Every organism, from humans and animals to plants and microbes, relies on water as a solvent for biochemical reactions.
Without it, cellular processes would cease within days.
Plants would wither and die almost instantly,
halting photosynthesis and stopping the production of atmospheric oxygen.
The global food web would collapse,
and terrestrial life would perish from dehydration within a few weeks.
Marine life would die even faster,
leaving behind vast, empty basins.
Geologically, the disappearance of oceans—which currently cover over 70% of the planet—would expose a massive, continuous landscape of oceanic crust.
The extreme weight of the world's oceans currently presses down on the tectonic plates beneath them.
Removing trillions of tons of water would cause the oceanic crust to buoyantly rebound and rise,
while the continental crust, now lacking the counterweight of the oceans, could subtly sink or shift.
This massive redistribution of planetary mass would trigger unprecedented, catastrophic earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, and tsunamis (of rock, not water)
as tectonic plates violently adjusted to the new pressures.
The climate and atmosphere would undergo radical shifts.
Without water vapor—the most abundant and potent greenhouse gas on Earth—the planet's ability to trap heat would plummet.
Global temperatures would swing to extremes:
searing, uninhabitable heat in areas exposed to the sun,
and freezing, sub-zero temperatures at night or in the shade.
The lack of moisture would completely halt the water cycle,
meaning no evaporation, no clouds, and no rain.
Without clouds to reflect sunlight, the Earth's albedo would change,
further exacerbating the temperature extremes.
Additionally, the exposed seabeds, rich in hydrated minerals and salts, would dry out and be swept up by intense, unobstructed global winds.
This would create colossal, toxic dust storms
that would choke the remaining atmosphere with salt and mineral particles,
eroding what little organic matter remained.
Ultimately, Earth would become a barren, sterilized rock bearing only the fossilized remnants of a biosphere,
resembling a harsh, extreme version of Mars or Venus.

items.question: How Long Could Humanity Survive on Cannibalism Alone?
human_answers: There are about 500 trillion calories of human in the world. If it could be frozen or otherwise preserved, that would be enough—at least in terms of raw calories—to keep a tiny breeding population (http://www.newscientist.com/article/dn1936-magic-number-for-space-pioneers-calculated.html#.U8a1mo2gFSE) alive for millions of years. [Image: image] Eating nothing but meat sounds bad, nutritionally, but the lack of vegetables wouldn't necessarily kill you. People can survive on high-meat or all-meat diets, especially if they eat things like organ meat and bone marrow; there are more vitamins and nutrients found in those which are missing from the narrower range of mammal skeletal muscle and fat in the typical western diet. The US experienced meat shortages during World War II because so much food was being diverted to soldiers and allies overseas. In response to this, the US government decided to encourage Americans to eat more organs and other animal body parts. They employed some of the world's best anthropologists, psychologists, social scientists, and food scientists to figure out a way to change American eating habits. One of the ideas the project had was that these foods should be rebranded as variety meats.[1]More on this in the hilarious Mary Roach book Gulp: Adventures on the Alimentary Canal (http://www.amazon.com/Gulp-Adventures-Alimentary-Mary-Roach/dp/0393081575) A Google Books search (https://books.google.com/ngrams/graph?content=variety+meats&year_start=1800&year_end=2008&corpus=17&smoothing=3) shows the phrase appearing suddenly in US books around that time (a pattern not seen in British books (https://books.google.com/ngrams/graph?content=variety+meats&year_start=1800&year_end=2008&corpus=18&smoothing=3).) When the war ended, many of these research efforts were dropped, but this 2002 article (https://books.google.com/ngrams/graph?content=variety+meats&year_start=1800&year_end=2008&corpus=15&smoothing=3) tries to piece together what they learned. There are a lot of things we don't understand (http://www.nature.com/news/nutrition-vitamins-on-trial-1.15459) about nutritional deficiencies, and—to put it mildly—a lot of dispute over what kind of diets are healthy or aren't healthy. But no matter what nutrients we would or wouldn't get in Quinn's scenario, we'd face a bigger problem: contaminated food. Even if you cooked your meat, it would be hard to avoid all kinds of disease exposure as you worked your way through the remains of the human population. [Image: image] In a small enough population, every outbreak is a pandemic; it wouldn't take long for something to wipe you out. There are also some obvious practical problems. Unless you're one of a small handful of people (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_briefcase), you have no way to kill the majority of living humans without some of them killing you first. Let's consider a different scenario, one probably more in line with what Quinn was imagining: What if half the population ate the other half?[2]On second thought, I really have no idea what specific scenario Quinn was imagining, and I'm not sure I want to know. If the average human weighs 50 kilograms and eats a couple thousand calories per day, then—according to Ryan North (http://www.topatoco.com/merchant.mvc?Screen=PROD&Store_Code=TO&Product_Code=QW-PERSON&Category_Code=QW)—then one person contains enough meat to feed another person for about a month. If, every month, half the population eats the other half, we could go for 32 months[3]Which should make sense to the computer science students out there, since "7 billion" is just barely too big to store in a 32-bit integer. of cannibalism before the second-to-last person was eaten by the last. Eating people who have eaten other people is a bad idea. For starters, it's a bad idea because you're eating people. Why are you eating people!? But it's also bad because it's an effective way to transmit prion diseases (https://www.cdc.gov/prions/). On the other hand, most prion diseases have lengthy incubation periods, so it might be a lesser concern in a world where you have a 50% chance of getting eaten every month. Lastly, we'd have to decide who got eaten in which round. We could fight it out, or—to be fair—we could pair off and flip coins. If we did, the result would be, literally, ... [Image: image] ... the tournament bracket (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bracket_(tournament)) to end all tournament brackets.

criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer grounds the survival estimate in plausible calorie/biomass arithmetic, distinguishing short-term population-wide cannibalism from tiny-population preservation scenarios.
criteria.1-2: Gives no quantitative estimate or offers wildly implausible numbers with no basis in human biomass or calorie needs.
criteria.3-4: Mentions calories or population size but uses crude or inconsistent math that cannot support the stated survival time.
criteria.5-6: Provides a rough calorie-based estimate, such as one person feeding another for weeks, but misses key scaling implications.
criteria.7-8: Correctly reasons that repeated halving yields only a few dozen months for the global population, while stored biomass could support a tiny group far longer.
criteria.9-10: Clearly separates scenarios and supports each with coherent order-of-magnitude math, including human caloric content, daily needs, preservation, and population decay.

criteria.name: Counterfactual Scenario Control
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates how well the answer defines and maintains the counterfactual premise: humanity relying on cannibalism alone, including who eats whom, whether food is preserved, and whether reproduction is possible.
criteria.1-2: Ignores the premise or replaces it with unrelated famine, agriculture, or ordinary survival scenarios.
criteria.3-4: Engages cannibalism but leaves the scenario so vague that the conclusion is ambiguous or contradictory.
criteria.5-6: Specifies a basic scenario, such as survivors eating the dead, but inconsistently applies assumptions about storage, killing, or population size.
criteria.7-8: Maintains a clear scenario and notes how different assumptions produce different survival durations.
criteria.9-10: Explicitly compares major premise variants—mass die-off with preserved bodies, half-eat-half cycles, and tiny breeding population—and keeps conclusions conditional on each.

criteria.name: Biological and Nutritional Mechanism Coverage
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses coverage of physiological constraints beyond raw calories, including micronutrients, organ meat, fat/protein balance, disease, prions, and contamination.
criteria.1-2: Treats human flesh as generic food and ignores nutrition, disease, and spoilage.
criteria.3-4: Mentions one biological issue, such as disease or protein, but with little causal explanation.
criteria.5-6: Covers calories plus some nutrition or disease risks, though important mechanisms are missing or oversimplified.
criteria.7-8: Explains that all-meat survival may be possible with organs/fat/marrow but that contamination, spoilage, and pathogens become serious limiting factors.
criteria.9-10: Integrates nutrition, organ consumption, vitamin/fat needs, prion risk, infectious disease, cooking limits, and preservation into the survival estimate.

criteria.name: Long-Range Population and Social Dynamics
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates reasoning about downstream consequences over months to generations, including violence, governance, breeding population size, pandemics in small groups, and extinction risks.
criteria.1-2: Only discusses immediate eating and ignores population dynamics or social consequences.
criteria.3-4: Notes that people would fight or die but does not connect this to survival duration.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes population decline and social breakdown, but the causal chain is incomplete or short-range.
criteria.7-8: Connects cannibalism to repeated population halving, conflict, disease amplification, and the fragility of small survivor groups.
criteria.9-10: Builds a coherent long-range chain from initial allocation through demographic collapse, violence, disease outbreaks, reproduction constraints, and eventual extinction or tiny-population persistence.

criteria.name: Uncertainty Calibration and Contradiction Control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer appropriately qualifies uncertain claims and avoids internal contradictions about feasibility, duration, disease timing, and nutritional adequacy.
criteria.1-2: Presents absolute claims that contradict basic biology or its own assumptions.
criteria.3-4: Includes some caveats but makes unsupported certainties or inconsistent survival estimates.
criteria.5-6: Acknowledges uncertainty but does not clearly indicate which factors dominate the answer.
criteria.7-8: Uses cautious, conditional language and avoids major contradictions while identifying the main uncertainties.
criteria.9-10: Precisely calibrates confidence, distinguishes hard arithmetic from speculative biology/social behavior, and keeps all estimates consistent with stated assumptions.

items.model_answer:
Humanity could survive on cannibalism alone for approximately 1-3 years before facing extinction, though the exact timeline depends on starting population size and logistical factors.

The fundamental problem is thermodynamic: without external energy input, you're simply recycling existing biomass with metabolic losses at each transfer. An average adult human body contains roughly 80,000-100,000 calories of edible tissue, while a living person needs about 2,000-2,500 calories daily. This means one consumed body sustains one person for roughly 40-50 days, but each meal permanently reduces the population.

The math is stark: if everyone must eat another human every ~45 days, the population roughly halves each cycle. Starting with 8 billion people, you'd reach extinction in approximately 4 years through pure exponential decline. However, practical realities would accelerate this timeline significantly.

Nutritional deficiencies would emerge quickly—human tissue lacks adequate vitamin C (leading to scurvy), calcium, and other micronutrients in necessary ratios. Prion diseases like kuru, which afflicted cannibalistic populations in Papua New Guinea, would spread. Without infrastructure for food preservation, spoilage would waste calories. Social collapse and conflict would further reduce efficiency.

The scenario is essentially a closed system with inevitable entropy—each metabolic conversion loses energy, and no new energy enters the cycle. Even optimal rationing and preservation would only modestly extend survival before the population crashes below sustainable thresholds.

items.question: What If I Fired an Infinitely Powerful Laser into the Sky?
human_answers: A lot of the time, if a question includes the word "infinity," the answer is "an infinite amount"—when there's an answer at all. An infinitely strong laser pointer would deliver an infinite amount of energy to the air in its path, which would in turn radiate an infinite amount of energy in all directions, which would destroy everything. For more on this, see What If #13 (http://what-if.xkcd.com/13/). Except that's not really the right answer to your question. Most of our equations don't really work when you put "infinity" in them. So the right answer is "an infinitely strong laser beam isn't a real thing." [Image: image] But if you made a laser pointer stronger and stronger, the result would look more and more like what I described. This is sort of like the mathematical idea of taking a limit; you can't say what happens at infinity, but you can see how it acts as you get closer and closer to it. Since we looked at the "destroying the world" consequence in question #13, let's look at the other part of your question: The random aiming. First of all, if you aimed in a truly random direction, you would have an almost 50% chance of hitting the Earth. Almost 50%, but not quite. If we assume you're on a spherical Earth, ignoring hills and trees,[1]And ignoring refraction. you have a slightly better chance of missing the ground than hitting it—because you're holding the laser above the surface, and the Earth curves away from you: [Image: image] If you miss the Earth, 89,999 times out of 90,000, your beam will pass right out of the galaxy without hitting anything. When it does hit something, it will almost always be the Sun or the Moon. The first time I met astronomer Phil Plait (http://www.slate.com/blogs/bad_astronomy.html) in person, he mentioned a clever trick for calculating the "area" of the sky:[2]"Learn This One Weird Trick,"" he said, "Invented By a Local Schoolteacher!"‌[3]He didn't say that. The area of a sphere is 4πr2. Ok, great, but what's the "radius" of the sky? Well, if the sky is a sphere around us, the radius is "one radian", because that's the radius of anything. But a radian is also 57.3 degrees, which means the sky is 57.3 degrees "away" from us. 4 times pi times 57.3 = 41,253 square degrees. The Moon and the Sun each take up about 0.2 square degrees, and so the chance of hitting either one of them is about 1 in 180,000. Those aren't great odds, but they're better than the odds of hitting anything else. [Image: image] To calculate the odds of hitting something else, we can use this handy angular size (http://xkcd.com/1276/) reference as a shortcut, dividing the rough angular size of the object in the chart by the Earth's total area to see how much of the sky it covers. The odds of hitting one of Jupiter's moons, for example, are on the order of one in a trillion. Stars are even worse. Your odds of hitting any star at all on your way out of the galaxy are almost zero, even if you aim for the core. This is good, though! If your odds of hitting a star were high, it would mean the galaxy would be opaque. Since most "lines of sight" would terminate on a star, it would be very hard or impossible to see past our galaxy (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubble_Ultra-Deep_Field).[4]There are only a few stars in our galaxy in the Hubble Ultra-Deep Field image. The fact that the night sky is dark is at the core of Olbers' Paradox (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olbers'_paradox).[5]I was so tempted to vandalize this article to put a [citation needed] after every claim that the night sky was dark. If you kept shooting long enough, eventually you'd hit a planet. Neptune would be the hardest to hit, followed by Uranus and Mercury. Pluto would be the hardest, but it might be worth it. An impossibly powerful laser would at least settle that debate. [Image: image]

rubrics.question_focus: What If I Fired an Infinitely Powerful Laser into the Sky?

criteria.name: Treatment of the Infinite-Power Premise
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer correctly handles the counterfactual premise of an infinitely powerful laser: recognizing physical impossibility, avoiding naive misuse of equations at infinity, and using finite-power limits to reason about consequences.
criteria.1-2: Treats an infinite laser as ordinary or gives a simple literal answer with no recognition of physical impossibility.
criteria.3-4: Mentions that infinity is unrealistic but still relies on confused or unsupported infinite-energy claims.
criteria.5-6: Acknowledges impossibility and gives a basic finite-limit interpretation, but with limited physical explanation.
criteria.7-8: Clearly distinguishes impossible infinity from increasingly powerful finite lasers and explains why equations break down.
criteria.9-10: Precisely frames the scenario as a limiting counterfactual, avoids invalid infinities, and uses that framing consistently throughout.

criteria.name: Near-Field Atmospheric and Terrestrial Effects
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates coverage of the immediate causal consequences of firing an extremely powerful laser through the atmosphere, including energy deposition, plasma formation, radiation, heating, and possible global destruction.
criteria.1-2: Ignores the atmosphere and local environment or claims the beam simply travels upward harmlessly.
criteria.3-4: Mentions heat or damage vaguely but lacks mechanisms such as ionization, plasma, or radiation.
criteria.5-6: Explains that the air and ground would absorb enormous energy, causing severe local or global effects, but incompletely.
criteria.7-8: Covers atmospheric ionization, intense radiation, explosive heating, and likely catastrophic effects before space propagation.
criteria.9-10: Gives a coherent mechanism chain from beam-air interaction to runaway energy release and correctly notes destruction dominates the scenario.

criteria.name: Random Aiming Geometry and Earth-Hit Probability
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer reasons correctly about aiming in a truly random direction from Earth’s surface, including the near-50% chance of hitting Earth and the slight asymmetry caused by elevation and curvature.
criteria.1-2: Does not address random aiming direction or gives a plainly wrong probability.
criteria.3-4: Says roughly half the directions hit Earth but gives no geometric reasoning or misses the surface-position nuance.
criteria.5-6: Correctly identifies an approximately 50% Earth-hit chance and distinguishes upward from downward directions.
criteria.7-8: Explains the spherical-Earth geometry and why being above the surface makes the miss chance slightly greater than 50%.
criteria.9-10: Accurately and succinctly derives or justifies the near-half probability while noting assumptions like ignoring terrain and refraction.

criteria.name: Sky-Target Probabilities and Astronomical Scale
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates reasoning about what the beam is likely to hit if it misses Earth, including angular size, Sun/Moon probabilities, planets, moons, stars, and the overwhelming likelihood of escaping the galaxy.
criteria.1-2: Claims the beam would probably hit a star, planet, or galaxy without scale-based justification.
criteria.3-4: Mentions space is mostly empty but gives little or inaccurate probability reasoning.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes that most beams miss everything and that the Sun or Moon are among the likeliest targets.
criteria.7-8: Uses angular-size or sky-area reasoning to compare odds for Sun, Moon, planets, moons, and stars.
criteria.9-10: Accurately conveys orders of magnitude: Sun/Moon dominate rare hits, planets are far rarer, stars are nearly impossible, and most paths leave the galaxy.

criteria.name: Long-Range Causal Coherence and Uncertainty Control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer maintains a consistent causal chain from impossible premise to local destruction to rare astronomical interactions, while calibrating uncertainty and avoiding contradictions.
criteria.1-2: Presents disconnected claims, contradicts itself, or ignores major stages of the scenario.
criteria.3-4: Has a partial chain but jumps between effects with weak causality or inconsistent assumptions.
criteria.5-6: Maintains a mostly plausible sequence but omits key caveats or mixes finite and infinite cases inconsistently.
criteria.7-8: Provides a coherent end-to-end chain with explicit assumptions and reasonable uncertainty about speculative effects.
criteria.9-10: Integrates physical limits, immediate destruction, geometric probabilities, and cosmic outcomes into a noncontradictory, well-calibrated counterfactual analysis.

items.model_answer: If you fired an infinitely powerful laser into the sky, the immediate consequence would be the complete destruction of the laser device itself, as the infinite energy required to operate it would instantly vaporize the mechanism. As the beam projected upward, it would not simply illuminate the atmosphere; the infinite intensity would instantly ionize, superheat, and vaporize the column of air directly above it, triggering runaway nuclear fusion and the photodisintegration of all atmospheric molecules into a plasma of fundamental particles. However, the ultimate and most profound consequence arises from general relativity. Because energy and mass are equivalent, an infinitely powerful laser beam possesses infinite mass-energy density. This infinite concentration of energy along the beam's axis would curve spacetime infinitely, instantly collapsing the local region into a black hole. Because the energy powering this black hole is infinite, its event horizon would expand at the speed of light, rapidly swallowing the atmosphere, the Earth, the solar system, and eventually the entire observable universe, resulting in the complete gravitational obliteration of all existence.

items.question: What If One Person Owned All the Money in the World?
human_answers: So you've somehow found a way to gather all the world's money. We won't worry about how you did it—let's just assume you invented some kind of money-summoning magic spell. [Image: image] Physical currency—coins and bills—represents just a small percentage of the world's wealth. In theory, you could edit all the property records on Earth to say that you own all the land and edit all the banking records to say you own all the money. But everyone else would disagree with those records, and they would edit them back or ignore them. Money is an idea, and you can't make the entire world respect your idea. Getting all the world's cash, on the other hand, is much more straightforward. There's a certain amount of cash in the world—it's about $4 trillion—and you want it all. It won't necessarily do anything for you, since—without the cooperation of the outside world—you probably won't be able to spend it. But maybe you can swim around in it, like Scrooge McDuck in his giant room full of gold. [Image: image] So you cast your magic spell and summon all the money. The pile of cash is the size of the Empire State Building, but heavier. You probably don't want to be standing under it, so let's assume you're standing over here, off to the side: [Image: image] The vast majority of the weight in the pile is coins, and the biggest single contributor is the US penny. Despite periodic efforts to kill off the penny (http://www.retirethepenny.org/), the US Mint keeps producing more of them. [Image: image] There are probably 150 billion pennies[1]A 1996 GAO report mentioned a US Mint estimate of the number of pennies in circulation: 132 billion. If you're excited by phrases like "General Accounting Office", "auditing standards", and "Subcommittee on Domestic and International Monetary Policy", you can read the report here (http://gao.gov/assets/110/106568.pdf). If you're so excited about penny statistics that the GAO report isn't enough for you, you're in luck: There's another way to derive this number. We can get an idea of the number of pennies in circulation by looking at all the change in our pockets, counting the dates, and using that to estimate a loss rate. In 1999, some statisticians recorded the dates on 1,000 pennies they had lying around, and published the data in the book Workshop Statistics: Discovery with Data and Fathom, page 389 (http://books.google.com/books?id=wGMRja1vE0kC&lpg=PA389&pg=PA389#v=onepage&q&f=false). By plotting the frequency with which they saw pennies of various ages against the frequency we'd expect from US Mint production numbers, we can estimate the rate at which older pennies drop out of circulation per year. Using their numbers, I come up with an estimate of about 190,000,000,000 pennies in circulation. We can then apply the same formula to previous dates, and come up with a number for 1996, to check against the GAO number. (I have a lot of spare time on my hands.) Surprisingly, this produces an estimate that's still about 190,000,000,000. Either number (190 billion or 132 billion) is probably a reasonable estimate, but if you're serious about your penny statistics—and if you've read this far, you must be—you should probably go with the US Mint guess. After all, they presumably know a thing or two about counting pennies. currently in circulation, for a total weight of over 300,000 tons. In total, US coins and bills are responsible for about 30% of the pile's weight, while the European Union—which has barely been minting coins for a decade—contributes 15%. Unfortunately for you, the pile doesn't stay a pile for long,[2]When you pour lots of loose material in a heap, it tends to form a cone. Different materials will form cones with different slopes; the steepness of the slope for a given material is called its angle of repose. I've never found the exact angle of repose for coins—or had enough of them to test it—but a forum poster with the username Master of Coin (who claims to be well-acquainted with "how piles of coins 'slish' about") says (http://asoiaf.westeros.org/index.php/topic/78114-the-hobbit-a-long-expected-spoiler-movie-thread/?p=3985923) that it's probably no more than 5 or 10 degrees. and what seems like a safe distance isn't so safe. In 1919, a tank of molasses in Boston collapsed. Molasses is thick, so you might think it would flow out slowly, but it didn't. The wave of molasses swept down the streets too fast to outrun, demolishing buildings and killing 21 people. Something similar happens with the pile of coins. As it collapses, the pile spreads outward, a wave of money carrying a staggering amount of momentum. The pennies, quarters, loonies, and euros scour the landscape in an expanding ring. Within seconds, the wave of coins engulfs you and you die. [Image: image] There are ways to avoid this. You could, say, build a wall around the coins to contain them. Unfortunately, then you might face a problem worse than death: Building code violations. Heavy skyscrapers need ground strong enough to support them. Places with large skyscrapers, like those in Manhattan, need bedrock sturdy enough to hold them up.[3]For a long time, people said that this was why there was a gap in Manhattan's skyline—the bedrock wasn't strong enough to support skyscrapers in the middle. However, a 2011 paper in the Journal of Economic History (http://journals.cambridge.org/action/displayAbstract?fromPage=online&aid=8429737) says that this is a myth, and the bedrock had little influence on the location of skyscrapers. A search through this giant PDF of NYC building codes (http://www2.iccsafe.org/states/newyorkcity/Building/PDFs/Chapter%2018_Soils%20and%20Foundations.pdf) suggests that if we went ahead with this plan, we would be in serious danger of violating section 1804 ("ALLOWABLE BEARING PRESSURES"). Which makes me wonder: Did Scrooge McDuck ever have to worry about this stuff? [Image: image]

rubrics.question_focus: What If One Person Owned All the Money in the World?

criteria.name: Counterfactual Premise Handling: Ownership, Money, and Social Recognition
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer correctly frames the counterfactual distinction between legally/socially owning all wealth, controlling bank/property records, and physically possessing all cash, and reasons from that distinction rather than treating money as inherently powerful by itself.
criteria.1-2: Treats owning all money as automatically granting unquestioned control of all goods and people; ignores that money depends on social recognition.
criteria.3-4: Mentions that others might resist but still largely assumes ownership records or cash possession would be universally honored.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes that financial/property records can be rejected or reversed, but only partially separates cash, deposits, assets, and social legitimacy.
criteria.7-8: Clearly distinguishes physical currency from broader wealth and explains why institutional cooperation is necessary for money to function.
criteria.9-10: Precisely anchors the scenario in money as a social/legal system, separates cash from wealth and records, and uses this framing to constrain all later consequences.

criteria.name: Physical-Scale and Engineering Consequences of Summoning All Cash
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer covers the concrete STEM implications of gathering global physical currency: mass, volume, coin dominance, structural loads, pile stability, flow/collapse, and direct hazards.
criteria.1-2: Provides little or no physical reasoning; treats the money pile as a cartoon treasure hoard with no mass or stability issues.
criteria.3-4: Notes that the pile would be very large or heavy but gives no meaningful mechanisms or consequences.
criteria.5-6: Discusses size, weight, or danger from a huge cash pile, but misses major factors such as coins dominating mass or collapse/spreading.
criteria.7-8: Explains that trillions in cash, especially coins, would form an enormous, unstable, extremely heavy pile with crushing or structural hazards.
criteria.9-10: Covers mass/volume estimates, coin-heavy composition, angle-of-repose or spreading behavior, ground-bearing limits, and lethal momentum/containment problems in a coherent physical chain.

criteria.name: Economic and Institutional Downstream Effects
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses the plausibility and depth of reasoning about what happens to economies, governments, banks, markets, payment systems, and ordinary people if all currency or monetary claims are concentrated in one person's hands.
criteria.1-2: Gives simplistic claims such as the person becomes infinitely rich or everyone else becomes permanently poor, with no institutional response.
criteria.3-4: Mentions inflation, poverty, or collapse in vague terms but lacks causal explanation or distinguishes poorly between cash and digital money.
criteria.5-6: Identifies some likely responses, such as governments replacing currency or freezing records, but leaves major systems unexplored.
criteria.7-8: Explains that authorities, banks, and societies would likely invalidate, replace, ignore, or forcibly reverse the concentration, limiting spendability.

items.model_answer:
If one person owned all the money in the world, the most paradoxical outcome would be that the money itself would become virtually worthless. Money derives its value from its function as a medium of exchange—it only has purchasing power because other people accept it in trade for goods, services, and labor. If no one else has any money, there's no one to trade with, and the entire monetary system collapses.

The immediate consequence would be global economic paralysis. No one could buy food, pay rent, or conduct business using money. Commerce would grind to a halt, and people would rapidly revert to barter systems, creating alternative currencies based on commodities, labor credits, or digital tokens. These new currencies would become the real functioning money, rendering the hoarded original currency irrelevant.

The owner would face an impossible paradox: they couldn't spend their money without giving it away, which would immediately mean they no longer owned "all" the money. Any attempt to purchase something would require transferring money to someone else, breaking the monopoly. They could only maintain total ownership by never spending, which means the money serves no purpose.

Governments would almost certainly intervene—issuing new currency, seizing assets, or imposing emergency redistribution. Mass social unrest would likely force political solutions before the scenario could persist. Ultimately, the situation reveals that money is inherently a shared social system, not a private possession. One person owning all of it is self-defeating, like one person owning all the words in a language—without others to speak with, the words have no meaning.

items.question: What If You Teleported to the Surface of the Sun for One Nanosecond?
human_answers: Believe it or not, this wouldn't even warm you. The temperature of the surface of the Sun is about 5,800 K,[1]Or °C. When temperatures start having many digits in them, it doesn't really matter. give or take. If you stayed there for a while, you'd be cooked to a cinder, but a nanosecond is not very long—it's enough time for light to travel almost exactly a foot.[2]A light-nanosecond is 11.8 inches (0.29981 meters), which is annoyingly close to a foot. I think it would be nice to redefine the foot as exactly 1 light nanosecond. Because we don't have enough unit confusion in the world already. This raises some obvious questions, like "Do we redefine the mile to keep it at 5,280 feet?" and "Do we redefine the inch?" and "Wait, why are we doing this?" But I figure other people can sort that out. I'm just the idea guy here. [Image: image] I'm going to assume you're facing toward the Sun. In general, you should avoid looking directly at the Sun, but it's hard to avoid when it takes up a full 180 degrees of your view. [Image: image] In that nanosecond, about a microjoule of energy would enter your eye. A microjoule of light is not a lot. If you stare at a computer monitor with your eyes closed, then open them and shut them quickly, your eye will take in about as much light from the screen during your reverse blink[3]Is there a word for that? There should be a word for that. as it would during a nanosecond on the Sun's surface. During the nanosecond on the Sun, photons from the Sun would flood into your eye and strike your retinal cells. Then, at the end of the nanosecond, you'd jump back home. At this point, the retinal cells wouldn't even have begun responding. Over the next few million nanoseconds (milliseconds) the retinal cells—having absorbed a bunch of light energy—would get into gear and start signaling your brain that something had happened. [Image: image] You would spend one nanosecond on the Sun, but it would take 30,000,000 nanoseconds for your brain to notice. From your point of view, all you would see was a flash. The flash would seem to last much longer than your time on the Sun, only fading as your retinal cells quieted down. The energy absorbed by your skin would be minor—about 10-5 joules per cm2 of exposed skin. For comparison, according to the IEEE P1584 standard (as quoted (http://www.arcadvisor.com/faq/threshold-incident-energy-second-degree-burn.html) on ArcAdvisor.com), holding your finger in the blue flame of a butane lighter for one second delivers about 5 joules per cm2 to the skin, which is roughly the threshold for receiving a second-degree burn. The heat during your Sun visit would be five orders of magnitude weaker. Other than the dim flash in your eyes, you wouldn't even notice. But what if you got the coordinates wrong? The Sun's surface is relatively cool. It's hotter than, like, Phoenix,[citation needed (https://www.google.com/search?tbm=isch&q=gibson+citation)] but compared to the interior, it's downright chilly. The surface is a few thousand degrees, but the interior is a few million degrees.[4]The corona, the thin gas high above the surface, is also several million degrees, and no one knows why (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corona#Coronal_heating_problem). What if you spent a nanosecond there? [Image: image] The Stefan-Boltzmann law (http://hyperphysics.phy-astr.gsu.edu/hbase/thermo/stefan.html) lets us calculate how much heat you'd be exposed to while inside the Sun.[5]There's also direct pressure from the heavy particles, protons and stuff, bouncing around, but the radiation turns out to be the dominant component. I'm going to hijack this note to ask another question: How does this transporter work, anyway? When you teleport somewhere, presumably it does gets rid of the matter that was in the way, so you don't end up combining yourself with whatever was there. A simple solution is to have the teleporters swap matter between the two locations. Kirk gets teleported down to the planet, a Kirk-sized chunk of air gets teleported up to the Enterprise. So what would happen if an AJ-shaped chunk of Sun-interior gets teleported to snowy Colorado, then we just left it there? The protons inside the Sun bounce around at speeds of about 350 km/s (about half of the Sun's escape velocity at that depth, for weird and deep (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virial_theorem) reasons.) Freed from their crushingly hot neighborhood, the whole collection of protons would burst outward, pouring light and heat energy into their surroundings. The energy released would be somewhere between a large bomb and a small nuclear weapon. It's not good. You would exceed the IEEE P1584B standard for second-degree burns after one femtosecond in the Sun.[6]Although it wouldn't be a second-degree burn until many picoseconds later, since the definition of a second-degree burn is one which damages some of the underlying layers of tissue—and in the first few femtoseconds, light wouldn't have time to reach the underlying tissue. A nanosecond—the time you're spending there—is 1,000,000 femtoseconds. This does not end well for you. There's some good news: Deep in the Sun, the photons carrying energy around have very short wavelengths—they're mostly a mix of what we'd consider hard and soft X-rays.[7]<what_if_book_reference>I wonder if there are more soft or hard x-ray photons in the universe.</what_if_book_reference> This means they penetrate your body to various depths, heating your internal organs and also ionizing your DNA, causing irreversible damage before they even start burning you. Looking back, I notice that I started this paragraph with "there's some good news." I don't know why I did that. [Image: image] In Greek legend, Icarus (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Icarus) flew too close to the Sun, and the heat melted his wings and he fell to his death. But "melting" is a phase change which is a function of temperature, a measure of internal energy, which is the integral of incident power flux over time. His wings didn't melt because he flew too close to the Sun, they melted because he spent too much time there. Visit briefly, in little hops, and you can go anywhere. [Image: image]

items.model_answer:
If you teleported to the Sun's surface (the photosphere) for exactly one nanosecond, you would survive essentially unharmed and might not even perceive the experience.

The key insight is that one nanosecond (10⁻⁹ seconds) is simply too brief for significant energy transfer to occur. While the photosphere temperature is about 5,500°C, heat diffusion into your skin would only penetrate roughly 12 nanometers—about the thickness of a single dead skin cell on your epidermis. The outermost layer of your skin is already dead tissue, so this minimal thermal exposure would cause no meaningful damage.

Radiation exposure would also be negligible. The Sun's surface emits about 63 megawatts per square meter, but over one nanosecond this translates to only about 0.06 joules per square meter. For a human body with roughly 2 square meters of surface area, you'd absorb approximately 0.13 joules total—comparable to the energy of a gentle tap. This is orders of magnitude below what would cause a sunburn or radiation injury.

The photosphere's density is actually extremely low—about one ten-thousandth of Earth's atmosphere at sea level—so there would be no crushing pressure effect.

You likely wouldn't even consciously register the event, as human neural processing operates on millisecond timescales, a million times slower. You'd teleport back with perhaps the most infinitesimal sunburn in history on your outermost dead skin cells, which you'd shed naturally within days anyway.

items.question: What If Auto Racing Had Only One Rule: The Driver Must Survive?
human_answers: The best you'll be able to do is about 90 minutes. There are lots of ways you could build your vehicle—an electric car,[1]With wheels designed to dig into the pavement on turns. a rocket sled, or a carriage that runs along a rail on the track—but in each case, it's pretty easy to develop the design to the point where the human is the weakest part. The problem is acceleration. On the curved parts of the track, drivers will feel powerful G forces.[2]Which you can broadly call either "centrifugal" or "centripetal" forces, depending on exactly which type of pedant you want to annoy. The Daytona Speedway in Florida has two main curves, and if the vehicles go around them too fast, the drivers will die from the acceleration alone. [Image: image] For extremely brief periods, such as during car accidents, people can experience hundreds of Gs and survive. (One G is the pull you feel when standing on the ground under Earth's gravity.) Fighter pilots can experience up to 10 Gs during maneuvers, and—perhaps because of that—10 Gs is often used as a rough limit for what people can handle. However, fighter pilots only experience 10 Gs very briefly. Our driver would be experiencing them, in pulses, for minutes and probably hours. There's a good NASA document on the physical effects of acceleration here (http://ntrs.nasa.gov/archive/nasa/casi.ntrs.nasa.gov/19930020462.pdf), and a particularly helpful chart in Figure 5 here (http://history.nasa.gov/conghand/mannedev.htm). But the most fun data comes from John Paul Stapp. Stapp was an Air Force officer who strapped himself into a rocket sled and pushed his body to the limit, taking careful notes after every run. You can read a great essay (http://www.ejectionsite.com/stapp.htm) about him on the Ejection Site (http://www.ejectionsite.com/). The whole story is fascinating, but my favorite line is, "... Stapp was promoted to the rank of major [and] reminded of the 18 G limit of human survivability ..." Stapp aside, the data shows that for periods on the order of an hour, normal humans can only handle 3-6 Gs of acceleration. If we limit our vehicle to 4 Gs, its top speed on the turns at Daytona will be about 240 mph. At this speed, the course will take about 2 hours to complete—which is definitely faster than anyone has driven it in an actual car, but not by that much. But wait! What about the straightaways? The vehicle will be accelerating during the turns, but coasting on the straightaways. We could instead accelerate the vehicle up to a higher speed while on straight segments, then decelerate it back down when approaching the end. This would result in a speed profile like this: [Image: image] This has the additional advantage that—with some clever back-and-forth maneuvering on the track—the driver can be kept at a relatively constant acceleration through the whole trip, hopefully making the forces easier to endure. [Image: image] Keep in mind that the direction of the acceleration will keep changing. Humans can survive acceleration best if they're accelerated forward, in the direction of their chest, like a driver accelerating forward. The body is least capable of being accelerated downward toward the feet, which causes blood to pile up in the head. To keep our driver alive, we'll need to swivel them around so they're always being pressed against their back. (But we have to be careful not to change direction too fast, or the centrifᵫtal[3]Splitting the difference. force from the swiveling of the seat will itself become deadly!) [Image: image] The fastest modern Daytona racers take about 3 hours to finish the 200 laps. If limited to 4 Gs, our driver will finish the course in a little under an hour and 45 minutes. If we raise the limit to 6 Gs, the time drops to an hour and 20. At 10 Gs—well past human tolerability—it would still take an hour. (It would also involve breaking the sound barrier on the backstretch.) So, barring dubious concepts like liquid breathing (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liquid_breathing), human biology limits us to Daytona finishing times over an hour. What if we drop the "survive" requirement? How fast can we get the vehicle to go around the track? Imagine a "vehicle" anchored with Kevlar straps to a pivot in the center, reinforced with a counterweight on the other side. In effect, this is a giant centrifuge. This lets us apply one of my favorite weird equations,[4]See footnote [8] in article #86 (http://what-if.xkcd.com/86/). which says that the edge of a spinning disc can't go faster than the square root of the specific strength[5](tensile strength divided by density) of the material it's made of. For strong materials like Kevlar, this speed is 1-2 km/s. At those speeds, a capsule could conceivably finish the race in about 10 minutes—although definitely not with a living driver inside. Ok, forget the centrifuge. What if we build a solid chute, like a bobsled course, and send a ball bearing (our "vehicle") rocketing down it? Sadly, the disc equation strikes again—the ball bearing can't roll faster than a couple km/s or it will be spinning too fast and will tear itself apart. Instead of making it roll, what if we make it slide? We could imagine a diamond cube sliding along a smooth diamond chute. Since it doesn't need to rotate, it could potentially survive more accelerations than a rolling ball bearing. However, the sliding would result in substantially more friction than the ball bearing example, and our diamond might catch fire (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WWpm6_Y7ASI). [Image: image] To defeat friction, we could levitate the capsule with magnetic fields, and make it progressively smaller and lighter to accelerate and steer it more easily. Oops—we've accidentally built a particle accelerator. And while it doesn't exactly fit the criteria in Hunter's question, a particle accelerator makes for a neat comparison. The particles in the LHC's beam go very close to the speed of light. At that speed, they complete 500 miles (30 laps) in 2.7 milliseconds. Wikipedia lists (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_motor_racing_tracks) about 850 motor racing tracks. The LHC beam could run the equivalent of a full Daytona 500 on each of those 850 tracks, one after another, in about 2 seconds, before the drivers had made it to the first turn. [Image: image] And that's really as fast as you can go.

rubrics.question_focus: What If Auto Racing Had Only One Rule: The Driver Must Survive?

criteria.name: Counterfactual Premise Fidelity and Scope Control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer correctly interprets the premise as removing racing regulations while retaining the requirement that a living human driver survives the full race, rather than treating it as ordinary racing, unmanned speed records, or arbitrary sci-fi.
criteria.1-2: Misreads the premise; ignores driver survival or treats the scenario as normal auto racing.
criteria.3-4: Acknowledges fewer rules but inconsistently applies survival or allows clearly non-survivable designs.
criteria.5-6: Maintains driver survival in most reasoning but occasionally drifts into unmanned or impossible cases.
criteria.7-8: Consistently centers the living driver constraint and distinguishes survivable from non-survivable designs.
criteria.9-10: Precisely frames the counterfactual, separates legal freedom from biological/physical limits, and avoids scope creep.

criteria.name: Human Acceleration and Biomechanics Modeling
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates how well the answer explains that the main bottleneck is sustained human tolerance to acceleration, especially lateral/centripetal forces on turns and changing acceleration direction.
criteria.1-2: Omits G-forces or gives biologically impossible claims about what drivers can survive.
criteria.3-4: Mentions G-forces superficially but lacks sustained-exposure limits or directional effects.
criteria.5-6: Identifies acceleration as a key limit and gives roughly plausible human tolerance ranges.
criteria.7-8: Explains sustained versus brief G exposure, turn forces, and driver orientation with good plausibility.
criteria.9-10: Uses acceleration biology rigorously, including duration, direction, pulsed loading, seat orientation, and survivability margins.

criteria.name: Vehicle, Track, and Speed-Profile Mechanism Coverage
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer develops plausible mechanisms for optimizing speed under the survival rule, including track curvature, straightaway acceleration/deceleration, rails/sleds/electric vehicles, and ways to manage driver loading.
criteria.1-2: Provides no meaningful mechanism for how the race would be run faster.
criteria.3-4: Suggests fast vehicles but ignores track geometry or how turns constrain speed.
criteria.5-6: Covers turns and straightaways but with limited detail or incomplete causal links.
criteria.7-8: Describes credible optimized speed profiles and vehicle concepts tied to track geometry.
criteria.9-10: Integrates vehicle design, banking/rails/traction, straightaway boosts, braking, and driver-position control into a coherent optimization.

criteria.name: Long-Range Consequence Coherence and Boundary Cases
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer follows downstream implications beyond the first design idea, including why stronger vehicles stop helping once the human is limiting, and what changes if survival or driver definitions are relaxed.
criteria.1-2: Stops at a single unsupported claim with no downstream reasoning.
criteria.3-4: Lists consequences but they are disconnected or causally weak.
criteria.5-6: Shows some chain reasoning from rule removal to faster vehicles to biological limits.
criteria.7-8: Develops a coherent chain through multiple designs and explains why each hits a limit.
criteria.9-10: Explores survivable and non-survivable boundary cases, such as centrifuges, chutes, magnetic levitation, or particle-like analogies, while keeping them logically separated.

criteria.name: Quantitative Plausibility, Uncertainty Calibration, and Contradiction Control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether estimates of speeds, times, accelerations, and material limits are physically plausible, appropriately qualified, and mutually consistent with the survival premise.
criteria.1-2: Contains major numerical or physical contradictions, such as unlimited speed with a surviving driver.
criteria.3-4: Uses numbers or claims that are mostly unsupported, inconsistent, or off by implausible orders of magnitude.
criteria.5-6: Provides rough plausible estimates but with weak uncertainty handling or minor inconsistencies.
criteria.7-8: Gives consistent order-of-magnitude reasoning for G limits, turn speeds, and race times with sensible caveats.
criteria.9-10: Calibrates uncertainty carefully, avoids overprecision, reconciles all estimates, and clearly flags speculative extensions.

items.model_answer:
If auto racing had only one rule—that the driver must survive—the sport would transform into something unrecognizable, essentially becoming a competition of human endurance engineering at the edge of physiological limits.

**Vehicle Evolution**
Cars would become survival pods strapped to propulsion systems. Without technical restrictions, teams would deploy jet engines, rocket thrusters, and fan-assisted ground effects. The only design constraint would be keeping the driver alive, leading to heavily armored cockpits with crash-attenuating materials, perhaps fluid-immersion systems to withstand extreme G-forces, and redundant life support. Vehicles could shed all conventional safety equipment meant to protect others—no crumple zones designed for opponent survival, no speed limiters, no restrictions on debris-generating designs.

**The G-Force Ceiling**
The ultimate limiting factor would become human physiology. Sustained G-forces above about 9G cause blackout and organ damage, so cornering speeds would hit a biological ceiling. Innovation would focus on G-suits, anti-G straining techniques, and possibly surgical or pharmaceutical enhancements. Drivers might be selected for genetic G-tolerance, and the sport could see pressure for cyborg-like integration between pilot and machine.

**Spectator and Bystander Danger**
With no rules protecting anyone else, cars could shed parts at 400+ mph, spray superheated exhaust, or crash into crowds. Races would likely move to remote locations, become fully remote-viewed, or shift to virtual spectatorship. Pit crews would face extreme hazard.

**Racing Format**
Wheel-to-wheel racing would become nearly impossible at such speeds and with such lethal vehicles. The sport would likely evolve into time trials or endurance challenges where survival itself becomes the victory condition.

The result: a sport that's less about driving skill and more about pushing the boundary of what human biology can endure while hurtling at the physics limit of ground-based propulsion.

items.question: What If Your Income Materialized around You in Cash?
human_answers: First, let's think about coins. The US federal minimum wage in the US is \$7.25/hour, which is about \$15,000/year for a full-time job. If you earn the minimum wage, you make a penny every 5 seconds during work hours, or every 20 seconds if you average it over your whole week. [Image: image] Someone making minimum wage in pennies would earn about 30 lbs of pennies per workday. Two weeks' worth of pay in pennies would fill a small carry-on suitcase. At 150 lbs, the suitcase would probably be too heavy to pick up. However, if they were paid in quarters instead of pennies, two weeks' pay would only weigh about 3 lbs. If paid in a typical mix of loose change,[1]The makeup of a "mix of loose change" depends on your spending habits. Lots of people have calculated this to estimate the amounts of change in a jar. One of the more careful theoretical calculation I've seen, which considers prices and sales tax, comes from Dan Kozikowski (http://dfkoz.tumblr.com/post/20389927354/whats-a-pound-of-change-worth). Since I've spent way too much time on this question over the years, for the record: If you're ever trying to guess the value of coins in a jar, my suggestion would be \$13.05/lb and \$468/gallon if the person doesn't use quarters for laundry or parking, \$9.53/lb and \$336/gallon if they do, and \$16.75/lb and \$611/gallon if they discard pennies. the US federal minimum wage is about one plastic water bottle full of coins per workday, and the median household earns three or four water bottles per workday. [Image: image] A CEO of a large company might make \$40,000 per workday (http://news.yahoo.com/median-ceo-pay-crosses-10-million-2013-104644141--finance.html). Assuming an 8-hour workday, that's 130 pennies per second. If paid in a mix of loose change, the CEO would earn about a water bottle of coins per minute, and a duffel bag full of loose change every hour, or 600 water bottles per workday: [Image: image] If you're a CEO working in a 300 ft2 office, the change would accumulate on the ground at a rate of about only half an inch per day. (If it were pennies, it would be more like 3" per day). It would mean frequently getting up to adjust your desk so it stayed on top of the pile, and I can't imagine your chair would be too stable, but it seems like it might be manageable. Lugging those 150-kg duffel bags to CoinStar every hour would be a hassle. If we allowed paper money, things would get easier. A dollar bill has a volume of about 1.55 mL, which means that a CEO paid in dollar bills would only need one large-ish duffel bag for a day's pay. If paid in \$100 bills, a CEO would only need a couple (http://xkcd.com/1070/) of duffel bags to carry home their year's salary. In either case, at 60-70 lbs, a duffel bag full of bills would be a little on the heavy side. [Image: image] Now, there are people who make a lot more than "typical CEOs". Mark Zuckerberg, Warren Buffett, and Bill Gates all made in the neighborhood of \$10 billion in 2013 (http://www.wealthx.com/articles/2013/revealed-billionaires-who-made-the-biggest-financial-gains-in-2013/). During the workday, that's a duffel bag full of \$100 bills every half-hour. Going back to our earlier metric, that's 25 water bottles full of change—one minimum-wage worker's daily salary—per second of the workday. [Image: image] If randomly dispensed from the ceiling in the form of loose change, Mark Zuckerberg's income would pile up at an inch every minute. There would be so many coins hitting the ground per second that it would meld into white noise.[2]The Mark Zuckerberg Money Pump would require over a kilowatt of power just to hoist the coins up to his ceiling and drop them. But that's not a problem. Even a penny is worth enough to pay for the electricity to hoist itself several thousand miles upward (http://www.wolframalpha.com/input/?i=1+penny+%2F+%28cost+of+electricity%29+%2F+%28penny+mass+*+earth+gravity%29). The downward force from the coins falling on Mark's head and shoulders would certainly be annoying, but not debilitating. It would be possible for him to walk around, but if he sat still for an hour, he'd be buried. [Image: image] It does sound awful.
