items.question: What If There Were Both a Space Elevator and a Stairway to Space?
human_answers: A week or two, if you're a champion stair-climber. Or 12 hours if you're on a motorcycle. A tower to space would be very different from a space elevator. A space elevator (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_elevator) would be about 100,000 kilometers tall, while a tower "to space" would only need to be 100 kilometers. As Ethan mentions, it would need to be pressurized, with an airlock every few miles. [Image: image] A stairway to space[1]If there's a bustle in your hedgerow, well, uh, boy, I don't know what to tell you. I guess ask it to leave? would have about half a million steps. World-champion stair-climbers[2]or "towerrunners" like Christian Riedl (http://stairsport.com/12h-stair-climbing-world-record-attempt-by-christian-riedl/) or Kristin Frey (http://www.kristinfrey.com/) can travel roughly a Mount Everest's height in a day; Riedl set the half-day record last October by climbing 13,145.65 meters (http://www.guinnessworldrecords.com/world-records/stair-climbing-vertical-height-%2812-hours%29) in 12 hours. At that pace—taking the other twelve hours to rest, eat, and sleep each day—it would take him a little over a week to reach the top. Climbing all those stairs would burn calories, which would mean you'd need to carry food. It turns out that the most efficient food you can carry, in terms of calories per pound, is butter—which is why Arctic explorers carry so much of it (http://abcnews.go.com/Technology/GlobalWarming/story?id=4853093). Suppose your backpack (http://www.amazon.co.uk/Disney-Frozen-Childrens-Multicoloured-FROZEN001018/dp/B00O2EO8XU) holds 9 liters. Climbing 10 stairs (http://journals.lww.com/acsm-msse/pages/articleviewer.aspx?year=2002&issue=04000&article=00021&type=abstract) burns about a calorie, which means climbing all the way up to space will burn about 72,000 calories. If you fill your backpack with butter, it would hold almost enough calories (http://www.wolframalpha.com/input/?i=9+liters+of+butter) to get you to the top. However, since it would take you weeks to climb all those stairs, you'd also need your normal dietary allowance of 2,000 calories (three sticks of butter) per day. Combining that with the 72,000 calories just from climbing the stairs, and you'd probably need to upgrade to a more serious 16-liter backpack (http://www.disneystore.com/anna-and-elsa-backpack-for-girls-personalizable/mp/1367267/1000290/). If you fill that backpack with butter, it will let you carry around 110,000 calories,[3]Coincidentally, about the amount you get (http://www.topatoco.com/merchant.mvc?Screen=PROD&Product_Code=QW-PERSON) from eating a human body. which should be enough to get you to the top if you're really dedicated. If you didn't want to eat 35 pounds of butter,[4]For whatever weird reason. you could try getting to the top by motorcycle. Based on how quickly this rider (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=k8CZiqEjQDk) ascends 45 stairs, a motorcycle could conceivably make it to the top in a day. [Image: image] Ok, so you got to the top. Now what? Getting up to space isn't that hard, after all—the hard part is getting into orbit (http://what-if.xkcd.com/58/), and the tower doesn't help you very much with that. So what else could you do? Michael Longuet-Higgins (http://noc.ac.uk/about-us/history/national-oceanography-centre-southampton/influential-scientists/professor-michael-s) was a research professor at the University of Cambridge and an expert in fluid dynamics, bubbles, and unusual types of waves.[5]Given his apparent research interests, this video (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=p70s1BNvBXI) would blow his mind.​[6]Or this one (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=711bZ_pLusQ), or this gadget (https://www.kickstarter.com/projects/creatableslabs/project-nesm-never-ending-slinky-machine), or this (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JwohMl9Toww). In 1953, Dr. Longuet-Higgins was shown, by a colleague, an "interesting toy" which had recently appeared on the market. This toy, "Slinky," had some unusual properties. The professor immediately set to work analyzing it, and wrote up his results in a paper (http://www2.eng.cam.ac.uk/~hemh/TV/On_Slinky_the_dynamics_of_a_loose_heavy_spring.pdf). Dr. Longuet-Higgins first determined through mathematical modeling that the rate at which the Slinky descends steps should depend only on the properties of the spring itself, and not the size or shape of the stairs. He and his colleague conducted a series of experiments "on five different flights of stairs, of various dimensions, in Trinity College, Cambridge." Their conclusion: The Slinky descended a constant rate of about 0.8 seconds per step.[7]Except on some wide, flat stairs, where the Slinky "came to rest after three or four steps at most," which gives me a wonderful mental image of two disappointed British professors at the bottom of a staircase.​[8]Sadly, this was before the invention of the StairMaster. Fun fact: After a surprise StairMaster management shakeup in 2011, for some reason not a single newspaper ran the headline "StairMaster CEO steps down". Dr. Longuet-Higgins determined that the Slinky quickly reached a constant descent rate after first few steps. This tells us that if you placed a Slinky (similar to his) at top of the stairway to space, and gave it just the right nudge ... [Image: image] ... it would make it back to the bottom in just over five days. Or, to put that in more appetizing units: [Image: image]

rubrics.question_focus: What If There Were Both a Space Elevator and a Stairway to Space?

criteria.name: Counterfactual setup fidelity: elevator vs stairway
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer correctly preserves the key physical distinction in the prompt: a space elevator and a stairway/tower to 'space' are not equivalent structures and imply very different scales, endpoints, and engineering constraints.
criteria.1-2: Treats the stairway and space elevator as the same thing, or assumes both simply reach orbit with no distinction.
criteria.3-4: Mentions a difference between them but gives major wrong scales or endpoints, such as a 100 km elevator or a stairway reaching geostationary orbit.
criteria.5-6: Correctly notes that the stairway only needs to reach near-space while the elevator must extend vastly farther, but gives limited detail.
criteria.7-8: Explains the approximate scale contrast, such as ~100 km for a stairway/tower to space versus tens of thousands to ~100,000 km for an elevator, and distinguishes reaching space from reaching orbit.
criteria.9-10: Precisely anchors the counterfactual around both structures coexisting, clearly separating the stairway's atmospheric/altitude role from the elevator's orbital transport role and using that distinction consistently throughout.

criteria.name: Mechanism coverage for human ascent on the stairway
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer plausibly reasons through what climbing or riding up a stairway to space would require, including atmosphere, pressure, food/energy, time, fatigue, and access infrastructure.
criteria.1-2: Ignores human survival and ascent mechanics, or says people can simply walk up into space unaided.
criteria.3-4: Mentions one issue such as oxygen or fatigue but leaves most survival and logistics mechanisms unexplained.
criteria.5-6: Covers several relevant constraints, such as pressurization, airlocks, time to climb, food, and rest, but with shallow or partially inconsistent reasoning.
criteria.7-8: Provides a coherent account of a pressurized stairway, repeated airlocks or stations, ascent times on the order of days to weeks for climbers, and energy/food requirements.
criteria.9-10: Integrates the stairway mechanics quantitatively and causally, including approximate step counts or altitude, climb-rate limits, calories, rest cycles, pressure management, and why vehicles might change the timescale.

criteria.name: Orbital mechanics and transport consequences
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer correctly reasons about the major downstream consequence: getting to 100 km altitude is not the same as achieving orbital velocity, while a true space elevator can provide access to orbital energy and momentum regimes.
criteria.1-2: Claims that reaching the top of the stairway automatically puts a person or payload safely in orbit.
criteria.3-4: Vaguely mentions orbit but confuses altitude, escape velocity, and orbital velocity in ways that undermine the answer.
criteria.5-6: States that the hard part is getting into orbit, not merely reaching space, but does not develop the implication for the two structures.
criteria.7-8: Explains that the stairway mainly saves altitude while leaving most orbital velocity needs, whereas the elevator could lift payloads to orbital or beyond-orbital radii.
criteria.9-10: Accurately connects altitude, tangential velocity, geostationary radius, tether rotation, and launch/reentry options, showing how the elevator and stairway would complement or fail to complement each other.

criteria.name: Long-range causal coherence under coexistence
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer follows a coherent chain of effects if both a stairway/tower to space and a space elevator existed, including infrastructure interaction, safety, economics, traffic, and plausible scientific or practical uses.
criteria.1-2: Lists disconnected jokes or effects with no causal chain and little relation to both structures existing.
criteria.3-4: Gives a few consequences but they are mostly isolated, speculative, or inconsistent with earlier assumptions.
criteria.5-6: Provides a plausible sequence of downstream effects, such as tourism, maintenance, launch support, or emergency access, but misses important interactions.
criteria.7-8: Develops multiple connected consequences: stairway as a novelty or access tower, elevator as cargo/orbit infrastructure, safety bottlenecks, maintenance, weather, and operational separation.
criteria.9-10: Builds a sustained long-range scenario in which physical constraints drive engineering design, costs, logistics, public use, failure modes, and societal or scientific impacts without losing the original premise.

criteria.name: Uncertainty calibration and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer uses appropriate confidence, avoids overclaiming in speculative areas, and remains internally consistent with known physics and the counterfactual assumptions.
criteria.1-2: Contains severe contradictions, impossible claims presented as certain, or ignores the counterfactual premise entirely.
criteria.3-4: Has several internal inconsistencies or unsupported exact claims, such as incompatible ascent times or changing structure heights.
criteria.5-6: Mostly consistent but includes some uncalibrated speculation, vague numbers, or minor contradictions.
criteria.7-8: Clearly separates approximate estimates from firm physical constraints and avoids major contradictions about altitude, pressure, orbit, and travel time.
criteria.9-10: Maintains tight consistency across all estimates and assumptions, flags uncertainty where materials or engineering are counterfactual, and never lets humor or speculation override causal plausibility.

items.model_answer:
If both a space elevator and a stairway to space existed simultaneously, they would serve fundamentally different purposes despite reaching the same destination.

The space elevator would function as the practical workhorse—efficiently transporting cargo and passengers via mechanical climbers along a tether at high speeds. It would be the industrial backbone of space access, moving tons of materials and hundreds of people quickly and economically.

The stairway, by contrast, would be extraordinarily impractical for transportation. Even reaching the Kármán line (100 km) would require climbing over 500,000 steps—far beyond human endurance. To geostationary orbit at 35,786 km, you'd face billions of steps requiring months of climbing. The stairway would instead become a symbolic and ceremonial structure, perhaps used for extreme endurance challenges, religious pilgrimages, or as the ultimate tourist experience with rest stations and pressurized habitats along the route.

Structurally, both would face similar engineering challenges—requiring materials like carbon nanotubes to withstand enormous tensile stresses—and both would be vulnerable to space debris, weather, and sabotage. However, having redundant access systems would provide critical safety benefits; if one system failed, the other could serve as an emergency evacuation route.

Economically, the stairway's maintenance costs would be staggering relative to its utility, likely requiring it to function as a luxury destination or cultural monument to justify its existence alongside the more practical elevator.

items.question: What If Tug-of-War Teams Pulled on an Iron Rod Instead of a Rope?
human_answers: A couple dozen people could pull a half-inch iron rod apart. Tug-of-war, a simple game in which two teams try to pull a rope in opposite directions, has a surprisingly bloody history. I don't mean that there's some kind of gruesome historical forerunner of modern tug-of-war.[1]Although it's definitely an ancient sport (http://www.usatowa.com/history.html), so I'm sure people have come up with all kinds of horrific variations over the centuries that I don't really want to spend hours reading about. Humans seem to be creative when it comes to that kind of thing. I mean that modern tug-of-war involves a lot more death and mutilation than you might expect—precisely because people underestimate how few people it takes to break "strong" things like heavy rope. As detailed in a riveting article (http://priceonomics.com/a-history-of-tug-of-war-fatalities/) in Priceonomics, recent games of tug-of-war have resulted in hundreds of serious injuries and numerous deaths—all caused, one way or another, by ropes snapping. In particular, this seems to happen when large groups of students try to set a world record for largest tug-of-war game. When a rope under many tons of tension suddenly snaps, the recoiling ends can—and do—cause a terrifying variety of injuries. [Image: image] Before we answer Markus's question, it's worth noting that the physics of tug-of-war can be a little tricky (https://www.lhup.edu/~dsimanek/scenario/insight.htm#mechanics). It seems like common sense that the "stronger" team has an advantage, but that's not quite right. To win, you need to resist sliding forward better than the other team. If you can't resist sliding, then increasing your arm strength means you'll just pull yourself forward. Since sliding friction is often proportional to weight, tug-of-war on many surfaces is simply a contest over who's heavier.[2]Champion tug-of-war teams focus on body angle, footwork, digging into the ground, and timing pulls to throw off the other team. The strongest team in the world would lose a tug-of-war with a six-year-old and a sack of bricks, as long as the sack had a firm grip. [Image: image] So, how much force can tug-of-war players exert? A 2011 paper (http://web.nchu.edu.tw/~biosimulation/journal/pdf/vol-3-no01/vol-3-no-1-b-0003.pdf) analyzing the immune systems of several "elite tug-of-war players"[3]The paper notes that "Few studies have been done to examine the effects of [the] tug-of-war sport on physiological responses," which seems likely enough to me. measured their average pull force (on a school gym floor) to be about 102.5 kilograms-force, or about 1.5x their body weight. The ultimate tensile strength (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ultimate_tensile_strength) of cast iron is about 200 megapascals (MPa), so we can use a simple formula to figure out how many players would be needed to break one. \[ \text{People required}=\frac{\pi\times\left(\tfrac{1}{4}\text{ inch} \right )^2\times200\text{ MPa}}{102.5\text{ kg}/\text{person}}\approx25\text{ people} \] Two teams of 25 people[4]I originally wrote 25 people total, forgetting that two people pulling with 100 units of force each will produce 100 units of tension on the rope, not 200! Thank you for Gordon McDonough for pointing this out. could probably pull a half-inch iron bar apart. An inch-thick iron bar could be torn in half by teams of 101 people,[5]People often play tug-of-war with their dogs. Going by weight alone, 30 humans would probably be about evenly matched against 101 dalmatians. and a 2-inch-diameter bar would need over 400. It's hard to have a tug-of-war with something thicker than about 2 inches. Since you're not allowed to install handles on the rope,[6]Or wrap it around your hand, for reasons which will become clear if you read some of the articles on tug-of-war injuries. it has to be narrow enough to grip easily. While "400 people" may be the limit for plain iron bars, there are much stronger substances out there. Common types of steel, for example, have a tensile strength about 10 times that of cast iron. Common half-inch rebar (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rebar), for example, would in theory take teams of over 200 people to pull apart, compared to 25 for cast iron. Other substances are even stronger; a half-inch shaft made from high-grade steel or a polymer like Kevlar (or, theoretically, a solid silicon crystal) could handle the pulling force from teams of anywhere between 500 and 800 competitive tug-of-war players. If we limit ourselves to a two-inch diameter rope, which seems to be about the maximum size for tug-of-wars,[7](William Safire (http://www.theonion.com/articles/william-safire-orders-two-whoppers-junior,3351/) returns from the grave to point out that it should really be tugs-of-war.) then the maximum number of tug-of-war players given a super-strong rope like Kevlar is in the neighborhood of 10,000.[8]Or several times that many, if they're not very athletic. If we figured out how to manufacture large ropes out of graphene ribbons, which have tensile strengths over 10 times higher (http://arxiv.org/pdf/0709.0992.pdf) than existing materials, we could theoretically support a tug-of-war between teams of up to 100,000 players each. Such a rope would be over 200 miles long, and could stretch from New York to Washington. [Image: image] If our experience with nylon ropes failing is any indication, when the graphene finally snapped, the death toll could be enormous among both players and bystanders. Lengths of graphene would crack across the landscape like bullwhips, slicing down forests and demolishing buildings. In the end, trying to develop stronger ropes leads only to greater danger to everyone, both participants and bystanders. In the ultimate game of tug-of-war ... [Image: image] ... the only winning move is not to pull.

items.model_answer:
If tug-of-war teams pulled on an iron rod instead of a rope, several fundamental changes would occur due to the rod's rigidity.

The most significant difference would be the introduction of bending forces. In standard tug-of-war, a rope naturally aligns all pulling forces along a single line of tension. A rigid rod, however, would act as a lever. As team members lean back and pull at different heights and angles—unavoidable in the sport—they would apply torque to the rod, causing it to bend. If the rod were thin enough to grip like a rope, it would likely bend permanently or snap under the combined lateral forces of two teams.

Grip would also become a decisive factor. A rope's rough texture and flexibility allow participants to wrap their hands around it and secure their hold. A smooth iron rod offers far less friction, meaning the contest would likely be decided by who slips off first rather than who generates more horizontal pulling force.

The center marker would also behave differently. With a rope, the center point moves linearly based on net force. With a rigid rod, the center could remain relatively stationary while the ends flex or rotate.

Finally, safety would be a severe concern. If a team suddenly lost grip or the rod broke, the stored elastic energy and momentum would launch the heavy metal object backward, creating a serious projectile hazard—unlike a rope, which simply goes slack.

items.question: What If the Moon Were Replaced by a Black Hole of the Same Mass?
human_answers: "Not much" and "not much." [Image: image] A black hole the mass of the Moon would have an event horizon about the size of a sand grain. Specifically, according to one of my favorite charts (http://pubs.usgs.gov/of/2003/of03-001/htmldocs/images/chart.pdf), a black hole moon would be a grain of fine to medium-fine sand, and could pass through a sieve of size ASTM No. 70 or larger. I mean, I guess a black hole with the mass of the Moon would pass right through any sieve, destroying it in the process, but that's neither here nor there.[1]The expression "that's neither here nor there" can be kind of confusing and ambiguous, but I guess that's neither here nor there. Since the Moon's mass and position wouldn't change, the tides on Earth wouldn't change, either. When you're floating outside a spherical mass, its pull on you is the same regardless of whether the mass is concentrated at the center of the sphere or spread out throughout it. If the Sun were replaced by a black hole of the same mass, the Earth's orbit wouldn't change, although life on Earth might (http://what-if.xkcd.com/49/). With the Moon gathered into a point, there'd be no moonlight, which would affect the life cycles of all kinds of nocturnal animals. But compared to a lot of the other (http://xkcd.com/1338/) things we've done, that would be fairly minor. The Earth's orbit is stabilized by the Moon (http://www.nature.com/nature/journal/v361/n6413/abs/361615a0.html), but the lunar-mass black hole would probably serve the same role. This black hole Moon (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3mbBbFH9fAg) would be pretty low-profile. If it were much smaller, it would evaporate through Hawking radiation (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawking_radiation), but a black hole the size of the Moon actually absorbs more energy from the cosmic background radiation than it emits through the Hawking mechanism. Our black hole would really be black. [Image: image] At least, if it didn't eat anything. If the black hole devoured any objects, it would let off a tremendous blast of radiation. Black holes burn brightly as they devour things; the whirlpool of matter heats up as it falls inward (http://www.gothosenterprises.com/black_holes/outside_black_holes.html), causing it to glow brightly.[2]A black hole can't devour matter too fast, though, because at some point it would be producing so much radiation that it would blast its own "food" away. This is called the Eddington limit (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddington_luminosity). If our black hole were devouring matter at the Eddington limit, it would be hot enough to sterilize the Earth. Fortunately, there's not a lot out there for it to eat, so it wouldn't glow very brightly for now. It would spend most of its time drastically altering the orbits of nearby dust particles—one sand grain pushing other sand grains around.[3]Even if it sucked in matter at the rate the Earth—with its much larger "collecting area"—sucks in interplanetary dust, it wouldn't necessarily be a problem for us. But there would be one interesting effect: In addition to getting darker, Earth would get colder, because moonlight warms the Earth. It's a very tiny contributor to our global energy balance; the Moon is five or six orders of magnitude dimmer than the Sun. But it's there. Measurements show that global temperature varies with a 28-day cycle (http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1029/2000GL011651/abstract); all else being equal, the Earth is hottest during the full moon. It's a tiny difference—small fractions of a degree—but it's there. But it turns out most of this effect is not due to moonlight. The largest contributor is the fact that the Earth is slightly closer to the Sun during a full Moon: [Image: image] Calculating the amount of energy radiated back to Earth by the Moon is deceptively tricky. The Moon reflects sunlight, but with some surprising twists. When the Moon is half-illuminated, you might think it would be half as bright as when full—but it's much less bright than that (http://home.earthlink.net/~kitathome/LunarLight/moonlight_gallery/technique/moonbright.htm). And once you account for that, there are even trickier effects to deal with, because science is the worst.[4]Like the fact that the waxing Moon is 20% brighter (http://www.jstor.org/discover/10.2307/2402251?sid=21105340972791&uid=2&uid=4&uid=3739808&uid=3739256) than the waning Moon, or that the Moon is a mild retroreflector (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opposition_surge). Then, on top of all the weird visible-light effects, the Moon also heats up under the Sun, then radiates that heat as infrared light. There's a great discussion of the Moon's effect on the Earth's energy budget in this article (http://scitation.aip.org/content/aapt/journal/ajp/67/12/10.1119/1.19109?ver=pdfcov) by Robert Knox. The upshot is that the Moon's infrared heat radiation turns out to affect Earth's temperature about 10 times more than the visible moonlight, but still about 10 times less than the effect from gravity moving Earth closer and farther from the Sun. Knox even quantifies the effect this has on Earth's radiation balance—the presence of infrared moonlight warms the planet by 1.2 milli-degrees Fahrenheit (m°F). [Image: image] Without moonlight, the planet would cool down slightly. But given the accelerating rate at which we're adding (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keeling_Curve) CO2 to the atmosphere—which changes the Earth's energy balance—we'd make up the difference in a couple of weeks. So all in all, the conversion of the Moon to a black hole might not even be that big of a deal. Unless, of course, it happened on certain days between 1969 and 1972, in which case Nixon (http://www.archives.gov/presidential-libraries/events/centennials/nixon/images/exhibit/rn100-6-1-2.pdf) would've needed yet another one of those speeches (http://xkcd.com/1484/). [Image: image]

items.model_answer: If the Moon were replaced by a black hole of the same mass, the most immediate consequence is that Earth's night sky would lose its brightest natural light source, as a Moon-mass black hole is incredibly tiny—only about 6 millimeters (roughly the size of a marble). Because the black hole exerts the exact same gravitational pull as the Moon, Earth's oceans would continue to experience the same tides, and our planet's orbit around the Sun would remain completely stable. The absence of the Moon's physical bulk, however, would eliminate its gravitational drag on Earth's rotation, causing our planet's days to gradually shorten over millions of years as Earth spins faster. Without the Moon's stabilizing gravitational influence, Earth's axial tilt would begin to wobble dramatically over long timescales, leading to extreme, unpredictable seasonal shifts and severe climate chaos that could eventually make the planet hostile to current life. In the immediate vicinity of the black hole, its extreme gravitational gradient would create a powerful and dangerous tidal field, destroying any spacecraft that approached too closely, but from Earth's surface, the only daily change would be perpetual, star-filled darkness at night.

items.question: What If You Mounted a High-Power Microwave on a Car to Melt Ice?
human_answers: Believe it or not, your flamethrower idea is actually the more practical of the two. The flamethrower also has the advantage that, unlike the microwave, it won't interfere with wifi (unless you aim it directly at the router). [Image: image] I'm writing this article from Boston, which is currently buried under a truly ridiculous amount of snow (http://www.buzzfeed.com/mjs538/please-stop-snowing). We've had more snow in the past 30 days (http://weather.ou.edu/~splillo/misc.html) than Anchorage, Alaska usually gets in an entire winter.[1]Meanwhile, Anchorage is on Twitter wondering (https://twitter.com/NWSBoston/status/567172928593485824) where their snow went and threatening revenge (https://twitter.com/NWSAnchorage/status/567566488517619712). Here's (https://twitter.com/EricHolthaus/status/567350490912931840) a neat visualization of the atmospheric pattern during these polar vortexes. Vortices. Whatever. Our transit system has broken down (http://www.bostonglobe.com/metro/2015/02/14/transportation/U7vNqP861gKQFRly2jmjdL/story.html) and our roofs[2]Tolkien prefers rooves. are collapsing (http://www.whdh.com/story/28133433/dozens-of-roof-collapses-reported-across-new-england). The mayor gave a press conference (http://www.boston.com/news/local/massachusetts/2015/02/15/boston-mayor-seems-pretty-tired-all-this-dang-snow/OYtAnLLNQ2iMBMRaxTJYzJ/story.html?s_campaign=bcom%3Asocialflow%3Atwitter) in which he announced, "I don't know what to say to anybody anymore. Hopefully it will stop eventually." So snow removal is on all our minds. But snow is hard to melt. (And we've been trying (https://twitter.com/NotifyBoston/status/564524089017401347)[3]I love that tweet because it sort of sounds like it comes from an alternate fairy-tale universe where cities farm snow and snow-melters form the base of the economy.) Your microwave idea certainly sounds like it should be more practical than a flamethrower. Microwaves seem clean and efficient; after all, we don't use flamethrowers in our kitchens. [Image: image] But there's a big problem: Microwaves heat water very well, but they don't really work on ice (http://www.thenakedscientists.com/HTML/content/kitchenscience/exp/-324719c1f8/). Fortunately, there are other ways to get energy into the ice. In addition to your flamethrower suggestion, you could, for example, use infrared heat lamps or lasers.[4]Pick a frequency where snow has a low albedo; otherwise, the FBI may hunt you down for lasering aircraft (http://www.nbcnews.com/tech/tech-news/why-its-terrible-idea-point-lasers-airplanes-n28841). But whatever you use, you'll run into another problem: It takes an awful lot of energy to melt snow. Melting a gram of snow takes about 335 joules of energy. To put that another way, a 60-watt lightbulb is capable of melting about a pound of snow an hour. A foot of snow contains roughly the same amount of water as an inch of rain, give or take (http://www.theweatherprediction.com/habyhints/346/). Let's assume you've had a decent snowstorm of about a foot[5]For the record, by this standard, Boston has had a "decent snowstorm" every few days for the past month.—meaning an inch worth of water—and that you want to melt a 9-foot-wide swath while driving along at 55 mph. Luckily, this happens to be one of those happy physics situations where we can just multiply together every number we're looking at, and the answer (http://www.wolframalpha.com/input/?i=55+mph+*+water+density+*+1+inch+*+9+feet+*+335+J%2Fgram) turns out to be the measurement we want: \[55\text{ mph}\times1\text{ inch}\times9\text{ feet}\times\text{water density}\times335\tfrac{\text{J}}{\text{gram}}=574\text{ megawatts}\] Unfortunately, it's not the answer we'd like. The nuclear reactor on an aircraft carrier, for example, produces less than 200 megawatts. To melt snow in front of your car, you'd need three of those. [Image: image] What about your your original flamethrower idea? Gasoline may have a phenomenally high energy density (http://what-if.xkcd.com/128/), but it's not high enough. No matter how big the tank on your flamethrower was, you'd run out of fuel constantly. Gas mileage in the US is often measured in "miles per gallon" of gasoline. With your flamethrower guzzling fuel, your mileage would be about 17 feet per gallon. You might be better off dropping the flamethrower entirely. Instead, take a cue from the rail agencies, who use jet-engine-powered snowblowers (http://www.boston.com/news/local/massachusetts/articles/2011/01/23/mbtas_mattapan_line_relies_on_snowzilla_in_worst_weather/) to clear train tracks. In the end, it's easier to just move the snow out of your way. [Image: image]

rubrics.question_focus: What If You Mounted a High-Power Microwave on a Car to Melt Ice?

criteria.name: Microwave-Ice Interaction Fidelity
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer correctly reasons about how high-power microwaves would couple to snow, ice, meltwater, and nearby materials under the proposed car-mounted scenario.
criteria.1-2: Claims microwaves would straightforwardly melt ice efficiently with no discussion of absorption or material response.
criteria.3-4: Mentions microwaves heat water but gives confused or oversimplified claims about ice, snow, or wet surfaces.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes that liquid water absorbs microwaves better than ice and that snow/ice heating would be uneven or inefficient.
criteria.7-8: Explains differential absorption by ice, snow, meltwater, dirt, and objects, including feedback as meltwater forms.
criteria.9-10: Accurately integrates microwave penetration, dielectric loss, wet-snow effects, uneven heating, reflection/scattering, and practical coupling losses.

criteria.name: Energy and Power Scaling
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer captures the dominant constraint: the enormous energy and power needed to melt road snow at driving speeds.
criteria.1-2: Ignores energy requirements or treats melting as easy with a powerful enough microwave.
criteria.3-4: States it would take a lot of power but provides no meaningful scale or uses implausible numbers.
criteria.5-6: Uses latent heat or rough snow volume reasoning to show the requirement is very large.
criteria.7-8: Estimates road width, snow water equivalent, vehicle speed, and latent heat to reach hundreds of megawatts scale.
criteria.9-10: Provides a coherent quantitative chain comparable to about 574 MW for a 9-foot swath, 1 inch water equivalent, at 55 mph, and explains assumptions.

criteria.name: Long-Range Consequence Chain
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer follows downstream effects beyond initial melting, including road conditions, vehicle operation, infrastructure, and environment.
criteria.1-2: Only answers whether the microwave melts ice, with no downstream consequences.
criteria.3-4: Lists a few hazards but without causal connection to the counterfactual setup.
criteria.5-6: Connects melting to runoff, refreezing, vehicle power needs, and limited usefulness.
criteria.7-8: Traces consequences such as slush formation, black ice, drainage load, visibility/steam, thermal damage, and vehicle impracticality.
criteria.9-10: Builds a coherent long-range chain from energy delivery to meltwater management, traffic safety, refreezing, infrastructure effects, regulatory concerns, and operational failure modes.

criteria.name: Comparison to Alternatives and Practical Endpoint
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer reaches a plausible practical conclusion and compares microwave melting with more realistic snow-removal methods.
criteria.1-2: Concludes the device is practical or superior without justification.
criteria.3-4: Says it is impractical but gives weak or unrelated reasons.
criteria.5-6: Correctly concludes it is impractical mainly due to power/efficiency limits.
criteria.7-8: Explains why mechanical removal, plows, snowblowers, heat lamps, lasers, or flamethrowers may be more plausible yet still energy-limited.
criteria.9-10: Clearly concludes that moving snow is generally easier than melting it, while fairly comparing microwaves, combustion heating, infrared/lasers, and plows under the same constraints.

criteria.name: Safety, Interference, and Contradiction Control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer handles hazards and uncertainties without contradicting established physics or the premise.
criteria.1-2: Contains major contradictions, impossible claims, or ignores obvious microwave hazards.
criteria.3-4: Mentions safety vaguely but includes questionable claims about radiation, power, or legality.
criteria.5-6: Identifies plausible hazards such as electromagnetic interference, burns, arcing, shielding needs, and bystander exposure.
criteria.7-8: Distinguishes ionizing from non-ionizing radiation, notes shielding/beam-control issues, and avoids overstating certainty.
criteria.9-10: Calibrates uncertainties while consistently addressing RF exposure, electronics/wifi interference, vehicle shielding, reflections, regulatory limits, and thermal/mechanical hazards without internal contradictions.

items.model_answer:
Mounting a high-power microwave on a car to melt ice would theoretically work on the ice, but the practical consequences would be catastrophic for the car, the driver, and the surrounding environment. The most immediate and insurmountable problem is power. Melting ice requires an enormous amount of energy to overcome the latent heat of fusion, which is roughly 334 kilojoules just to turn a kilogram of ice at zero degrees into water, plus whatever energy is required to raise the ice temperature to its melting point. To melt a meaningful layer of ice on a road while driving at any reasonable speed would require megawatts of continuous power. A standard car alternator produces only about one to two kilowatts, meaning the microwave would demand thousands of times more electrical energy than the car could possibly provide without towing a dedicated, trailer-sized power plant. 

Even if you could generate the required power, the electromagnetic interference would instantly fry the car's own electronic control units, sensors, and ignition systems, bringing the vehicle to a dead halt. Modern cars rely on delicate microprocessors that are highly vulnerable to high-power microwave radiation. Furthermore, while the car's metal body acts as a Faraday cage that would generally shield the driver from external microwaves, the system would be incredibly dangerous. Reflections from the wet, melting ice or metal objects on the road could bounce radiation back into the vehicle, and any gaps, cracks, or windows in the car's shielding could allow microwaves to leak into the cabin, potentially injuring the driver.

The interaction with the road itself would also be highly destructive and inefficient. Liquid water absorbs microwaves much more readily than pure ice. As soon as a tiny patch of ice melted, the resulting water would superheat, rapidly boiling and potentially causing steam explosions that would damage the asphalt or concrete. Any metal embedded in the road, such as rebar, manhole covers, or sewer grates, would act as antennas for the microwave radiation, arcing violently and potentially starting fires or causing small explosions. Finally, the device would be lethally dangerous to anything in front of the car, instantly causing severe internal burns to pedestrians, animals, or anyone in nearby vehicles. Ultimately, while the physics of microwave heating would indeed melt the ice, the car would stall, its electronics would be destroyed, the road would be damaged, and the driver would be in immense danger long before a significant stretch of ice was cleared.

items.question: What Would Happen to a Human Body Left in Orbit?
human_answers: This isn't really relevant, but I have to ask: Is there a reason you specifically wanted your corpse to be naked? Just making things extra weird for the technicians loading up the capsule and/or throwing you out of the airlock? [Image: image] If you tried this, the first thing that would happen to your corpse would be that it would dry out. This would probably start before you made it to space; the dry, climate-controlled air in the pre-launch waiting area would help draw moisture from your body. In the Manual of Forensic Taphonomy, Franklin Damann and David Carter outline the process of human decomposition. According to them, it takes a lot of effort to keep corpses from drying out during the embalming process.[1]The citation they give for that fact is "(C. A. Wacker, pers. comm.)," which I like to think means it was shared in a conversation that totally broke up the dinner party they were both at. In extremely dry environments like the Atacama Desert in Chile, "spontaneous mummification" can occur—and space is even drier than Chile.[2]The space tourism industry has not adopted this as a slogan. Also, "Chile: Not as Dry as Space!" was probably nixed by the Chilean tourism board. Once your body made it to space, this process would ramp up quickly. Most of the "ecology" responsible for decomposing your corpse would be killed off quickly by the drying process (along with the lack of oxygen, temperature swings, and solar radiation levels), so your body wouldn't decay very much. Instead, you'd become a freeze-dried mummy, after losing about 80% of your body weight in water.[3]This is how much liquid you can remove from fresh animal tissue, according to lab experiments reported in Arthur C. Aufderheide's book The Scientific Study of Mummies. That makes sense; after all, according to that commonly-repeated piece of trivia, human bodies are around 70% water. Or is it 65%? Or 80%? The exact number is a little vague, and seems to depend on who you ask. In a footnote in her wonderful book, Stiff: The Curious Lives of Human Cadavers, writer Mary Roach mentioned that she had methodically Googled the phrase "human body is <X> percent water", for X from 0 to 100. She reported a wide range of claims, including several pages asserting that we're 98% water. It's really gratifying to know I'm not the only person who spends a lot of time carefully cataloging weird stuff like that. What happens next depends on exactly where in space you are. If you're in an orbit that passes near the Earth, your orbit will quickly decay, and before long you'll re-enter the atmosphere and burn up. If you're in a slightly higher orbit, you'll last longer, but you'd also be in the zone where space debris (http://commons.erau.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1000&context=stm) was thickest. Impacts with small bits of debris would start to leave pits and scars on your surface; they would often find these on Space Shuttle windows after a flight. Eventually, probably after a few decades, you'd probably have a violent collision with something. Higher orbits are safer. If you were some distance away from the Earth, near where geosynchronous satellites orbit, there would be less debris to run into. Furthermore, for large, dense objects, orbits out there are stable (http://www.readcube.com/articles/10.1029%2F92JE00032?show_checkout=1) for a very long time. You could spend centuries drifting among TV broadcast satellites. [Image: image] If you wanted to last even longer, you could launch yourself away from Earth completely, finding a quiet and stable orbit somewhere in interplanetary space. There, over the course of millennia, you'd be slowly baked by the Sun's radiation and pitted and powdered by micrometeorites. But if your goal is to weird out future space travelers, that might not be the best plan. Space is big; if someone randomly stumbles on your corpse, it suggests that there must be a lot of people zipping around the solar system. And if space travel has become that common, there will be lots of corpses floating around;[4]Weird that "lots of corpses floating around" is somehow an optimistic prediction about the future of space travel. discovering yours will be more archaeologically exciting than anything. You'll be stuck in a lab or museum somewhere and contribute to someone's research paper—a bland end to your exciting prank. Unless, of course, you happen to be found by the only people in space even weirder than you. [Image: image]
items.original_question: 我经常开玩笑说我希望将我的遗体送入轨道。不是“撒我的骨灰”的意思，而是“把我赤裸的尸体扔出气闸”的意思。老实说，我的主要动机是让遥远的未来的某人感到困惑，但这是一个有趣的科学问题：在几年、几十年或几个世纪的过程中，我在轨道上的身体会发生什么？

items.model_answer:
If a human body were left in Earth's orbit, its condition would be dictated by the extreme environment of space, primarily whether it is exposed to the vacuum or protected by a spacesuit. If exposed directly to the vacuum without a suit, the lack of atmospheric pressure would cause the water in the body's tissues to vaporize, a process known as ebullism. This would cause the body to swell to roughly twice its normal size, though the skin is strong enough to prevent it from bursting. Simultaneously, the lungs would rupture if the person held their breath, and the lack of oxygen would lead to unconsciousness within seconds and death within a few minutes. 

If the body were inside a spacesuit, the initial breakdown would be driven by anaerobic bacteria from the gut, which would begin consuming the soft tissues. However, this decomposition would be short-lived; once the bacteria exhausted the available oxygen and nutrients, they would die off. In both scenarios, the extreme temperatures of orbit would quickly halt all biological activity. As the body orbits Earth, it cycles between intense sunlight and deep shadow. In the sun, temperatures can exceed 120°C (250°F), which would slowly cook and desiccate the tissues. In the shadow, temperatures plummet to roughly minus 150°C (-240°F), freezing the body solid. This continuous freeze-thaw cycle would eventually mummify and freeze-dry the remains.

Over longer periods, the unfiltered radiation of space would alter the body's appearance. Ultraviolet light and cosmic rays would break down the chemical bonds in the skin and muscles, causing the remains to slowly bleach to a pale, grayish-white and develop a leathery texture. If the body is in a suit, the material would eventually degrade or be punctured by micrometeoroids, exposing the mummified remains to the vacuum. Ultimately, the body's fate would be determined by orbital mechanics. In low Earth orbit, the slight but persistent drag from the upper atmosphere would cause the body to slowly lose altitude. Over the course of months, years, or decades—depending on the exact altitude—the body would re-enter Earth's atmosphere. Because it would be traveling at orbital velocities of roughly 28,000 km/h (17,500 mph), the intense friction and heat of re-entry would almost entirely incinerate the remains, leaving no trace.

edus.text: If a human body were left in Earth's orbit, its condition would be dictated by the extreme environment of space, primarily whether it is exposed to the vacuum or protected by a spacesuit.
If exposed directly to the vacuum without a suit, the lack of atmospheric pressure would cause the water in the body's tissues to vaporize, a process known as ebullism.
This would cause the body to swell to roughly twice its normal size,
though the skin is strong enough to prevent it from bursting.
Simultaneously, the lungs would rupture if the person held their breath,
and the lack of oxygen would lead to unconsciousness within seconds and death within a few minutes.
If the body were inside a spacesuit, the initial breakdown would be driven by anaerobic bacteria from the gut,
which would begin consuming the soft tissues.
However, this decomposition would be short-lived;
once the bacteria exhausted the available oxygen and nutrients, they would die off.
In both scenarios, the extreme temperatures of orbit would quickly halt all biological activity.
As the body orbits Earth, it cycles between intense sunlight and deep shadow.
In the sun, temperatures can exceed 120°C (250°F),
which would slowly cook and desiccate the tissues.
In the shadow, temperatures plummet to roughly minus 150°C (-240°F),
freezing the body solid.
This continuous freeze-thaw cycle would eventually mummify and freeze-dry the remains.
Over longer periods, the unfiltered radiation of space would alter the body's appearance.
Ultraviolet light and cosmic rays would break down the chemical bonds in the skin and muscles,
causing the remains to slowly bleach to a pale, grayish-white and develop a leathery texture.
If the body is in a suit, the material would eventually degrade or be punctured by micrometeoroids,
exposing the mummified remains to the vacuum.
Ultimately, the body's fate would be determined by orbital mechanics.
In low Earth orbit, the slight but persistent drag from the upper atmosphere would cause the body to slowly lose altitude.
Over the course of months, years, or decades—depending on the exact altitude—the body would re-enter Earth's atmosphere.
Because it would be traveling at orbital velocities of roughly 28,000 km/h (17,500 mph), the intense friction and heat of re-entry would almost entirely incinerate the remains,
leaving no trace.

items.question: What If You Dug Straight Down at One Foot per Second?
human_answers: This question is the reverse of question #64 (http://what-if.xkcd.com/64/), which asked how you'd die if you rose steadily at a foot per second. Digging at the same rate would kill you more quickly. [Image: image] After you get through the surface layers,[1]See question #132 (http://what-if.xkcd.com/132/) for more on that. temperatures rise pretty steadily as you go deeper, a trend that continues all the way to the core. In some areas, where the hot magma[2](Lava (http://xkcd.com/1405/).) is closer to the surface, the ground gets hotter more quickly. The Southern Methodist University Geothermal Lab has produced some superb maps (http://www.smu.edu/Dedman/Academics/Programs/GeothermalLab/DataMaps/TemperatureMaps) showing the temperature of deep rocks in different parts of the United States. If you look at the map of the 3.5 km layer (http://www.smu.edu/~/media/Site/Dedman/Academics/Programs/Geothermal%20Lab/Graphics/TemperatureMaps/SMU_2011_35kmTemperature.ashx?la=en), you see that at that depth, most of the US is colored greenish-yellow, representing temperatures somewhere around 100°C—with one glaring exception. In northwest Wyoming, there's a circle of ground colored bright red, where the rock is much hotter than normal. That circle is the Yellowstone supervolcano (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellowstone_Caldera). [Image: image] The SMU maps show that even if you avoided digging in Yellowstone, you'd quickly encounter temperatures too hot for an unprotected human. The ground typically gets hotter at an average of about 35°C per kilometer, so at a rate of a foot per second, you'd encounter lethal heat within an hour or two. But wait a moment. Let's say your hole is about a meter wide. At the rate you're digging, you have to remove roughly half a ton of material every second. No human would be capable of lifting that first foot of material out of the hole so quickly, and it only gets worse after that. After a minute of digging, you'd be 60 feet down, and would have to lift all that rock and dirt a huge distance vertically to get it out of the hole. The power required to do that lifting—just after the first minute—would be roughly 150 horsepower. [Image: image] Even if you're not doing the lifting yourself, the way your question is worded makes it pretty clear that you are in this hole. Whatever process you're using is going to require huge amounts of energy to lift all that rock, and that energy is inevitably going to result in the hole being heated somehow. Even if the layer you're digging through wasn't hot when you started, it will be. What if we assume you're protected against the heat from the ground (and the digging mechanism)? Well, in that case, the pressure would become a problem. As you go deeper, air pressure increases. Below about 5 km, the pressure is high enough that oxygen (http://www.scuba-doc.com/oxygentox.html) becomes toxic (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LOZuxwVk7TU). So what if you're protected against the heat, pressure, and the digging process? Well, at that point, we've redefined the rules so much that I'm not sure it makes sense to try to calculate an answer. The question—"what would kill you if you kept digging downward"—has left the realm of physics and become fantasy. Which, come to think of it, makes the answer perfectly clear. [Image: image]

items.model_answer:
If you dug straight down into the Earth at a constant rate of one foot per second, you would complete the roughly 7,918-mile journey to the opposite side of the planet in about 484 days, assuming you had indestructible equipment and a way to survive the extreme conditions. At this speed, you would travel about 16.4 miles per day. For the first couple of days, you would dig through the Earth's crust, passing through soil, sediment, and solid granite bedrock while the temperature steadily increases. Once you enter the mantle, you would spend the next several months boring through high-pressure, viscous silicate rocks that behave like a very thick fluid over geological timescales. About 110 days into your journey, you would reach the outer core, a churning ocean of liquid iron and nickel heated to between 4,000 and 5,000 degrees Celsius. Here, traditional digging would be impossible; you would essentially be tunneling through a dense, metallic fluid. After about 85 days of traversing the outer core, you would hit the inner core, a solid sphere of iron and nickel under mind-bending pressure, where you would spend the final 45 days of your descent to the center enduring temperatures as hot as the surface of the sun. 

As you pass the exact center of the Earth, the physics of your journey would fundamentally change. Gravity is generated by the mass beneath you, so as you dig deeper, gravity steadily decreases. At the very center, you would experience zero gravity. Once you dig past the center, the bulk of the Earth's mass is now above you, meaning gravity pulls you back toward the center. Because of this, the second half of your journey would feel like digging straight uphill. You would have to actively pull yourself and your equipment upward against the pull of gravity, which would gradually increase until you reach the surface on the other side of the globe. Finally, after a year and four months of continuous digging, you would break through the crust, emerging into the open air or ocean of the opposite hemisphere.

edus.text: If you dug straight down into the Earth at a constant rate of one foot per second,
you would complete the roughly 7,918-mile journey to the opposite side of the planet in about 484 days,
assuming you had indestructible equipment and a way to survive the extreme conditions.
At this speed, you would travel about 16.4 miles per day.
For the first couple of days, you would dig through the Earth's crust,
passing through soil, sediment, and solid granite bedrock
while the temperature steadily increases.
Once you enter the mantle, you would spend the next several months boring through high-pressure, viscous silicate rocks
that behave like a very thick fluid over geological timescales.
About 110 days into your journey, you would reach the outer core,
a churning ocean of liquid iron and nickel heated to between 4,000 and 5,000 degrees Celsius.
Here, traditional digging would be impossible;
you would essentially be tunneling through a dense, metallic fluid.
After about 85 days of traversing the outer core, you would hit the inner core,
a solid sphere of iron and nickel under mind-bending pressure,
where you would spend the final 45 days of your descent to the center
enduring temperatures as hot as the surface of the sun.
As you pass the exact center of the Earth, the physics of your journey would fundamentally change.
Gravity is generated by the mass beneath you,
so as you dig deeper, gravity steadily decreases.
At the very center, you would experience zero gravity.
Once you dig past the center, the bulk of the Earth's mass is now above you,
meaning gravity pulls you back toward the center.
Because of this, the second half of your journey would feel like digging straight uphill.
You would have to actively pull yourself and your equipment upward against the pull of gravity,
which would gradually increase until you reach the surface on the other side of the globe.
Finally, after a year and four months of continuous digging, you would break through the crust,
emerging into the open air or ocean of the opposite hemisphere.

items.question: What If You Dropped a Submarine into Jupiter?
human_answers: Nope! Jupiter's pressure, density, and temperature curves are different from ours. At the point in Jupiter's atmosphere where the density is high enough for a submarine to float, the pressure is high enough to crush the submarine,[1]Which makes it more dense. and the temperature is high enough to melt it.[2]Which makes it harder to drive. [Image: image] But there's another problem: Jupiter is a gas giant, but submarines—as you can figure out from etymology—go under water. [Image: image] Air and water are different. This seems straightforward enough, but they're also the same in a lot of ways. They're both "fluids," and some of the same rules apply to each. In some sense, when you look up at the sky (http://xkcd.com/1556/), you're looking up from the bottom of a deep sea of air. Things float when they're less dense than the fluid around them. This works the same for balloons in air and boats in water. The late Terry Pratchett wrote a truly beautiful passage about this, in the prologue to his book Going Postal. He says that since water is in many respects a wetter form of air,[3]Sounds reasonable enough to me. as ships sink, eventually they reach a point where the water was too dense to sink any further. This layer forms an underwater surface on which shipwrecks collect, drifting around beneath the waves but far above the sea floor:It’s calm there. Dead calm.Some stricken ships have rigging; some even have sails. Many still have crew, tangled in the rigging or lashed to the wheel.But the voyages still continue, aimlessly, with no harbour in sight, because there are currents under the ocean and so the dead ships with their skeleton crews sail on around the world, over sunken cities and between drowned mountains, until rot and shipworms eat them away and they disintegrate.Sometimes an anchor drops, all the way to the dark, cold calmness of the abyssal plain, and disturbs the stillness of centuries by throwing up a cloud of silt. I love that passage. It's also completely wrong. Ships sink all the way to the bottom. (Sir Terry knew this, as the rest of the passage makes clear, but he's describing how ships work on Discworld, not Earth.) Air follows the ideal gas law (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ideal_gas_law). The more pressure you put on it, the smaller (and denser) it gets. Water, on the other hand, is pretty much incompressible. When you dive into the ocean, the pressure increases as you go deeper (rising by one atmosphere every 10 meters or so) but the water's density barely changes all the way down to the sea floor. Buoyancy depends on density, not pressure. There's a point in Jupiter's atmosphere where the pressure is equal to a little more than an Earth atmosphere—which is the pressure a submarine is used to—but the air there is barely a tenth as dense as ours. A submarine in that layer would fall even faster than it would in the air on Earth. [Image: image] To reach a depth where it could "float" in Jupiter, the submarine would have to go halfway to the center of the planet, where the intense pressure turns the air into a metallic soup (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metallic_hydrogen) that's hotter than the surface of the Sun. The pressure there would be so high that not only would the submarine be crushed, the substances that make it up would probably be converted into new and exciting forms. It's hard to create those kinds of conditions in a lab, so we don't know a lot about how materials behave with that much pressure pushing down on them. [Image: image] In the sea, on the other hand, the density of the fluid stays relatively constant. That means the submarine can find its appropriate pressure range and float there. In other words, submarines only work because water doesn't follow the ideal gas law. But there's one more twist: Water sort of does obey the ideal gas law. The equations governing water under normal pressure are similar to (http://arxiv.org/pdf/1311.0534.pdf) the equation for a gas under about twenty thousand atmospheres of pressure. In a sense, this is why water seems incompressible to us—it behaves as if it's already compressed so much that an extra atmosphere or two hardly makes a difference. So, in some ways, water and air are more similar than they seem, but in the ways that matter for a submarine, they really are different. Which, of course, brings us back to why it's called a submarine—it operates under a "mare". A vehicle designed to operate beneath a sea of air would be called a subaerine.[5]The "gas" in "gas giant" is from the Greek word for void (χάος, kháos), so maybe a vessel (σκάφη, skáphē) that travels through a gas giant's atmosphere would be a khaoskaphe. criteria.7-8: Correctly explains that low-density upper layers cannot support a submarine and that sufficient density occurs only at extreme depths and pressures.
criteria.9-10: Precisely connects buoyancy to displaced fluid density, contrasts compressible Jovian gas with nearly incompressible seawater, and avoids ocean-like analogies except as clarified comparisons.

criteria.9-10: Clearly sequences the long-range descent through Jovian layers, including low-density upper atmosphere, increasing drag/density, extreme pressure-temperature regimes, and possible metallic-hydrogen-like conditions.

criteria.name: Structural, Thermal, and Material Fate of the Submarine

criteria.7-8: Explains that the hull would fail under external pressure long before reaching a buoyant layer, with later heating/melting/chemical or phase changes.
criteria.9-10: Integrates pressure collapse, compression of internal spaces, thermal destruction, possible chemical/material transformation, and the disappearance of any submarine-like structure.

criteria.name: Long-Range Causal Coherence and Endpoint Plausibility

items.model_answer: If you dropped a submarine into Jupiter, it would almost immediately burn up and vaporize in the planet's upper atmosphere due to the intense friction of atmospheric entry, as submarines lack the thermal shielding required to survive re-entry speeds. However, if we assume the submarine is magically protected from the heat of entry, its journey would be a rapid, crushing descent. Jupiter has no solid surface, only an atmosphere that grows denser and hotter the deeper you go. As the submarine falls through the ammonia and water-ice clouds, Jupiter's strong gravity—about 2.5 times that of Earth—would accelerate its descent. A submarine hull is designed to resist external pressure pushing inward, but even the deepest-diving military submarines collapse around 700 to 800 meters down in Earth's ocean, and specialized research submersibles max out around 11,000 meters (about 1,100 atmospheres of pressure). On Jupiter, that equivalent pressure is reached at a depth of roughly 100 to 200 kilometers below the cloud tops. At this point, the atmospheric pressure would overwhelm the hull, causing the submarine to violently implode and crush into a compact ball of metal. If the submarine were somehow indestructible, it would continue sinking as the surrounding hydrogen and helium transition from a gas into a supercritical fluid, and eventually into a bizarre liquid metallic hydrogen ocean. It would finally come to rest on Jupiter's core, a region where pressures reach tens of millions of atmospheres and temperatures exceed the surface of the Sun, leaving the indestructible sub sitting forever in a superheated, slushy mixture of rock and exotic matter.

items.question: What Would It Be Like to Ride a Submarine into Jupiter?
human_answers: We don't know! We've only flown spacecraft into a gas planet's atmosphere twice (both Jupiter). One had no cameras, and one went in at night (and was being disposed of, so wasn't taking pictures anyway). If you took a submarine to Jupiter, it would burn up. Jupiter has a deep gravity well; after falling down toward it from space, you're going very fast. There's no easy way to shed that speed other than slamming into the atmosphere and letting it slow you down, but the entry is about four times faster than the Space Shuttle or Apollo Earth reentries. Only the Galileo probe has survived a Jupiter atmospheric entry. [Image: image] The Galileo probe survived by being a bullet with a big heat shield, and several inches of the shield were burned away before it finished slowing down and started falling vertically by parachute. The probe only sent back about half a megabyte of data to the Galileo orbiter, and had no camera, so we don't know what it saw. We could, I guess, try to do the same thing with a submarine—by mounting a giant heat shield on the front—but it would probably qualify as the most Kerbal (https://youtu.be/vwrLR2kv5KA?t=1119) vehicle ever built. [Image: image] If our submarine survived, what would we see?[1]I mean, submarines don't usually have a lot of windows, but we at least have a periscope, right? The best pictures we have of Jupiter's atmosphere are probably these carefully processed mosaics (http://www.planetary.org/blogs/emily-lakdawalla/2010/2644.html) of the Great Red Spot, but they're still taken from very far away. At those resolutions, a huge Earth thunderstorm would appear as roughly one pixel. Trying to figure out what Jupiter's clouds would look like from those pictures is like using this (http://visibleearth.nasa.gov/view.php?id=78314) to reconstruct these (http://stormandsky.smugmug.com/Thumbnail-Galleries). By combining the pictures with other science data, we've been able to put together a pretty good idea of what Jupiter's atmosphere is like, but there are some pretty big questions still unanswered which make it hard to be too confident about what it would actually look like. For example, you know the Great Red Spot? We don't know what all that red stuff is. [Image: image] Author Michael Carroll has done a lot of thinking about planetary atmospheres, and his book Drifting on Alien Winds (http://www.amazon.com/Drifting-Alien-Winds-Exploring-Weather/dp/1441969160) vividly describes of what it would be like to descend through Jupiter's clouds. He was also kind enough to answer some of my questions about Jupiter. Here's a rough sketch of what you'd see as you descended through the clouds; for more, definitely check out his book (http://www.amazon.com/Drifting-Alien-Winds-Exploring-Weather/dp/1441969160). [Image: image] Jupiter's upper atmosphere (the part we would see before we died (http://what-if.xkcd.com/138/)) has three main layers—an upper layer of haze and ammonia clouds, similar to cirrostratus (https://www.google.com/search?q=cirrostratus&tbm=isch) clouds on Earth. Below that is a thick, reddish-brown ammonium hydrosulfide cloud layer. The lowest layer consists of white water clouds, which occasionally rise into towering thunderstorms that occasionally push through the middle layer. Between these cloud layers, the air is probably pretty clear. At those levels, it would be less dense than the air on Earth, so you could see a long way. Thanks to Rayleigh scattering (https://xkcd.com/1145/), the sky would be blue, and objects far off in the distance would fade to blue just like they do on Earth (http://thehelpfulartteacher.blogspot.com/2010/11/landscapes-continuedatmospheric.html). But since Jupiter is so huge, we might not see the clouds disappear over the horizon; the towers might just fade off into the distance. We don't really know how accurate these pictures are, though, until we send a camera to fly down into Jupiter's atmosphere and send pictures back. Juno, scheduled to reach Jupiter next year, carries a pretty nice camera (http://www.msss.com/all_projects/junocam.php),[2]Thank you to Emily Lakdawalla for her helpful background about various spacecraft cameras, including her many thorough spreadsheets. which should give us slightly better-resolution pictures, but it still won't really give us a sense of what the cloud decks look like from within them. For that, we need to send in a probe with a camera—and there's nothing like that on the horizon. There's certainly more science value in visiting Europa than in satisfying our curiosity about the Jovian sky. But with interplanetary cubesats (http://www.nasa.gov/directorates/spacetech/niac/staehle_interplanetary_cubesats.html) soon to make their debut, who knows—maybe someone out there will put together a camera, heat shield, and parachute, and hitch a ride on the next outer planets mission. And then, finally, we'll get to look at Jupiter's clouds from both sides (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=v9j_j-cUwKc). [Image: image]

rubrics.question_focus: What Would It Be Like to Ride a Submarine into Jupiter?

criteria.name: Entry and Survival Physics
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer correctly reasons from the premise of bringing a submarine to Jupiter through the unavoidable high-speed atmospheric entry, heating, deceleration, and structural survival issues.
criteria.1-2: Treats Jupiter entry like ordinary diving or flight; ignores orbital/fall speed, heating, pressure, or the submarine's likely destruction.
criteria.3-4: Mentions danger or crushing/burning vaguely but gives little causal explanation or uses Earth-ocean analogies incorrectly.
criteria.5-6: Identifies that the submarine would probably burn up or be destroyed during entry, with some reference to high speed, atmosphere, or pressure.
criteria.7-8: Explains the long-range chain from Jupiter's gravity well to very fast entry, intense heating, need for extreme heat shielding, deceleration, then later pressure/temperature hazards.
criteria.9-10: Accurately compares Jupiter entry to extreme spacecraft reentry, notes Galileo-like heat-shield requirements, and clearly separates entry heating, deceleration, parachute/fall dynamics, and later atmospheric crushing/heating.

criteria.name: Jovian Atmospheric Structure and Visual Experience
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates coverage of what a surviving observer might plausibly see while descending through Jupiter's cloud layers, including haze, ammonia clouds, ammonium hydrosulfide clouds, water clouds, storms, visibility, and sky color.
criteria.1-2: Describes an ocean, solid surface, or generic darkness with no Jupiter-specific atmospheric features.
criteria.3-4: Mentions clouds or storms but with little distinction between layers or with major misconceptions such as liquid water seas.
criteria.5-6: Covers some plausible Jovian visuals, such as colored clouds, storms, haze, or limited visibility, but omits important layering or scale effects.
criteria.7-8: Describes multiple cloud decks and likely visual effects, including upper haze/ammonia, reddish-brown middle clouds, lower water clouds, storm towers, and clear regions between layers.
criteria.9-10: Gives a vivid but scientifically grounded descent sequence, including blue Rayleigh-scattered sky in clearer layers, enormous cloud towers fading into distance, uncertain colors, and lack of a solid surface view.

criteria.name: Long-Range Causal Chain Coherence
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer maintains a coherent sequence from approach to entry to descent to deeper atmospheric fate without skipping or contradicting necessary intermediate mechanisms.
criteria.1-2: Presents disconnected claims or impossible jumps, such as instantly diving into a Jovian sea or safely touring the planet.
criteria.3-4: Has a rough sequence but major causal gaps, e.g., ignores how the submarine slows down or why conditions worsen with depth.
criteria.5-6: Provides a mostly ordered narrative from entry to descent to destruction, though some transitions are shallow or underspecified.
criteria.7-8: Maintains a clear causal progression: gravity-driven acceleration, atmospheric braking, heat-shield survival problem, cloud-layer descent, increasing pressure/temperature, communications/visibility limits.
criteria.9-10: Integrates all major stages into a tightly reasoned chain, showing how each physical constraint determines the next and why even a modified submarine would only briefly function as a probe.

criteria.name: Uncertainty Calibration and Evidence Use
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer distinguishes known science from speculation, reflects the limited direct observations of Jupiter's atmosphere, and uses relevant probes or missions appropriately.
criteria.1-2: States speculative visuals as certain facts or invents unsupported details without acknowledging observational limits.
criteria.3-4: Includes a token caveat but mostly overclaims what we know about views inside Jupiter's atmosphere.
criteria.5-6: Acknowledges uncertainty and mentions limited observations or spacecraft data, but does not connect this to specific visual or atmospheric claims.
criteria.7-8: Correctly notes that only limited probes have entered Jupiter, that imagery from within the atmosphere is lacking, and that cloud appearance is partly inferred.
criteria.9-10: Carefully calibrates confidence throughout, referencing Galileo/Juno or remote imaging limits where relevant, and frames the submarine-view description as plausible extrapolation rather than settled fact.

criteria.name: Contradiction Control and Counterfactual Discipline
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer preserves the counterfactual premise without introducing contradictions about submarines, Jupiter, or planetary physics.
criteria.1-2: Contradicts basic facts, such as giving Jupiter a normal ocean floor, breathable air, survivable open hatches, or submarine propulsion working normally.
criteria.3-4: Avoids some obvious errors but still includes incompatible claims, such as both immediate destruction and extended normal exploration without modification.
criteria.5-6: Mostly respects the premise and physics, with minor inconsistencies about buoyancy, pressure, windows, propulsion, or survivability.
criteria.7-8: Clearly distinguishes an ordinary submarine's fate from a heavily modified probe-like version and avoids claims of solid-surface landing or oceanic navigation.
criteria.9-10: Consistently handles the absurd premise by explaining what must be modified, what remains impossible, and what observations could occur only under tightly qualified survival assumptions.

items.model_answer:
Riding a submarine into Jupiter would be a journey of increasingly extreme environments, ultimately ending in catastrophic destruction long before you reached anything resembling a solid surface. Jupiter is a gas giant with no true boundary between its atmosphere and its interior—density just increases continuously until the gas behaves like a liquid.

As your submarine descends from space into Jupiter's upper atmosphere, you would first encounter violent weather. Jet streams whip around the planet at hundreds of miles per hour, and you would be tossed through massive ammonia clouds and colossal thunderstorms where lightning flashes are hundreds of times more powerful than on Earth. 

Assuming your vessel survives the turbulence, the descent would grow darker and colder as thick clouds obscure the sunlight. Eventually, you would cross the zero-altitude reference point where Jupiter's atmospheric pressure equals 1 bar (Earth's surface pressure). Continuing down, the pressure would rapidly mount. At around 1,000 miles deep, the pressure reaches roughly 1,000 atmospheres. The surrounding hydrogen and helium gas would become so compressed that it transitions into a supercritical fluid—a bizarre state where it has the density of a liquid but still permeates gas. Your submarine would essentially be "floating" in a crushing ocean of supercritical hydrogen.

The deeper you go, the more hostile the conditions become. At roughly 3,000 miles down, the pressure hits a million atmospheres. The temperature soars to thousands of degrees—hot enough to melt tungsten. The surrounding fluid is now a dense, metallic liquid hydrogen, which is so compressed that its electrons flow freely, making it electrically conductive. This metallic ocean is what generates Jupiter's immense magnetic field. At these pressures, the hull of even the most advanced deep-sea military submarine—built to withstand perhaps 40 atmospheres—would be instantly crumpled like tin foil, and the intense heat would vaporize you and the vessel.

If you somehow miraculously survived this, your final destination would be Jupiter's core. At the very center, roughly 18,000 miles down, the pressure reaches tens of millions of atmospheres and the temperature exceeds 40,000 degrees Fahrenheit (hotter than the surface of the Sun). Here, the extreme pressure forces the metallic hydrogen to mix with heavier elements like rock and ice, forming a sludgy, partially solid core. You would never reach a clear ocean floor to land on; your submarine would simply be crushed and dissolved into the planet's extreme, churning interior.

nodes.text: Riding a submarine into Jupiter would be a journey of increasingly extreme environments,
ultimately ending in catastrophic destruction long before you reached anything resembling a solid surface.
Jupiter is a gas giant with no true boundary between its atmosphere and its interior
density just increases continuously until the gas behaves like a liquid.
As your submarine descends from space into Jupiter's upper atmosphere,
you would first encounter violent weather.
Jet streams whip around the planet at hundreds of miles per hour,
and you would be tossed through massive ammonia clouds and colossal thunderstorms
where lightning flashes are hundreds of times more powerful than on Earth.
Assuming your vessel survives the turbulence,
the descent would grow darker and colder
as thick clouds obscure the sunlight.
Eventually, you would cross the zero-altitude reference point
where Jupiter's atmospheric pressure equals 1 bar (Earth's surface pressure).
Continuing down, the pressure would rapidly mount.
At around 1,000 miles deep, the pressure reaches roughly 1,000 atmospheres.
The surrounding hydrogen and helium gas would become so compressed
that it transitions into a supercritical fluid
a bizarre state where it has the density of a liquid but still permeates gas.
Your submarine would essentially be "floating" in a crushing ocean of supercritical hydrogen.
The deeper you go, the more hostile the conditions become.
At roughly 3,000 miles down, the pressure hits a million atmospheres.
The temperature soars to thousands of degrees
hot enough to melt tungsten.
The surrounding fluid is now a dense, metallic liquid hydrogen,
which is so compressed that its electrons flow freely,
making it electrically conductive.
This metallic ocean is what generates Jupiter's immense magnetic field.
At these pressures, the hull of even the most advanced deep-sea military submarine—built to withstand perhaps 40 atmospheres—would be instantly crumpled like tin foil,
and the intense heat would vaporize you and the vessel.
If you somehow miraculously survived this,
your final destination would be Jupiter's core.
At the very center, roughly 18,000 miles down, the pressure reaches tens of millions of atmospheres
and the temperature exceeds 40,000 degrees Fahrenheit (hotter than the surface of the Sun).
Here, the extreme pressure forces the metallic hydrogen to mix with heavier elements like rock and ice,
forming a sludgy, partially solid core.
You would never reach a clear ocean floor to land on;
your submarine would simply be crushed and dissolved into the planet's extreme, churning interior.
