human_answers: This one doesn't end well for us. But—unlike most scenarios involving the word "antimatter"—the end is surprisingly slow and drawn-out. [Image: image] The whole universe is matter, as far as we can tell. No one is sure why (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baryon_asymmetry) there's more matter than antimatter, since the laws of physics are pretty (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CP_violation#CP-symmetry) symmetrical, and so there's no reason to expect there to be more of one than the other.[1]Although when it comes down to it, there's no reason to expect anything at all. It's possible that galaxies are made of antimatter, and we just haven't noticed because we haven't tried to touch them. This is a cool idea, but if there are zones of matter and zones of antimatter, we should see a telltale gamma-ray glow from the boundary between the zones. So far, we haven't (http://www.researchgate.net/publication/1746009_When_Clusters_Collide_Constraints_On_Antimatter_On_The_Largest_Scales) seen that, although another telescope (http://arxiv.org/abs/1401.7258) might help. [Image: image] If the rest of the universe were swapped out for antimatter, we'd be in trouble. Outer space isn't really "space";[2]As far as I know, it really is "outer", for what that's worth. it's full of a thin gas.[3]Technically, plasma.​[4]Technically, there's also a substantial quantity of solid grains of dust.​[5]Look, there's a bunch of little bits that are hard to see, ok?.​[6]Ok, they're not always (https://www.flickr.com/groups/northernlight/) hard to see (https://www.google.com/search?q=1833+leonids&tbm=isch). The Earth's magnetic field (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Magnetic_Fields) protects us from the solar wind, and would protect us from an anti-solar wind, too. A tiny fraction of the particles from the Sun do reach the Earth, funneled down by our magnetic field, and create the aurora. In this scenario, the aurora would get a lot brighter, but most of the time not bright enough to really cause problems. Meteorites would be the real problem. The Earth sweeps up space dust as it travels around its orbit.[7]Unfortunately for us, antimatter is probably (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gravitational_interaction_of_antimatter) attracted to matter by gravity. About 100 tons of dust per day enters the atmosphere in the form of tiny grains, most weighing about 10^-5 grams. An additional similar (http://books.google.com/books?id=eqd4e34uE-MC&pg=PA78) average per-day amount arrives in giant clumps all at once (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicxulub_impactor). This inflow of antimatter dust would collide with the top of our atmosphere and be annihilated. The interactions between the nuclei and antinuclei and protons and antiprotons would be complex,[8]A lot (http://www.iaps.inaf.it/sz/integral2013/talks-posters/40-2013_10%20Antimatter%20Universe_von%20Ballmoos.pdf) of the energy would be carried away by neutrinos (http://turtlepedia.wikia.com/wiki/Neutrinos). but the end result would be a lot of gamma rays, which would turn into a lot of heat. This steady flow of material would be worst around dawn, when your house was facing in the direction of Earth's motion. The heat and light added by the antimatter would most likely be enough to tip the Earth into a "runaway greenhouse (http://www.nature.com/nature/journal/v504/n7479/full/nature12827.html?WT.ec_id=NATURE-20131212)" scenario, turning the Earth into something resembling Venus. But the big asteroids would get us first. Even a relatively small object like the Chelyabinsk meteor (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chelyabinsk_meteor) would deliver as much energy as the meteor that killed the dinosaurs.[9]Although it would deliver it to the top of the atmosphere, so in some ways it wouldn't be as bad. Fairly large asteroids enter the atmosphere every few months (http://www.nature.com/nature/journal/v503/n7475/full/nature12741.html)—mostly unnoticed. If they were all antimatter, each one would trigger a tremendous pulse of energy in the sky and ignite a massive firestorm.[10]If an antimatter meteor is large enough, encountering a cloud could launch some of it backward without completely destroying it (http://books.google.com/books?id=gI-nZdadvJ4C&pg=PA140). However, it's hard to come up with a practical (http://weeklyworldnews.com/headlines/43206/asteroid-to-bounce-off-earth-today/) scenario in which a meteor would exhibit this effect in Earth's atmosphere—unless it were so large that it would have basically destroyed the planet anyway. Right now, it's still an open question whether any significant percentage of the stuff in the sky is made of antimatter. It's probably not, but we'd need to build another orbiting gamma-ray telescope to really be sure. However, it's easy to use a telescope to rule out one possibility: That everything in the sky is antimatter. [Image: image] If you have a telescope, maybe you can get that result published.

rubrics.question_focus: What If Everything except Earth Were Made of Antimatter?

criteria.name: Counterfactual premise fidelity and physical setup
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer correctly interprets the premise that Earth remains matter while the Sun, solar wind, interplanetary dust, meteoroids, and the wider universe are antimatter, and applies known matter-antimatter physics without changing the scenario.
criteria.1-2: Misreads the premise, e.g. makes Earth antimatter too, assumes instant universal contact, or treats antimatter as magic.
criteria.3-4: Recognizes Earth-versus-rest antimatter but makes major setup errors such as ignoring space dust or claiming photons from the anti-Sun annihilate.
criteria.5-6: Mostly preserves the premise and basic annihilation idea, but omits important environmental details or introduces some unsupported assumptions.
criteria.7-8: Accurately frames Earth as matter in an antimatter environment, including anti-solar wind, dust, meteoroids, and normal radiation/gravity.
criteria.9-10: Precisely maintains the counterfactual setup across scales and explicitly distinguishes harmless or weak interactions from dangerous matter-antimatter contacts.

criteria.name: Matter-antimatter mechanism coverage
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates coverage and correctness of the key mechanisms: annihilation of antimatter particles with the atmosphere/Earth, gamma rays and secondary heating, magnetic-field shielding, auroral effects, and energy release from antimatter dust and meteoroids.
criteria.1-2: Provides little or no mechanism beyond vague explosions or apocalypse language.
criteria.3-4: Mentions annihilation but badly misstates where it happens, what energy forms result, or why Earth is affected.
criteria.5-6: Explains annihilation and energy release in general terms but misses several central mechanisms such as atmospheric interception, gamma rays, or magnetic shielding.
criteria.7-8: Covers most mechanisms correctly, including anti-solar wind shielding, atmospheric annihilation, gamma-ray heating, dust influx, and meteoroid energy.
criteria.9-10: Gives a detailed, physically grounded mechanism chain with appropriate nuances such as neutrino losses, upper-atmosphere deposition, and variable particle/meteoroid flux.

criteria.name: Long-range causal chain and downstream effects
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer develops a coherent progression from immediate particle interactions to environmental consequences and eventual habitability outcomes for Earth.
criteria.1-2: Jumps directly to an unsupported ending with no causal sequence.
criteria.3-4: Has a rough sequence but relies on large gaps, reversals, or arbitrary disasters.
criteria.5-6: Presents a plausible broad arc but underdevelops the transition from small fluxes to climate or impact consequences.
criteria.7-8: Builds a coherent chain: limited solar-wind effects, enhanced aurora, continuous dust annihilation, atmospheric heating, climate stress, and dangerous antimatter meteors.
criteria.9-10: Integrates short-, medium-, and long-term effects into a clear timeline, explaining why the end is severe but not necessarily instantaneous.

criteria.name: Scale, magnitude, and comparative reasoning
criteria.criteria_description: Judges whether the answer uses appropriate scale estimates or comparisons for antimatter fluxes, dust mass, meteor frequency, annihilation energy, and climate or impact severity.
criteria.1-2: Uses no scale reasoning or gives wildly impossible magnitudes.
criteria.3-4: Includes some quantities or comparisons but they are mostly incorrect or misleading.
criteria.5-6: Uses qualitative scale distinctions correctly but lacks concrete comparisons or has minor magnitude errors.
criteria.7-8: Correctly distinguishes small anti-solar-wind effects from serious dust and meteoroid effects, with reasonable energy or frequency comparisons.
criteria.9-10: Employs strong order-of-magnitude reasoning, e.g. daily dust infall, antimatter annihilation energy, Chelyabinsk-scale objects, firestorms, and runaway-greenhouse plausibility.

criteria.name: Uncertainty calibration and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer states uncertainties appropriately and avoids contradictions about antimatter gravity, cosmic antimatter observability, annihilation boundaries, and Earth’s survival timescale.
criteria.1-2: Contains major contradictions or presents false certainties, such as guaranteed antigravity or immediate total annihilation without contact.
criteria.3-4: Shows limited uncertainty awareness and includes several conflicting claims about antimatter behavior or observational evidence.
criteria.5-6: Avoids the worst contradictions but overstates some conclusions or leaves assumptions unclear.
criteria.7-8: Calibrates uncertainty well, noting likely gravity attraction, complex annihilation products, observational gamma-ray constraints, and approximate rather than exact outcomes.
criteria.9-10: Maintains rigorous consistency throughout while clearly separating established physics, plausible extrapolation, and open questions about antimatter distribution and detailed atmospheric effects.

failures.question: What If a Falling Person Grabbed a Flagpole and Swung Back to the Roof?
human_answers: If you're like me, your first thought on hearing this question was, "That's ridiculous; there's no way that could work." Your first thought is right. But just to be sure, let's take a closer look. Grip strength depends on a lot of factors, like hand slickness and surface material. But for the moment, let's assume Rex's hands are able to grab the pole tightly. What happens to the rest of his body? [Image: image] It's hard to find good numbers on how much force it takes to tear off a person's arm.[1]Which is probably a good thing, to be honest. There are threads on the question on MetaFilter (http://ask.metafilter.com/133821/How-much-force-to-tear-off-a-limb) and the Straight Dope message boards (http://boards.straightdope.com/sdmb/showthread.php?t=515612), and frequent discussion of the death of Robert-François Damiens (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert-Fran%C3%A7ois_Damiens),[2]Damiens was tortured to death for attempting to assassinate Louis XV, but a team of horses had trouble tearing him limb from limb. but not too much hard data. For the record, there are lots (https://journals.biologists.com/jeb/article/215/20/3552/11014/Tendon-material-properties-vary-and-are) of studies (http://www.udel.edu/PT/PT%20Clinical%20Services/journalclub/sojc/95_96/apr96/itoi.pdf) and lectures (http://wings.buffalo.edu/eng/mae/courses/417-517/Orthopaedic%20Biomechanics/Lecture%203u.pdf) on the breaking strength of tendons, which tend to give values of around 50-150 MPa. That's stronger than skin (27 MPa (http://www.ircobi.org/downloads/irc12/pdf_files/59.pdf)) but weaker than bone (120 MPa (http://www.robmech.co.za/proceed/ROBMECH2011_Unene%20N.%20MAnganyi_Biological%20considerations%20in%20the%20structural%20design%20of%20smart%20prosthetics.pdf)). However, to figure out the overall strength of the arm, we need to tally up all the tendons, muscles, and tissues in the wrist, arm, and shoulder, their cross-sectional area, and figure out which parts would be put under strain in what order. Instead, it might be easier to consider people who try to pull off this maneuver in real life: Gymnasts. A gymnast on the uneven parallel bars pushes the human body to its limits while performing maneuvers very similar to Rex's flagpole stunt.[3]In some ways, at least. A 2009 study (http://www.jbiomech.com/article/S0021-9290(09)00609-5/fulltext) used 3D motion capture to measure the forces involved in an elite gymnast's routine. They found that the athlete's hands exerted a force of over 3 kN on the bar at the bottom of a swing. In other words, the gymnast was briefly supporting almost 700 lbs of weight. Let's be generous and assume that Rex is even better than the elite gymnast in the study. (After all, the gymnast has to worry about long-term injury, while Rex's concerns are a lot more short-term). Suppose Rex's arms can handle a swing force of over 10 kN, three times more than the gymnast (and twice as much as these (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=V1JBx2Mm9e8) guys (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iJYOs5VFjwk)!). How will he do? Let's see how much force Rex needs to withstand. The "tallest building in town" here in Boston is the 240-meter-tall Hancock Tower (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Hancock_Tower); if he jumped off the top, he'd be going nearly 100 mph by the time he was halfway down. At that speed, the force on his arms (speed squared over the radius of his turn[4]Which is effectively somewhere between 1 and 2 meters here.) would be around ... 100 kN (http://www.wolframalpha.com/input/?i=100+lbs+*+(100+mph)%5E2+%2F+(1.5+meters)). [Image: image] Really, the numbers are just telling us what common sense told us from the start: You can't grab hold of something while going 100 mph, much less swing around it. If you want get a more vivid intuitive sense of the forces involved, consider this: In 2006, GQ put baseball star Albert Pujols in a lab and measured his swing. They clocked the speed of his bat at 87 mph, similar to the speed of the flagpole relative to our falling person. So if you want to pull off Rex's stunt, first go find Albert Pujols, have him swing his bat as hard as you can ... and try to grab it. [Image: image] And remember: You're just trying to stop the momentum of a 31-ounce piece of wood. When you're falling past the flagpole, you're going to be catching your whole body, so it's going to be up to 100 times worse. Good luck! [Image: image]

rubrics.question_focus: What If a Falling Person Grabbed a Flagpole and Swung Back to the Roof?

criteria.name: Core physical plausibility and conclusion
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer reaches a physically defensible conclusion about a falling person grabbing a flagpole at high speed and swinging back to the roof.
criteria.1-2: Claims the stunt would likely work or treats it as easy, with little or no physical justification.
criteria.3-4: Expresses doubt but leaves the outcome ambiguous or bases the conclusion on weak intuition only.
criteria.5-6: Concludes it is very unlikely or impossible, citing excessive force or speed in general terms.
criteria.7-8: Clearly explains that the person could not safely grab and swing back because the required deceleration/centripetal force far exceeds human limits.
criteria.9-10: Gives a decisive, physically grounded conclusion: grip, arms, shoulders, or tissues would fail or the person would be severely injured long before a successful swing back to the roof.

criteria.name: Force and motion mechanism coverage
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates coverage of the relevant mechanics: fall speed, momentum change, circular motion around the pole, radius of swing, and forces transmitted through the hands and arms.
criteria.1-2: Ignores mechanics or relies on unrelated ideas such as bravery, agility, or cinematic timing.
criteria.3-4: Mentions falling speed or impact force but does not connect them to the pole grab or swing dynamics.
criteria.5-6: Identifies that grabbing the pole would require stopping or redirecting the body's momentum, but with limited detail.
criteria.7-8: Explains that the body must undergo rapid centripetal acceleration around a small radius, creating forces many times body weight.
criteria.9-10: Integrates fall velocity, swing radius, centripetal acceleration, grip load, and body-momentum redirection into a coherent mechanical account.

criteria.name: Biomechanical realism
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer realistically treats human grip, tendons, shoulders, arms, and injury thresholds in the flagpole scenario.
criteria.1-2: Assumes hands and arms can withstand arbitrary loads or ignores injury entirely.
criteria.3-4: Mentions possible injury but does not specify what would fail or why.
criteria.5-6: Notes that grip strength or arm strength would be insufficient under the load.
criteria.7-8: Discusses likely failure modes such as losing grip, dislocated shoulders, torn tendons/ligaments, broken bones, or severe soft-tissue injury.
criteria.9-10: Compares the required loads to realistic human or gymnast-level capabilities and explains that even exceptional strength would be overwhelmed.

criteria.name: Counterfactual chain coherence
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates the logical sequence from the counterfactual premise—successfully contacting or gripping the flagpole—to downstream consequences such as swing path, roof return, or failure.
criteria.1-2: Presents disconnected claims or jumps directly to an unsupported outcome.
criteria.3-4: Gives a partial sequence but skips key transitions between grabbing, loading, swinging, and landing.
criteria.5-6: Provides a mostly logical chain showing that grabbing leads to extreme forces and likely failure.
criteria.7-8: Maintains a coherent cause-effect chain from fall speed to pole contact to force spike to bodily failure or loss of grip.
criteria.9-10: Explores both the realistic failure path and the hypothetical idealized path, showing that even if grip initially holds, the swing geometry and loads still prevent a safe return to the roof.

criteria.name: Uncertainty calibration and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer uses estimates appropriately, avoids overclaiming beyond available data, and remains internally consistent with the scenario.
criteria.1-2: Contains major contradictions, impossible numbers, or confident claims that violate basic physics.
criteria.3-4: Uses vague or inconsistent estimates, or alternates between saying the stunt works and cannot work.
criteria.5-6: Acknowledges approximate values and avoids the most serious contradictions.
criteria.7-8: Uses order-of-magnitude reasoning sensibly, distinguishing assumptions such as fall height, body mass, speed, and pole radius.
criteria.9-10: Calibrates uncertainty well while preserving the robust conclusion: across plausible heights, speeds, and human strength limits, the stunt remains catastrophically implausible.

failures.question: What If Earth Were Made Entirely of Protons and the Moon of Electrons?
human_answers: This is, by far, the most destructive What-If scenario to date. You might imagine an electron Moon orbiting a proton Earth, sort of like a gigantic hydrogen atom. On one level, it makes a kind of sense; after all, electrons orbit protons, and moons orbit planets. In fact, a planetary model of the atom (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bohr_model) was briefly popular (although it turned out not to be very useful for understanding atoms.[1]This model was (mostly (http://scitation.aip.org/content/aapt/journal/ajp/81/2/10.1119/1.4769785)) obsolete by the 1920s, but lived on in an elaborate foam-and-pipe-cleaner diorama I made in 6th grade science class.) [Image: image] If you put two electrons together, they try to fly apart. Electrons are negatively charged, and the force of repulsion from this charge is about 20 orders of magnitude stronger than the force of gravity pulling them together. If you put 1052 electrons together—to build a Moon—they push each other apart really hard. In fact, they push each other apart so hard, each electron would be shoved away with an unbelievable amount of energy. It turns out that, for the proton Earth and electron Moon in Noah's scenario, the planetary model is even more wrong than usual. The Moon wouldn't orbit the Earth because they'd barely have a chance to influence each other;[2]I interpreted the question to mean that the Moon was replaced with a sphere of electrons the size and mass of the Moon, and ditto for the Earth. There are other interpretations, but practically speaking the end result is the same. the forces trying to blow each one apart would be far more powerful than any attractive force between the two. If we ignore general relativity for a moment—we'll come back to it—we can calculate that the energy from these electrons all pushing on each other would be enough to accelerate all of them outward at near the speed of light.[3]But not past it; we're ignoring general relativity, but not special relativity. Accelerating particles to those speeds isn't unusual; a desktop particle accelerator (http://www.amazon.com/s/?field-keywords=crt+monitor) can accelerate electrons to a reasonable fraction of the speed of light. But the electrons in Noah's Moon would each be carrying much, much more energy than those in a normal accelerator—orders of magnitude more than the Planck energy, which is itself many orders of magnitude larger than the energies we can reach in our largest accelerators. In other words, Noah's question takes us pretty far outside normal physics, into the highly theoretical realm of things like quantum gravity and string theory. So I contacted Dr. Cindy Keeler, a string theorist with the Niels Bohr Institute. I explained Noah's scenario, and she was kind enough to offer some thoughts. [Image: image] Dr. Keeler agreed that we shouldn't rely on any calculations that involve putting that much energy in each electron, since it's so far beyond what we're able to test in our accelerators. "I don't trust anything with energy per particle over the Planck scale. The most energy we've really observed is in cosmic rays; more than LHC by circa 106, I think, but still not close to the Planck energy. Being a string theorist, I'm tempted to say something stringy would happen—but the truth is we just don't know." Luckily, that's not the end of the story. Remember how we're ignoring general relativity? Well, this is one of the very, very rare situations where bringing in general relativity makes a problem easier to solve. [Image: image] There's a huge amount of potential energy in this scenario—the energy that we imagined would blast all these electrons apart. That energy warps space and time just like mass does.[4]If we let the energy blast the electrons apart at near the speed of light, we'd see that energy actually take the form of mass, as the electrons gained mass relativistically. That is, until something stringy happened. The amount of energy in our electron Moon, it turns out, is about equal to the total mass and energy of the entire visible universe. An entire universe worth of mass-energy—concentrated into the space of our (relatively small) Moon—would warp space-time so strongly that it would overpower even the repulsion of those 1052 electrons. Dr. Keeler's diagnosis: "Yup, black hole." But this is no an ordinary black hole; it's a black hole with a lot of electric charge.[5]The proton Earth, which would also be part of this black hole, would reduce the charge, but since an Earth-mass of protons has much less charge than a Moon-mass of electrons, it doesn't affect the result much. And for that, you need a different set of equations—rather than the standard Schwarzschild equations (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schwarzschild_radius), you need the Reissner–Nordström ones (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reissner%E2%80%93Nordstr%C3%B6m_metric). In a sense, the Reissner-Nordström equations compare the outward force of the charge to the inward pull of gravity. If the outward push from the charge is large enough, it's possible the event horizon surrounding the black hole can disappear completely. That would leave behind an infinitely-dense object (http://www.amazon.com/s/?url=search-alias%3Dindustrial&field-keywords=infinitely+dense+object) from which light can escape—a naked singularity (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naked_singularity). Once you have a naked singularity, physics starts breaking down in very big ways. Quantum mechanics and general relativity give absurd answers, and they're not even the same absurd answers. Some people have argued (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmic_censorship_hypothesis) that the laws of physics don't allow that kind of situation to arise. As Dr. Keeler put it, "Nobody likes a naked singularity." In the case of an electron Moon, the energy from all those electrons pushing on each other is so large that the gravitational pull wins, and our singularity would form a normal black hole. At least, "normal" in some sense; it would be a black hole as massive as the observable universe.[6]A black hole with the mass of the observable universe would have a radius of 13.8 billion light-years, and the universe is 13.8 billion years old, which has led some people to say "the Universe is a black hole!" (It's not (http://www.preposterousuniverse.com/blog/2010/04/28/the-universe-is-not-a-black-hole/).) Would this black hole cause the universe to collapse? Hard to say. The answer depends on what the deal with dark energy (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_energy) is, and nobody knows what the deal with dark energy is. But for now, at least, nearby galaxies would be safe. Since the gravitational influence of the black hole can only expand outward at the speed of light, much of the universe around us would remain blissfully unaware of our ridiculous electron experiment. [Image: image]

rubrics.question_focus: What If Earth Were Made Entirely of Protons and the Moon of Electrons?

criteria.name: Initial charge-forces and instability of proton Earth/electron Moon
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer correctly identifies the dominant early physics: enormous like-charge repulsion within each body, vastly exceeding gravity and preventing any ordinary Earth-Moon or atom-like orbital behavior.
criteria.1-2: Treats the system as a stable giant atom, normal orbit, or ordinary charged planet-moon pair with little disruption.
criteria.3-4: Mentions electrical effects but underestimates them or focuses mainly on Earth-Moon attraction rather than internal self-repulsion.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes both bodies would violently destabilize from like-charge repulsion, but gives only qualitative or incomplete scale comparison.
criteria.7-8: Clearly explains that electrostatic repulsion within the electron Moon and proton Earth overwhelms gravity by enormous orders of magnitude and dominates before orbital dynamics matter.
criteria.9-10: Precisely frames the premise as catastrophically unstable, rejects the giant-atom analogy, and explains why internal Coulomb energy/repulsion dwarfs both gravity and mutual Earth-Moon attraction.

criteria.name: Mass-energy scale and relativistic/Planck-regime consequences
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer traces the energy stored in the separated charges to extreme relativistic scales, including near-light-speed expansion in non-GR reasoning and the limits of tested particle physics.
criteria.1-2: Ignores energy scale or describes only conventional explosions, radiation, or chemical/nuclear effects.
criteria.3-4: States the explosion would be huge but gives no credible mechanism or scale beyond ordinary astrophysical destruction.
criteria.5-6: Notes particles would be accelerated to relativistic speeds or enormous energies, but does not connect this to untested Planck-scale physics.
criteria.7-8: Explains that Coulomb potential energy would drive particles toward near-light-speed energies far beyond accelerator scales, with special relativity limiting speeds.
criteria.9-10: Accurately connects the charge energy to trans-Planckian per-particle regimes, notes standard calculations become unreliable, and distinguishes special-relativistic limits from speculative quantum-gravity/string effects.

criteria.name: General-relativistic endpoint: charged black hole rather than simple explosion
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer captures the key long-range outcome that the charge-field energy itself gravitates so strongly that the system forms an enormous charged black hole, with appropriate Reissner-Nordström/naked-singularity considerations.
criteria.1-2: Concludes only that Earth and Moon explode or annihilate, with no role for gravity from field energy.
criteria.3-4: Mentions a black hole vaguely but gives the wrong cause, wrong scale, or treats it as a normal Earth/Moon-mass black hole.
criteria.5-6: Identifies black-hole formation from immense energy density but omits charge-specific issues or the competition between charge repulsion and gravity.
criteria.7-8: Explains that the electromagnetic potential energy gravitates, producing a black hole vastly larger/more massive than Earth or Moon, and notes high electric charge matters.
criteria.9-10: Correctly presents the endpoint as a Reissner-Nordström-like charged black hole, discusses why charge could in principle threaten the horizon/naked singularity but gravity from the enormous energy wins.

criteria.name: Long-range causal chain and downstream cosmic effects
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer gives a coherent sequence from premise to immediate instability to relativistic/GR outcome to effects on the wider universe, without skipping causally important stages.
criteria.1-2: Provides a disconnected list of disasters or an unsupported final claim with no causal progression.
criteria.3-4: Has a rough sequence but major steps are missing, reversed, or physically inconsistent.
criteria.5-6: Gives a plausible chain from charge repulsion to catastrophic energy release, but only weakly addresses the final cosmic-scale consequences.
criteria.7-8: Coherently traces the sequence through self-repulsion, extreme energy density, black-hole formation, and limited causal influence propagating outward at light speed.
criteria.9-10: Builds a tight long-range chain covering local destruction, collapse into a universe-mass-scale charged black hole, horizon/cosmic scale implications, and why distant galaxies are not affected instantly.

criteria.name: Uncertainty calibration and contradiction control under extreme physics
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer avoids overclaiming beyond known physics, flags speculative regimes, and remains internally consistent about charge, gravity, relativity, annihilation, and causality.
criteria.1-2: Makes confident false claims such as electron-proton annihilation, faster-than-light effects, stable matter, or ordinary electromagnetism applying unmodified at all scales.
criteria.3-4: Includes some correct ideas but also serious contradictions, such as both stable orbit and immediate total collapse, or instantaneous universal destruction.
criteria.5-6: Mostly consistent but overstates uncertain details or fails to distinguish known physics from speculative quantum-gravity territory.

failures.question: How Many Gravity Assists Would It Take to Stop Jupiter?
human_answers: More than we can afford. Spacecraft sometimes perform close flybys of heavy, fast-moving planets, which can let them gain speed without using fuel.[1]It may sound strange that you could gain speed by flying toward a planet and then away from it, since intuitively it seems like any speed you gain from flying toward it, you should lose flying away. But it's not really about gravity at all; gravity assists could work just as well with ropes or springs, if you could make them big enough. When you you fly toward a planet, swing around it, and fly back in the direction you came, it's as if you "bounced off" the planet. If the planet is moving, this bounce can give you an extra kick—like a tennis ball thrown at the windshield of a passing truck. You can check out What If #38 (http://what-if.xkcd.com/38/) for details—or, at least, a drawing of the tennis ball thing. Due to conservation of momentum, the maneuver also slows the planet down very slightly, but no one really worries about that. [Image: image] Planets don't slow down much during a flyby because they're so much heavier than spacecraft. When New Horizons flew by Jupiter, it gained about 4,000 m/s of velocity, while Jupiter lost about 10-21 m/s.[2]The geometry is a little complicated, since they were changing both speed and direction. If you want to learn more, look for a copy of this paper (http://scitation.aip.org/content/aapt/journal/ajp/71/5/10.1119/1.1539102); it's a great tutorial. 10-21 meters per second may not sound like much, but it very slightly changed Jupiter's orbit, shortening its year and bringing it slightly closer to the Sun. Thanks to that flyby, by the time the Sun goes supernova, Jupiter's calendar will be several dozen nanoseconds out of sync from where it would be otherwise! [Image: image] "Several dozen nanoseconds out of sync" isn't really satisfying, so we'll definitely need more than one flyby. How many can we pull off? The New Horizons mission cost the US government about \$700,000,000 over the full planned lifetime of the mission from 2001 to 2016. Over that same period, the government spent about \$47,879,840,000,000 on other things. If we cut all the spending on those other things[3]It's probably nothing important. and funneled it all into New Horizons probes, we could have launched 68,000 identical New Horizons probes. This would create some problems. For one, New Horizons carries a chunk of plutonium for power. This chunk—about 10 kg of it—was made from uranium in a reactor (http://www.nature.com/news/nuclear-power-desperately-seeking-plutonium-1.16411). To make enough plutonium for 68,000 New Horizons would require a substantial chunk of the world's uranium reserves. But it gets worse.[4]It always seems to, with plutonium. When NASA launches a spacecraft carrying plutonium, they estimate the odds of a launch accident which would release radioactive material into the atmosphere. Usually, these odds are around 1 in 300. With 68,000 launches, then, we can expect a little over 200 nuclear accidents, which probably isn't good. [Image: image] But it would all be worth it if we could slow down Jupiter! Sadly, 68,000 New Horizons probes aren't nearly enough. We'd still only rob Jupiter of a tiny fraction of its speed. Over the lifetime of the Solar System, the error in Jupiter's calendar would only add up to 2 milliseconds. If we made the spacecraft cheaper, we could send more of them, but sooner or later we'd start running out of materials. We'd definitely run out of fuel for all these rocket launches, but let's assume we've built some kind of space elevator to make launches cheap. We'd run out of uranium (to make the plutonium) pretty quickly, but we could replace the uranium with a chunk of lead—after all, this spacecraft doesn't really need to work. Eventually, though, we'd start running out of lead, too. If we replaced the lead with something else—say, rocks, or old garbage—we'd run out of that, too. At some point, in our desperate attempts to reduce Jupiter's forward speed, we'd be reduced to stuffing handfuls of rocks and dirt into a burlap sack with a NASA logo on the side. [Image: image] Then, believe it or not, we would run out of rocks. The Earth's crust only has so much stuff[5]This is the technical term. in it. Even if we peeled up the upper few dozen kilometers of crust and flung it at Jupiter—and for the record, I do not recommend we do this—it would trim less than a single mile per hour off Jupiter's speed. Really, it makes sense that this plan doesn't work. Earth weighs a lot less than Jupiter,[6]Earth weighs almost exactly pi milliJupiters. so even if we throw the entire Earth at Jupiter, it would still only reduce Jupiter's speed by a fraction of a percent—on the order of a few dozen miles per hour. The situation is similar to the one in the tennis ball analogy from earlier: If you want to stop a truck with tennis balls, the tennis balls need more momentum than the truck, which means they need to be extremely heavy, fast, or both. And at the core, that's the problem with this idea. Gravity assists are just like throwing a tennis ball at a speeding truck, and to stop a truck ... [Image: image] ... you need an awfully big tennis ball.

rubrics.question_focus: How Many Gravity Assists Would It Take to Stop Jupiter?

criteria.name: Gravity-assist momentum-transfer mechanism
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer correctly explains how a spacecraft flyby can change Jupiter's velocity through conservation of momentum, including the 'bounce off a moving planet' analogy and the fact that Jupiter is slowed only minutely per encounter.
criteria.1-2: Misstates gravity assists as free energy, pure fuel thrust, or a way to remove Jupiter's speed without momentum exchange.
criteria.3-4: Mentions gravity assists can speed spacecraft or slow Jupiter, but gives little or incorrect causal explanation.
criteria.5-6: Explains momentum exchange qualitatively, but omits key geometry or why Jupiter's change is extremely small.
criteria.7-8: Accurately describes flyby momentum transfer, spacecraft gain, Jupiter loss, and mass-ratio scaling.
criteria.9-10: Gives a precise, coherent account of the moving-planet bounce mechanism, conservation laws, directional dependence, and why each assist barely affects Jupiter.

criteria.name: Quantitative order-of-magnitude reasoning
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer uses plausible magnitudes for Jupiter's mass and orbital speed, spacecraft mass/speed changes, and the resulting enormous number of assists needed, rather than relying on vague claims.
criteria.1-2: Provides no quantitative reasoning or gives wildly impossible numbers without justification.
criteria.3-4: Uses some numbers, but they are inconsistent with planetary or spacecraft scales by many orders of magnitude.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes the number is astronomically large and uses approximate scaling, but lacks a defensible calculation.
criteria.7-8: Uses credible order-of-magnitude estimates showing why human-scale missions fall vastly short.
criteria.9-10: Connects mass, velocity change, and momentum conservation to a defensible estimate, showing that stopping Jupiter requires momentum comparable to Jupiter's orbital momentum.

criteria.name: Resource and feasibility chain under the counterfactual
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer traces downstream practical limits of launching enough spacecraft, including cost, launch capacity, propellant/material needs, plutonium or power-source constraints, and eventually planetary-scale mass limits.
criteria.1-2: Ignores feasibility and treats unlimited spacecraft or launches as trivial.
criteria.3-4: Mentions cost or difficulty only superficially, without connecting it to the number of assists.
criteria.5-6: Identifies several constraints, but the chain is incomplete or not tied to momentum requirements.
criteria.7-8: Coherently explains why budget, launch accidents, fuel, power sources, and materials fail long before Jupiter is stopped.
criteria.9-10: Develops a robust long-range feasibility chain showing that even extreme assumptions, such as cheap launch or using Earth's crust as payload, still cannot supply enough momentum.

criteria.name: Long-range consequences and orbital interpretation
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer correctly interprets what 'stop Jupiter' means in orbital terms and follows the consequences of partially reducing Jupiter's heliocentric velocity, such as orbit changes rather than an immediate simple halt.
criteria.1-2: Treats stopping Jupiter as a local braking problem with no orbital or solar-system consequences.
criteria.3-4: Mentions Jupiter's orbit but confuses velocity reduction with destroying, ejecting, or instantly freezing Jupiter.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes that slowing changes Jupiter's orbit, but gives limited or partially muddled downstream effects.
criteria.7-8: Explains that small velocity losses alter Jupiter's semimajor axis/period slightly and that complete stopping relative to the Sun would have catastrophic orbital implications.
criteria.9-10: Clearly distinguishes tiny cumulative perturbations from true cancellation of orbital motion and reasons coherently about resulting inward fall/orbital transformation and solar-system-scale consequences.

criteria.name: Uncertainty calibration and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer states assumptions, handles ambiguity in 'how many,' avoids overclaiming precision, and remains internally consistent with conservation laws and the open-ended nature of the problem.
criteria.1-2: Gives a confident exact answer that contradicts its own assumptions or violates conservation of momentum/energy.
criteria.3-4: Shows some awareness of uncertainty, but contains major internal inconsistencies or unsupported precision.
criteria.5-6: Uses cautious language and plausible assumptions, though some estimates or implications are under-specified.
criteria.7-8: Clearly states assumptions about spacecraft type, flyby geometry, and definition of stopping, while avoiding false precision.
criteria.9-10: Maintains tight consistency across all claims, calibrates uncertainty well, and frames the result as an order-of-magnitude impossibility rather than a precise engineering count.
